abstract: A prominent international agenda for land governance reform has a particular focus on making land governance more gender equal, and situating land governance within communities. Research on land governance reform suggest that the process is rife with contestation, specifically involving de facto authority. Rather than assume that de facto authority operates in preexisting, bounded spaces, this article considers how de facto authorities create spaces that challenge reforms for gender equality. Liberia offers a clear example of a place where this international agenda is being pursued. The article explores how two de facto authorities construct spaces that limit gender equality provisions. One of these was used to subvert the expectation that newly formed land governance bodies would resolve disputes in open community meetings, rather than ‘the bush’ (a site women are excluded from). Another is that of ‘community development associations,’ which span geographic space between ‘the community’ and the capital city. Through considering how these de facto authorities constitute the community in space and time, this paper shows the limitations to thinking ‘the community’ as a bounded space for land governance, and rather shows it as made up of several overlapping spaces, some of which uphold gendered exclusions.

title: The impact of pension reforms and rapid aging on savings and labor supply: The case of China
Reintegrating Influencer Media Logic into the Study of Political Influencers
abstract: Political influencers are an emerging epistemic authority in politics. Yet, existing scholarship risks conceptually misspecifying them by focusing on their political nature and neglecting their communicative practices established in broader social media influencer literature. This article advances a theoretical intervention to reintegrate influencer studies into the study of political influencers in political communication. Drawing on the media logic tradition, we discuss “influencer media logic” as communication principles that distinguish political influencers from other political media actors and that underpin their persuasiveness. We discuss three principles of influencer media logic, authenticity, intimacy, and platform expertise, and their contribution to restructuring visibility, credibility, and trust in politics. By foregrounding these communicative practices, we address the limitations of existing conceptualizations and clarify mechanisms of influence beyond the political aspect of their content. We discuss research directions to systematically study political influencers and examine their implications for political communication and democratic engagement.

title: Fines, Not Fares: The Punitive Nature of Transit Enforcement in Canadian Cities
abstract: Despite calls for reform, many transit agencies rely heavily on enforcement to increase fare revenue and perceptions of safety. Both fare evasion and behavior violations (like loitering and public intoxication) can carry heavy fines, and lead to debt collection and criminal justice system involvement. Yet there has been limited examination of the financial and social costs of transit fines, and whether enforcement programs can achieve promised revenue goals. Using administrative data obtained through freedom of information requests, I use an exploratory approach to document the nature and extent of transit enforcement and fines in sixteen Canadian cities. Enforcement varies considerably between cities, ranging from no enforcement to high rates of bans and tickets. I find that transit fines are excessively punitive when compared with parking violations, as transit fines are on average five times higher than comparable parking infractions. While there may be deterrence value from enforcement, few transit fines are paid, and the costs of enforcing transit violations are likely significantly greater than revenue from payments. Given this, transit agencies should evaluate the goals, impacts, and outcomes of enforcement programs, with a full accounting of both the financial and social costs, and consideration of alternative programs.

title: Breaking Out of Low‐Effort Traps: Bureaucratic Leadership by Persuasion
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper tests if bureaucratic leadership impacts the quality of service provision of a difficult‐to‐monitor task: learning in public schools. Using the empirical case of rural India, it exploits an administrative setup with two types of bureaucrats for the same spatial unit, the district, that either have more authority or more ability to engage in time‐intensive persuasion. Utilizing blocked randomization inference and bias‐corrected variance decomposition on bureaucratic postings linked to independent learning data from household surveys across 10 years, it shows that only those bureaucrats with less authority but more ability to engage in persuasion impact learning. Drawing on novel interview data, it illustrates how bureaucratic leaders can increase effort levels of subordinates through persuasion to overcome collective action problems rather than relying on orders and monitoring as principal‐agent frameworks would suggest. The findings illustrate that for difficult‐to‐monitor tasks managerial intensity and persistence trump formal authority.

title: Striking multiple balances in cross-sector collaborations: How leaders navigate institutional complexity with interdependent leadership behaviors
abstract: Abstract In cross-sector collaborations (CSCs), leaders must navigate the complex and often conflicting demands of the public, business, and nonprofit sectors. This study explores how leaders manage this institutional complexity through a multi-level framework, drawing on a case study of a tri-sector partnership developing technology for disaster management. Based on evidence from 27 interviews, observations, and documentary material, we identify the leadership repertoire and, as our core contribution, uncover four distinct types of interdependencies between these behaviors: enabling, substituting, stabilizing, and inhibiting. Our findings reveal that leadership in CSCs goes beyond adopting a single style; rather, it requires a strategic orchestration of how different behaviors interact. We identify two overarching strategies (selective targeting and sequential switching) that leaders use to combine complementary behaviors while preventing them from undermining each other. By focusing on leaders’ micro-level agency in response to macro-level sector differences, this study provides a clearer understanding of how interdependent leadership behaviors converge into what we theorize as institutional leadership in CSCs.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Coordination Capacity and Performance in Fighting Antimicrobial Resistance
The costs of caring: understanding the lived experience of unpaid caregiving and risks to financial wellbeing
abstract: Abstract Unpaid carers face significant financial risks, yet how caring shapes financial wellbeing (FWB) over time has been poorly understood. Drawing on qualitative research with fifty unpaid carers in Britain, purposively sampled across age, life stage, gender, caring intensity and socio-economic status, this paper applies and extends an ecological framework of FWB for the first time in a care context. It makes three contributions. First, it provides original empirical evidence showing that the financial consequences of caregiving are cumulative, uneven and experienced differently across the life course. Second, it develops a life course conceptualisation of carer FWB, highlighting dynamic interactions between individual circumstances, family situations and work, welfare and care systems. Third, it reframes policy debates by demonstrating how care costs are systematically individualised, making structural life stage sensitive interventions essential. Effective policy responses must therefore reflect carers’ differing needs across the life course and address cumulative financial risks. This includes support with saving and affordable housing for young adult carers; clearer pension information and protection from long term care related employment breaks in mid life; and more generous, flexible benefits and trusted care services. Our conceptualisation has international relevance in contexts where reliance on unpaid care is high, and formal support remains limited.

title: A framework for fragility: guiding measurement for policy
The sources of particularistic tax policy: evidence from legislator amendments in Argentina
abstract: The literature on the political economy of tax policymaking argues that particularistic tax policies are generated by the combination of interest group pressures on legislators and legislator incentives to represent the economic interests of their constituencies. This literature has produced scant longitudinal evidence in support of these propositions, due to the difficulties in collecting cross-time data on tax bills and their legislative processes, which has led scholars to focus on case studies or small-N comparisons. This paper overcomes those difficulties by using a database on all executive-sponsored tax bills and all legislator-sponsored bills reported by committees in the Argentine Chamber of Deputies between 1983 and 2011, which includes complete information about all substantive dimensions of tax policy, all amendments proposed and introduced through the lawmaking process, and the final outcomes. In contrast with case study findings, our analysis shows that particularistic tax bills and amendments are introduced and passed by legislators regardless of ideology, macroeconomic contexts, partisan configurations of Congress and the executive, and the existence of majority or plurality legislative cartels. We contribute to the literature on the political economy of tax lawmaking by proposing a methodology for cross-time analysis and generating theoretically consistent large-scale evidence on tax particularism.

title: Understanding ethics advisory bodies in Australia through a policy advisory systems lens
abstract: Outside of bioethics, ethics advice in policy is often poorly defined, yet it plays a crucial role in guiding governments through morally complex policy decisions. This paper draws on PAS typology dimensions as an analytical heuristic to map ethics advisory bodies (EABs) in Australia across several structural and functional dimensions (temporality, government control, expertise, transparency, consensus, and demand–supply) to organize and interpret a largely unmapped domain of expert advice – ethics advice. Using a mixed-methods approach combining documentary analysis and interviews with providers and recipients of ethics advice for governments, the study reveals an ethics advisory landscape driven by definitional ambiguity combined with the absence of a national, institutionalized ethics advisory centre. These factors weaken the visibility and influence of ethics advice in Australia and increase the risk of politicized “shopping” for favourable expertise. The findings highlight the importance of building a better understanding of ethics advice as a form of advisory work that is difficult to capture using formal system categories alone, to support improved policy design and implementation in the future.

title: The accountability–blame avoidance nexus: Experimental evidence from public employees in China
abstract: Research on blame avoidance of public employees primarily focuses on its reactive nature, referring to justifying failures after they happen, while its anticipatory side has received less attention. Using data from 781 Chinese public employees, this study examines how four accountability features, namely, the number of forums, the type of authority, the initiation source, and the evaluative focus, shape their perceptions of anticipatory blame avoidance. Results indicate that political authority and outcome-focused accountability reduce the perceived likelihood of blame avoidance of public employees, whereas the number of forums and the initiation source have little effect. These findings contribute to the governance and policy literature by demonstrating how accountability features shape public employees’ anticipation of blame avoidance before misconduct.

title: Electoral contests over voter beliefs
abstract: Abstract Voter perceptions of candidates are the substrate on which campaigns act. It is costly, however, for voters to devote enough attention to politics to change their own perceptions of candidates. This paper views campaigns—and the time, effort, and money they expend—as subsidizing rationally inattentive voters' adoption of new beliefs about candidate platforms. We employ an all‐pay contest to model costly competition over voter perceptions. In our baseline model, campaigns seek to improve perceptions of their own candidates. In a variant, candidates engage in negative campaigning. Among other results, we observe platform divergence under more reasonable informational assumptions than previous spatial models, replacing candidate uncertainty about voters with voter uncertainty about candidates. This model serves as a bridge between behavioral research on campaigns and theoretical literature on elections, offering a richer set of empirical predictions while preserving the insights of the canonical Downsian framework as a limiting case.

title: Contesting repression in divided democracies: Can counternarratives reduce support for police violence?
abstract: Abstract Democracies often struggle to contain police violence, which undermines the rule of law and reproduces inequality by targeting marginalized citizens. Yet, scholars have shown that repressive policing enjoys considerable public support. Focusing on Brazil, we demonstrate that attitudes toward police violence mirror polarization between left‐ and right‐wing voters, and investigate how competing narratives change attitudes toward police violence through multiple mechanisms. We argue that marginalized victims’ counternarratives can counteract police discourses justifying violence through perspective‐getting, enabling citizens to hear about the experiences of stigmatized groups. Using a nationwide survey experiment, we find that although police narratives increase endorsement of lethal violence, statements from victims’ mothers emphasizing innocence and disadvantage reduce support for police killings—even among right‐wing voters—by increasing empathy and reducing victim‐blaming. We demonstrate that, even in deeply unequal and polarized democracies where exclusionary attitudes align with entrenched ideological divides, counternarratives from marginalized groups can shape public attitudes toward injustices.

title: Property Rights and Social Institutions in Urban Africa: Experimental Evidence From a Land Formalization Program in the DRC
abstract: Formal property rights to land remain rare in sub-Saharan Africa. We argue that social institutions shape citizens’ demand for land formalization. When offered the opportunity to formalize, citizens weigh the insurance and tenure-security benefits of informal institutions against their monetary and social obligations. We study a randomized land titling program in a large Congolese city that sharply reduced the costs of acquiring a title. The program caused large increases in both initiation and receipt of titles. Demand was strongest among citizens more engaged in social institutions and more connected to city chiefs, yet such ties did not predict completion of the titling process. Program assignment also reduced citizens’ participation in social institutions and worsened their evaluations of chiefs. These findings suggest that, in urban settings where land values are higher and social institutions are more costly, citizens may exit social institutions when formal alternatives become available, illustrating how formalization can reshape engagement with informal authority.

title: From instability to hostility: Coalition collapse and affective polarization
abstract: How do sudden coalition breakdowns shape affective polarization in multiparty democracies? While a growing body of work examines how coalition cooperation structure partisan affect, comparatively little is known about how citizens react when coalitions break apart. We argue that coalition collapse is associated with affective polarization. More specifically, we contend that through a dynamic of scapegoating and blame-attribution, this overall difference is concentrated in greater out-party hostility rather than in-party favorability. We test these expectations by exploiting the abrupt collapse of the German “traffic light” coalition in November 2024, using an Unexpected Event during Survey Design comparing respondents interviewed before and after the collapse. We find that the post-collapse period is associated with higher levels of affective polarization, concentrated in greater hostility toward out-parties rather than stronger in-party attachment. Disaggregating to party-dyads reveals that this hostility is targeted, with dislike rising significantly toward the party publicly blamed for the breakdown, and toward anti-establishment parties, while evaluations of other parties remain stable. Subgroup analyses indicate that this targeted hostility is concentrated among supporters of left-wing parties. Coalition collapses, we argue, do not polarize multiparty electorates uniformly but selectively, along ideologically structured lines. The findings contribute to the literature on affective polarization in multiparty systems by highlighting coalition collapse as a distinct, blame-attribution-based mechanism that is associated with targeted rather than diffuse out-party hostility.

title: The online transnationalisation of populist radical right publics
abstract: Abstract International cooperation between radical right populists has escalated over the last decade as parties and leaders worldwide increasingly establish formal and informal connections. Although studies have investigated the role of populist radical right parties (PRRPs) in transnationalisation processes, we know little about the transnationalisation of their online audiences, who are key to amplifying the circulation of PRR narratives across countries. This article therefore addresses the following research question: Which factors explain transnational online engagement with PRR communications? I argue that their digital publics play a role in constructing a transnational network for the PRR, facilitated by online spaces. I hypothesise that engagement varies according to party strategies, platform architectures, and linguistic and geographical factors. To investigate my research question, I analyse YouTube data from 2016 to 2024 of nine PRRPs in eight countries across three continents – the Americas, Europe, and Oceania. Using content and social network analysis, I find transnational engagement is on the rise, that it intensifies around public joint appearances of PRR actors from various countries, and is driven by language and content popularity. These results indicate that transnationalisation is not only catalysed by party elites but is shaped from below and by the architecture of digital platforms amidst a complex interplay of grassroots activity, algorithmic visibility, and party communications.

title: Announcements
From foe to friend? Government–opposition conflict and the appointment of cabinet ministers
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a dynamic theory of ministerial appointments in coalition governments, arguing that party leaders reward members of parliament (MPs) who fulfilled their expected roles in the prior government–opposition conflict. Using all speeches from the German Bundestag of six decades (1961–2021), we estimate MPs’ expressed positions on the government–opposition conflict dimension and assess their effect on cabinet selection. Contrary to the expectation that party leaders prefer moderate ministers to foster cooperation, we find that more loyal MPs—strong government defenders or fierce critics—are more likely to be appointed. These findings highlight how past parliamentary behavior affects future cabinet formation and suggest that ministerial appointments are shaped by partisan loyalty and role fulfillment.

title: Jumping on the Bandwagon or Off the Sinking Ship: Electoral Support and Candidate Supply
abstract: ABSTRACT Local candidates are essential for democratic representation in local elections, yet the number of individuals willing to run for office continues to decline. This study examines the reciprocal relationship between electoral performance and candidate supply, arguing that electoral victories enhance a party's ability to attract candidates through a bandwagon effect, while losses drive both voter and candidate withdrawal. These dynamics are especially pronounced for niche parties which face heightened recruitment challenges when electoral support weakens. Drawing on a novel dataset covering more than 30 years of Swedish local elections, and using OLS, logit, and heterogeneous difference‐in‐differences models, the study demonstrates that electoral gains significantly increase the number of nominated candidates and reduce the probability of fielding no candidates at all, while losses sharply increase the risk of candidate shortages. In turn, parties that fail to nominate candidates experience a significant electoral decline, lasting up to three electoral cycles. These findings underscore the self‐reinforcing nature of candidate shortages and highlight how the inability to field candidates poses risks not only for individual parties but for the quality of local democratic competition.

title: Large Industrial Clusters in the Long Run: Evidence from Million-Rouble Plants in China
abstract: Abstract We study the impact of large, successful manufacturing plants on other local producers in China, focusing on “Million-Rouble Plants” built in the 1950s during a brief alliance with the U.S.S.R. The ephemeral geopolitical situation and the locations of allied and enemy airbases provide exogenous variation in plant siting. We find a boom-and-bust pattern: Counties hosting these plants were 80% more productive than control counties in 1982 but 20% less productive by 2010. This decline reflects the performance of local establishments, which exhibit low productivity, limited innovation, and high markup. Specialization hindered spillovers, preventing the emergence of new clusters and local entrepreneurship.

title: Editorial Board
Fickle fossils: Economic growth, coal, and the European oil invasion, 1900–2015
Political Fact-Checking Efforts are Constrained by Deficiencies in Coverage, Speed, and Reach
abstract: Fact-checking has been promoted as a key method for combating political misinformation. Comparing the spread of election-related misinformation narratives along with their relevant political fact-checks, this study provides the most comprehensive assessment to date of the real-world limitations faced by political fact-checking efforts. To examine barriers to impact, this study extends recent work from laboratory and experimental settings to the wider online information ecosystem present during the 2022 U.S. midterm elections. From analyses conducted within this context, we find that fact-checks as currently developed and distributed are severely inhibited in election contexts by constraints on their i. coverage, ii. speed, and, iii. reach. Specifically, we provide evidence that fewer than half of all prominent election-related misinformation narratives were fact-checked. Within the subset of fact-checked claims, we find that the median fact-check was released a full four days after the initial appearance of a narrative. Using network analysis to estimate user partisanship and dynamics of information spread, we additionally find evidence that fact-checks make up less than 1.2\% of narrative conversations and that even when shared, fact-checks are nearly always shared within,rather than between, partisan communities. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence which runs contrary to the assumption that misinformation moderation is politically biased against the political right. In full, through this assessment of the real-world influence of political fact-checking efforts, our findings underscore how limitations in coverage, speed, and reach necessitate further examination of the potential use of fact-checks as the primary method for combating the spread of political misinformation.

title: Memory in Motion: The Configuration of Korean War Memory in Chinese Popular Representations
abstract: China’s Korean War memory moves in and out of view, but rarely returns unchanged. This article asks how Chinese popular representations of the Korean War vary as the foreign relationships embedded in the war shift. It develops a configurational account of wartime memory, emphasizing activation, selection, and mediation across state priorities, nationalist repertoires, and media institutions. Drawing on a near-comprehensive corpus of theatrically released Chinese Korean War films, alongside close readings of influential print and screen texts, it traces three periods: canonization, latency, and security revival. Chinese sacrifice and victory endure; the United States remains central, but negative portrayals of US soldiers become less common; solidarity with North Korea recedes; Soviet participation remains largely unmentioned; and China’s intervention is increasingly framed as national defense.

title: Does bureaucrat bashing diminish the performance of public servants? Evidence from a survey experiment in The Netherlands
abstract: Bureaucrat bashing—the negative views expressed about public servants—is a widespread phenomenon. Does this bureaucrat bashing diminish the performance of public servants, as theoretically expected? We answer this question with a preregistered, original survey experiment among Dutch public servants. Our main results show that bureaucrat bashing does not significantly lower self-reported overall performance. Additional analyses confirm our main results. We discuss how our findings provide valuable insights into bureaucrat bashing and its possible effects in the public sector.

title: The social media paradox: Political expression and the bifurcation of bureaucratic values
abstract: Bureaucrats’ political activity on social media has received growing attention from various observers who have debated whether such behavior is weakening the bureaucracy’s reputed impartiality, or creating public value by contributing to public discussions. To advance this debate, this article investigates bureaucrats’ political activity on social media with survey data from Canada. Testing hypotheses drawn from four ideal-types depicting different approaches towards social media—imperatively impartial; politically minded, mindfully impartial; megaphone bureaucracy; promiscuously partisan—the empirical results suggest that bureaucrats’ social media activity has led to a paradoxical bifurcation of the bureaucracy into radically different realms of being imperatively impartial and promiscuously partisan. Responding to risk-averse messages from the bureaucracy itself, nonexecutive federal bureaucrats display remarkably low levels of political activity on social media. In contrast, responding to political pressure to promote the government’s messaging, top-ranking federal bureaucrats display high levels of political activity on social media, especially when it comes to partisan content such as reposting official party messages. This social media paradox points to a potentially tragic portrait for the future of governance in the twenty-first century, whereby the integrity of the bureaucracy’s reputed impartiality and the vitality of democratic society, both stand to lose.

title: Bureaucratic interest in academic evidence: a field experiment in Tanzania, India and Peru
abstract: We investigate how different types of messaging by academics impact public servants’ behavioral demand for access to academic evidence by inviting nearly 9,000 national-level government bureaucrats in Tanzania, India and Peru to receive training on an original website that summarizes and graphically depicts findings from hundreds of randomized controlled trials. Implementing well-known interventions from the psychology of choice literature, we sought to test whether “nudges” might work across different national and bureaucratic contexts. We tested randomly assigned messaging characteristics related to messenger identity and social proof. In particular, we randomized whether invitations came from U.S. researchers on location or similar local researchers. We find that bureaucrats were significantly more responsive to U.S. researchers in Peru but not in India or Tanzania. We also randomly assigned information that other bureaucrats in the same ministry had previously expressed interest. Contrary to findings from other populations with similar “social proof” treatments, bureaucrats were less interested when informed that others had already accepted the demonstration. This novel finding is likely due to the institutional context of bureaucracies, where knowledge is more likely to be either a shared resource or a competitive advantage. In this context, others’ access to knowledge disincentivizes individual action rather than communicating a norm. This study offers evidence about some possible approaches and pitfalls to effective dissemination of academic evidence.

title: Using community values and evidence to respond to homelessness together: a case for methodological flexibility
abstract: Background Canada’s homelessness crisis has deepened due to policy failures, structural inequities and systemic neglect. In Ontario, mid-sized cities face growing pressures with housing and homelessness responsibilities downloaded to municipalities and under-resourced community organizations. These intersecting challenges underscore the need for coordinated, community-driven and evidence-informed responses that transcend traditional policy and research silos. Aims and objectives This article examines collaborative efforts to address homelessness within Peterborough, Ontario, and distils a local research-to-action process to inform evidence-led problem-solving in other contexts. It explores how researchers can balance academic and activist frameworks with community values to foster meaningful social change. Methods Aligned with institutional ethnography, the process integrated community-based participatory research, knowledge mobilization and community organizing. Two coordinated research projects culminated in a half-day community forum and a two-day community symposium, co-designed with local people with lived experience, Indigenous organizations, service providers and municipal staff. Structured facilitation supported collective problem identification, priority setting and coordinated planning. Findings The forum mobilized local evidence, allowing participants to identify key policy and practice priorities. The symposium generated community actions and future directions, including a living resource hub, a coordinated advocacy committee and enhanced access to justice supports. Participants reported strengthened collaboration, mutual accountability and solidarity across sectors. Discussion and conclusion Although the process did not directly reduce homelessness, it built local agency and collective capacity for policy advocacy and resource coordination. Grounded in local evidence and shared values, it offers an adaptable model for communities addressing complex social challenges.

title: Review of Economics and Statistics 2026 Annual Report
The magic of secularization
abstract: Abstract Institutional secularization does not necessitate a secular public. In fact, as church memberships decline, more individualized sources of supernatural belief can emerge. Using a nationally representative survey of American adults (n = 1812), we analyze the popularity of “secular rationalism” and how it relates to belief in non-Divine supernatural causation, i.e., magic. Our findings suggest that belief in magic is not simply the inverse of religiosity or secular rationalism. Instead, belief in magic emerges most strongly among those who are both scientifically oriented and residually religious. Secular rationalism does not erase belief in supernatural mechanisms—it affirms the individual’s agency to decide what they are. In short, magic thrives where reason and spirituality meet, suggesting that modernity’s rational turn does not disenchant so much as release faith from institutional restraints.

title: University expansion, academic fields, and the match between the degree and the job
abstract: Abstract Academic knowledge—such as biology, psychology, and economics—is found both in university majors and specific occupations. When educational attainment expands in the population, does it improve or weaken the academic match between university majors and occupations? Using nationally representative data from Great Britain and Canada, we find heterogeneous effects by field of study that are consistent across countries. Increases in the proportion of individuals with university degrees improves matches for economics, mathematics, and fine arts majors, such that they enter occupations that utilize more of their major-specific academic knowledge. The reverse is true for graduates in philosophy and theology, sociology and anthropology, and several majors in the natural and physical sciences. While some high-status fields see stronger matches between major and occupation as education expands, the natural and physical sciences remain a clear exception. These idiosyncratic results suggest that field-level prestige partly explains the heterogeneous effects of educational expansion on major-occupation matching, but that more research is needed on shifts in academic knowledge usage in the labor market.

title: Nudging Across Borders? A Collaborative Governance Framework of European Cross-Border Public Procurement
abstract: While scholars have debated the utility of performance measures in monitoring public procurement, few have explored how policy nudges align political goals with contracting decisions. This article leverages insight from collaborative governance to assess how principal policy intentions may ultimately fail due to contracting authority preferences and suggest how policy nudges can help close the gap between policy objectives and implementation within public procurement decision-making. This research theoretically applies cross-border contracting as a collaborative arrangement between European countries abiding by agency theory tenets and empirically evaluates the degree to which governments engage in cross-border contracting in support of European integration. Analyzing award data reported on Tenders Electronic Daily from 2010 to 2019, findings suggest interorganizational processes, centralization of decision-making, fiscal and political environments, and social partnership dynamics matter in cross-border contracting decision-making. Recommendations for using policy nudges and public-facing performance measures to incentivize contracting authorities to procure cross-border are discussed.

title: Assessing policy priorities for Level 3–4 autonomous driving in Korea: expert consultation and AHP analysis
Jumping the Gun: The Effects of Permitless Concealed Carry Laws on Crime
abstract: ABSTRACT In the last decade, one of the most substantial changes to firearm policy is the widespread adoption of permitless concealed carry laws. Since 2015, more than 20 states have adopted a permitless carry law. Permitless carry laws allow firearm owners to carry a concealed handgun in public without first obtaining a license and undergoing a background check. This article estimates the causal impact of permitless carry laws on crime using stacked event study estimators. I find that violent crime increases by 7% in the 12 months following the law's adoption, with increases beginning shortly after passage, or several months before the law formally takes effect. I find no evidence of offsetting deterrence in property crime. The rise in violence is driven by a 12% increase in aggravated assaults involving firearms. These effects are accompanied by a 22% decline in police enforcement of weapons law violations and modest increases in reports of stolen firearms.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: The Fertility Effects of Reducing Implicit Childcare Subsidies: The Case of School Schedules
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite governments’ efforts to raise fertility through family‐support policies, birth rates continue to decline in high‐ and middle‐income countries. Some policies designed for other purposes, however, may function as implicit childcare subsidies. This article examines the impact of reducing such support on fertility by exploiting a large‐scale reform in Spain that shortened the elementary school day, shifting from full‐day to morning‐only sessions. Using provincial‐level data from 1981 to 2016 and a synthetic difference‐in‐differences identification strategy, I find that the reform reduced the total fertility rate by 0.12 children per woman and delayed maternal age at first birth by approximately 4 months. The delay is significantly larger in provinces with weaker pre‐reform female labor market integration, although fertility declines are similar across labor market contexts. These findings suggest that removing an implicit childcare subsidy increased the cost of childbearing, with fertility timing particularly sensitive to local labor market conditions.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: The democratic ideal under stress: Citizen commitment to democratic rights and procedures in challenging times
abstract: Abstract To what extent do citizens support democratic rights and procedures in the face of major societal challenges? Drawing on a Dahlian ideal of democracy, we exploit the context of the Covid-19 pandemic to address this question with two preregistered survey experiments covering 9,000 respondents in six countries (Germany, Hungary, Japan, Poland, South Korea, and Spain). A conjoint experiment on preferences for pandemic policies reveals that citizens strongly oppose restrictions that interfere with their private lives but are largely indifferent to constraints on core democratic rights (elections, rallies, freedom of the press). A framing experiment assessing citizens’ procedural preferences, elicited using best-worst scaling, shows that expert and business input are consistently ranked higher than parliamentary votes or partisan consensus – regardless of whether Covid-19, climate change, or generic ‘societal challenges’ are at stake. We discuss alternative readings of our results and conclude that commitment to democracy does not appear particularly robust when citizens confront concrete crisis-related trade-offs, with largely similar patterns across countries. While our findings diverge from those of some other experimental studies, they are broadly consistent with accounts that point to rising technocratic preferences, concerns about stealth democracy, and risks of gradual democratic erosion rather than abrupt autocratic shifts.

title: Fair enough? Citizens’ preferences on refugee distribution in the EU
abstract: Abstract How should asylum seekers be distributed across EU member states? And can EU citizens agree on the principles underlying such distribution? While scholars have proposed various fairness principles – such as allocation based on population size, wealth, or past intake – we know little about which principles citizens support. Using an original population survey in six EU member states, this study examines public preferences for distributive fairness in asylum governance. We find widespread dissatisfaction with the status quo of large asymmetries in refugee numbers and broad support for European responsibility sharing based on fair distribution. However, there are significant differences between member states in the principles that citizens support, and these preferences are also affected by the principles that would keep the number of refugees in their own country at a minimum. These findings suggest that while there is a transnational consensus on the need to move to a fairer distribution of refugees in the EU, its practical operationalisation reveals the deeper political divides on the matter.

title: Education and Political Attitudes: The Power and Limits of Field Theory
abstract: A growing body of research suggests that a person’s field of education shapes their political worldview. Yet basic questions remain unanswered. How strongly is the content of education associated with political attitudes relative to income, gender, ethnicity, and, most importantly, level of education? Which political orientations are most closely linked to field, and which are not? Using original and public surveys from the United States and Europe, we show that the human-centeredness of a field is strongly related to liberal positions on a wide range of political attitudes. The association with field is comparable to, and sometimes larger than, the association with level of education. However, the theory we propose has clear scope conditions: field of education is not systematically associated with interest in politics, efficacy, participation, or affective party identification.

title: Encompassing Authority in Election Campaign Mobilization
abstract: Where central state authority is limited, local leaders play a crucial role in political mobilization. But why are some leaders more effective than others? Dominant explanations emphasize leader characteristics, such as social centrality and shared social identity with voters, or individuals’ traits like wealth and gender. We argue that a critical factor has been overlooked: the breadth of leaders’ perceived influence across various domains of individuals’ lives. We introduce and test the concept of encompassing authority – the extent to which individuals perceive a leader as influencing multiple aspects of their lives. Drawing on original survey data from Zambia’s 2021 elections, we examine three types of local mobilizers: religious leaders, chiefs, and local councillors. We show that encompassing authority predicts mobilization in campaigns and community meetings independently of leader and individual characteristics. We identify three mechanisms that explain this effect: belief in the leader’s legitimacy, fear of sanctions for noncompliance, and confidence in the leader’s ability to coordinate collective action. By conceptualizing authority as a dyadic, relational property rather than fixed characteristics of leaders or individuals, our study offers new insights into the underpinnings of political mobilization and opens avenues for future work.

title: Fearing Not Belonging: How Local Attitudes and Policies Shape Refugees’ Destination Preferences
Fiscal capacity and the flypaper effect
Rule of law or rule of ties? Interregional rotation of law enforcement officials and market integration in China
From catastrophe to culture: The role of historical disasters in shaping long-term orientation
Who drives inequality?
abstract: Which countries drive global inequality? Which states drive US inequality? We characterize the class of inequality measures that can answer these questions, permitting both an additive decomposition by subgroup and a multiplicative decomposition into within- and between-group components. Its central measure is simply the expected ratio of incomes between two randomly selected individuals. We show that global inequality fell since 1990, driven by declining disparities between countries. Inequality is primarily driven by large middle-income countries (India, China) and poor countries (Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia). In the US, rising inequality is explained by widening gaps within states, while between-state inequality remains limited.

title: Social networks, language, and material culture on New Guinea
abstract: It is common in both the popular imagination and in scientific research to treat humans as members of distinctive ethnolinguistic groups, populations, or races with different histories. How to best model human diversity has reemerged as a significant issue owing to the prominence of ancient genetic evidence now being used to study the human past. The island of New Guinea, where people speak more than 800 languages or dialects, has served as a test case of competing models of how human biocultural diversity is created and maintained. We present a new test of the degree to which language and material cultural patterning align, using a sample of elaborately decorated bone daggers from museum collections spanning large areas of New Guinea and its surrounds. We compare technological and stylistic variability in these daggers to language as well as a large ethnographically modelled social network. We find that how people socially engage with each other is more predictive of how they make daggers than what language they speak, particularly for daggers dating to the later 19th and early 20th century. While it is often assumed that ancient communities were relatively socially isolated from one another, we argue that there is no reason to assume this default hypothesis about ancient social life. Empirical studies of material culture, and emerging archaeological and genetic understanding of the New Guinean past suggests that language diversity there was developed and maintained within structured social networks linking communities to one another.

title: The Anatomy of Earnings Conference Calls: An Integrative Framework for Management Research
abstract: The use of earnings conference calls in management research has exploded over recent years, yet insights remain fragmented due to differing assumptions about how calls should be analyzed and interpreted. To synthesize this work, we review 207 articles across management, accounting, and finance journals and map how prior studies have drawn on specific call components—structural attributes, prepared remarks, and question-and-answer exchanges. Building on this anatomical mapping, we inductively identify three epistemic roles through which earnings calls have been mobilized in management research: communicative disclosure (“window”), performative communication (“stage”), and communicative trace (“fingerprint”). Each role reflects distinct assumptions about how earnings calls reveal, enact, or encode managerial and organizational phenomena, and each highlights different opportunities for future theorizing. By making these inferential logics explicit, our framework provides a conceptual foundation for more precise and cumulative use of earnings conference calls as a data source in management scholarship and outlines promising areas for future research.

title: Digital Institutions and Occupational Fraud
abstract: How do a country’s digital institutions influence the magnitude of occupational fraud within firms? Leveraging and extending the institution-based view, we address this understudied question by conceptualizing digital institutions as a new genre of institutions that condition the deterrence calculus within firms. We define digital institutions as the foundational structures and resources that shape a country’s digital environment along three key dimensions: (1) digital infrastructure, (2) digital governance, and (3) digital innovation. While strengthening digital institutions has become a priority for policymakers worldwide, the unintended consequences of doing so, such as the potential to facilitate occupational fraud within firms, remain insufficiently understood. Using a unique dataset of 3,974 cases from 41 countries, we find that digital infrastructure is linked to higher fraud magnitude in firms, whereas digital governance is associated with lower occupational fraud magnitude. Our analysis further uncovers the nuanced ways in which digital institutions condition the effectiveness of firm-level internal controls. Overall, policymakers must recognize that digital institutions are a “double-edged sword,” as developing digital infrastructure without reinforcing digital governance can negate efforts to control occupational fraud at the firm level.

title: Aspirational technologies of the (disabled) self: Confessional, self-examinatory, and ascetic masculinities among food delivery riders on China’s digital platforms
abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly offering new employment and social participation opportunities for people with disabilities (PWDs). This study examines the intersections of digital platforms, disability, and masculinity in China. Drawing on in-depth interviews and ethnography with 12 disabled male food delivery riders, it explores how platform-based delivery work serves as a site to negotiate masculinity and social recognition. The findings indicate that platforms not only offer relatively accessible and flexible income opportunities, enabling participants to engage in socially valued work and gendered responsibility, but also mobilize aspirational discourses that promise future inclusion and moral recognition while demanding intensified temporal discipline, bodily endurance, and the willingness to “eat bitterness.” Thus, digital platforms constitute an ambivalent space where inclusion and constraint coexist, enabling gendered self-formation while introducing new forms of discipline. Ultimately, this study calls for greater attention to the challenges faced by PWDs in digital labor.

title: Learning the algorithm: Responsibilization and the limits of agency on YouTube
abstract: Content creators invest extensive effort in “learning the algorithm” to secure visibility and growth. While existing research documents the proliferation of folk theories and optimization strategies, less attention has been paid to the structural conditions under which such learning unfolds. Drawing on a computational analysis of 179 YouTube videos discussing the platform’s algorithm, this article identifies recurring interpretive patterns that frame visibility as optimizable through metrics, strategic adjustment, and disciplined self-management. This paper argues that attempts at algorithmic learning are sustained by an asymmetry between epistemic agency – the capacity to interpret metrics and hypothesize about system behavior, and effective agency – the capacity to reliably influence outcomes. Because large-scale machine-learning systems are probabilistic, multi-objective, and continuously recalibrated, effective control remains systemically indeterminate. This asymmetry produces governance through responsibilization: creators internalize responsibility for unstable outcomes, sustaining engagement because the system appears responsive while remaining structurally uncontrollable.

title: Mapping worker-led AI governance in the global cultural industries
abstract: Between 2022 and early 2026, hundreds of cultural workers’ organizations around the world have mobilized in response to generative AI. From the Hollywood strikes of 2023 to voice actors’ protests in Mexico City, from pan-European game workers’ declarations to the first workers’ appendix to Brazil’s national AI bill, these mobilizations are reshaping how AI is deployed across cultural industries. This article presents a tracker of worker-led AI governance, documenting 142 worker organizations in 34 countries across eight cultural sectors. The tracker’s evidence suggests that collective bargaining is one of eight repertoires documented in the field, and not the most frequent; that most organizations target the state rather than employers or AI companies; that workers’ claims cluster around compensation, consent and copyright, with unauthorized training on creative output as the most cited harm; and that voice acting, the sector with most presence of Majority World, mobilizes a cultural-identity register that tracks the sector’s position in global screen value chains.

title: Bridging Public Services Co-Production: Exploring the Roles of NGOs in Ecological Governance and Rural Revitalization in China
abstract: While co-production theory is deeply rooted in Western democratic norms, its applicability to state-centric regimes with managed participation and constrained civil society remains under-theorized. Addressing this gap, this study examines how an environmental NGO facilitates co-production in China’s Guanba Nature Reserve. Integrating Ostrom’s multi-level ecosystem framework with Social Network Analysis, we reveal that co-production here is not a static arrangement but a dynamic evolutionary process. Acting as a strategic “boundary spanner,” the NGO orchestrates resource flows and translates state imperatives into community-led actions, propelling engagement from an initial material-driven phase, through value evolution, to institutional lock-in. Our findings demonstrate the successful transfer of bridging and linking social capital to indigenous actors, converting passive recipients into active co-producers—a process we term “intermediated participation.” This study advances co-production theory by revealing context-dependent engagement pathways and provides a novel framework for understanding participatory governance beyond Western-centric models.

title: Digital transformations in public welfare services: risks and benefits of digital co-production
abstract: Digital technologies have the potential to transform public services by enabling digital co-production. This paper presents an illustrative case study set in the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Services (Nav) to explore how these transformations can be conceptualized and theorized. The study contributes by building an integrative framework that can be used to guide research and decision-making on digital co-production across diverse public service sectors. The framework explicates the underlying dilemmas, benefits and risks – and, consequently, the value conflicts and trade-offs involved in digital transformations centred on co-production of services.

title: Debate: Defence spending accountability and the SDGs amid geostrategic shifts
abstract: In 2015, all United Nations member states adopted the Sustainable Development Agenda and its 17 goals (SDGs), which are to be reviewed by 2030 (United Nations, 2015). Among these goals, Goal 16 (‘p...

title: Governing generative AI in public administration: Productivity, work redesign and reflective human–AI collaboration
abstract: IMPACTThe authors’ findings will be helpful for public managers, policy-makers and practitioners responsible for digital transformation in public services. The study provides empirical evidence on the conditions under which generative AI can successfully contribute to value for money in public administration, while also showing that productivity gains will be limited unless the technology is integrated into work processes, training systems and governance arrangements. The greatest benefits of generative AI arise in text-based, collaborative and document-intensive activities, such as drafting, standardizing, information retrieval and internal communication. However, tasks involving legal judgment, institutional discretion or complex interpretation continue to require strong human oversight. For public managers, the key implication is that generative AI should not be treated as a plug-and-play efficiency tool. Its public value depends on role redesign, human validation, service-quality monitoring, and the development of professional capabilities that allow public employees to question, contextualize and verify AI-generated outputs.

title: Digital innovation adoption under wartime conditions: Enacting entrepreneurial orientation through proactive intergovernmental bureaucratic mechanisms
abstract: IMPACTThis article will be of value to public managers, digital government practitioners, emergency management professionals, local government executives, chief information officers, and officials responsible for intergovernmental co-ordination. Drawing on evidence from 175 local governments during wartime conditions, the study demonstrates that the success of emergency digital transformation depends not only on the availability of technology but also on proactive bureaucratic engagement. The findings show that direct outreach, hands-on support for implementation, and the active removal of administrative barriers can significantly accelerate digital adoption, particularly among local governments with limited digital capacity. The article highlights practical strategies that central government agencies can use to strengthen local preparedness, improve the uptake of digital tools, and foster collaborative relationships during crises. More broadly, it suggests that proactive intergovernmental support can serve as a mechanism for building trust and enhancing resilience across levels of government. These insights offer actionable lessons for practitioners seeking to improve emergency response capabilities and implement digital innovation under conditions of uncertainty.

title: Defence spending in the war economy: a comparative fiscal and governance analysis
Improving Governance to Reduce Administrative Burden and Increase Funding for School-Based Health Services
abstract: Public schools are critical sites to address children’s emergent health needs, yet they face ongoing challenges to finance and sustain health initiatives. Medicaid is an important funding source for school-based health services, accounting for over $8 billion in revenue for school-based health services in 2024 (Furtado et al., Citation2026), but it is underutilized. Drawing on interviews with state Medicaid and local educational agency personnel, this study illuminates administrative burdens in school Medicaid billing and the collaborative governance arrangements developed among states, localities, and third-party organizations to ease burdens. We find that cooperation between educational service agencies and school districts increased billing capacity and shifted administrative burdens up to higher-level educational units better equipped to manage them. Adopting collaborative governance models that leverage the comparative strengths and scaling capacities of public and private organizations may lessen administrative burdens and increase school Medicaid billing, although low Medicaid reimbursement remains a significant disincentive.

title: Emergent Coordination in Public Sector HRM: COVID-19 and the Reconfiguration of Accountability, Predictability, and Common Understanding
abstract: Coordination is a critical yet challenging aspect of organizational functioning, particularly in public sector organizations characterized by formalized structures and siloed operations. These challenges are exacerbated during crises, which often disrupt established practices and require adaptive responses. Despite the significant role HR managers are assumed to play in navigating such disruptions, limited research has explored how their coordination practices evolve in times of crisis. This in-depth qualitative study draws on interviews with senior HR managers across Swedish public sector municipalities during the COVID-19 pandemic to address this gap. According to HR managers’ accounts, the pandemic disrupted traditional coordination arrangements by challenging the three integrating conditions of coordination: accountability, predictability, and common understanding. Prior to the pandemic, coordination was described as relying heavily on formal, predefined mechanisms tied to specialization and hierarchical structures. During the pandemic, however, HR managers experienced a shift toward more emergent and relational forms of coordination characterized by cross-boundary collaboration and adaptive, real-time problem-solving. The study contributes to the literature by demonstrating how crises can reconfigure coordination practices within public sector organizations and by highlighting the importance of flexibility and emergent coordination even in traditionally bureaucratic contexts. Furthermore, the findings advance our understanding of HR managers as boundary-spanning coordinators who facilitate organizational adaptability and integration during disruptive events.

title: Virtues of Regulatory Criminology
abstract: ABSTRACT This special issue demonstrates that regulatory studies and criminology both have virtue. Regulatory criminology has neglected virtues that exceed the sum of its parts. The editors did a splendid job of pointing out in their introduction that criminology created a number of theoretical traditions that have had moments of passing value and relevance to regulatory studies. In both fields, and at their intersections, one of these traditions, an economism of rational choice, even enjoyed periods of domination. At times, this narrowed scholarly imagination has won Nobel Prizes in economics. Today economists are less present at criminology, law and society, and regulation and governance conferences. Economists must be attracted back so that intellectual renewal on offer from regulatory studies and criminology might broaden their imaginations, and they ours. Regulation and governance can benefit greatly from noting how criminologists integrate insights from micro and macro levels by fine‐grained studies of the modus operandi of lawbreakers that are connected to a historical imagination for the longue durée and a sociological imagination of macrostructures.

title: Power and Participation: Assessing Collaborative Governance of Organic Standards in Canada
abstract: ABSTRACT Against a backdrop of increasing political, economic, and ecological volatility, participatory governance could provide a valuable mechanism to counteract democratic backsliding caused by unchecked power and regulatory capture. Food systems in particular are a site where many interests and sectors converge—including health, agriculture, land use, labor, environment, and climate change—and where there has been increasing interest and experimentation in forms of participatory governance. This research uses the example of the organic standards governance process to understand how governance structures can enable transitions to more sustainable and just systems (including but not limited to food systems), and what we can learn from existing participatory governance approaches about how to govern complex systems in a collaborative and inclusive way. We conducted 20 semi‐structured interviews with individuals who have participated in recent organic standards review processes and analyzed key documents to characterize the sources and arenas of power at play. We found that formal authority and discursive legitimacy are enabling some participants to maintain influence at a time when increasing professionalization and resource‐based power would otherwise dominate the process. In particular, the processes in place to ensure opportunities for public comment, diverse sector representation, and limited political influence all contribute to a collaborative, participatory process. At the same time, the organic sector is facing significant challenges due to the high costs of administering such a labor‐intensive process, a lack of consistent funding, and the imminent closure of the Canadian General Standards Board as an institutional structure to support the organic standards review process. Despite these challenges, the governance of the Canadian organic standards has been a robust and unique instance of participatory governance that merits continued support.

title: Reinterpreting intra-household bargaining over childcare through a capability-informed lens: a study of Taiwanese couples
abstract: Despite the expansion of family policies in East Asia, gendered patterns of childcare remain persistent. Incorporating the capability approach into the intra-household bargaining model, this study reinterprets observed patterns of parental leave-taking among Taiwanese couples. Using dyadic data from the Kids in Taiwan Survey and estimating a bivariate probit model, the analysis explores how relative resources and conversion factors are associated with these outcomes. The findings indicate that mothers’ relative advantages in working time are associated with a higher likelihood of departing from default maternal caregiving, whereas fathers’ advantages in occupational status are associated with lower predicted probabilities of taking leave, which may be consistent with the constrained scope of paternal participation. Among highly educated couples, mothers’ perception of access to high-quality, subsidized babysitting services is associated with greater room for manoeuvre on childcare arrangements. Taken together, these associations have important implications, through a capability-informed lens, for policies promoting gender equality in childcare: policymakers may need to move beyond expanding leave entitlements to trying to improve the bargaining conditions under which families negotiate childcare arrangements.

title: How is platform subordination being reconfigured? Algorithmic dependency among overnight delivery workers in the South Korean welfare state
abstract: Platform work creates a fundamental paradox. Algorithmic management intensifies control, yet workers’ subordination is increasingly invisible to legal and social security systems. This study operationalizes algorithmic dependency and asks how the subordination of platform delivery labour is being reconfigured. We examine whether organizational, economic, and algorithmic dependency are empirically distinct, how they interrelate, and what their configuration implies for employment-based social protection. We draw on the Korean Working Conditions Survey (KWCS, 2017–2023) and an original survey of 942 overnight delivery platform workers performing last-mile e-commerce delivery under heterogeneous employment statuses. The KWCS shows dependent self-employment is structurally embedded in Korea’s labour market, with delivery workers exhibiting exceptionally high dependency (74.1%). Exploratory factor analysis indicates algorithmic and economic dependency load onto a single latent dimension, while organizational dependency remains distinct. We interpret this convergence as algorithmised economic dependency, a hybrid form in which algorithmic control and economic reliance jointly intensify and obscure subordination while evading employment-based protections. Inherited concepts of subordination, built around visible and direct command, cannot fully capture this reconfigured dependency. Because income security in welfare states like Korea presupposes employment relationships defined by traditional subordination, recognizing it is a precondition for extending social protection to platform workers.

title: The Basic Income for Care Leavers in Wales pilot: perceptions of deservingness amongst recipients and professionals
abstract: Abstract This paper explores recipients’ and professionals’ attitudes towards the Basic Income for Care Leavers in Wales pilot. Qualitative interviews were conducted with forty-one professionals and forty-four basic income recipients in the first year of the scheme (2022/2023). The findings are situated within Van Oorshot’s CARIN framework that aids analysis of attitudes towards the ‘deservingness’ of others. The findings indicate that there was an almost unified agreement among these participants that care leavers deserve additional support but much less agreement on whether the basic income pilot is the right way to provide this support. The findings are situated in a context where strong views have been expressed by a small number of politicians and media outlets who question the deservingness more overtly, especially when considering former unaccompanied child asylum seekers. Meanwhile, the Welsh Government, which implemented the pilot, emphasises the state’s obligations to this population and the opportunities that a basic income might facilitate. Implications of the findings relate to how future basic income schemes are justified to the public, recipients and those administering the scheme at a local level.

title: Beyond pilots and policy labs: institutionalizing experimentation through transformative partnerships
abstract: This paper conceptualizes the upscaling challenge in Transformative Innovation Policy (TIP) as a distinct governance problem. While experimentation is central to TIP, much of the literature focuses on pilots, policy labs, and bounded policy trials, paying less attention to how experimentation can be institutionalized once the objective is system-level change. We argue that pilots remain useful for testing narrowly specified interventions. However, they offer an incomplete institutional solution for transformative programmes that support socio-technical and territorial change. Scaling changes actor behavior, accountability demands, coordination requirements, and the political basis of legitimacy; it also unfolds over timeframes in which technologies, markets, and initial assumptions may change substantially. However, allowing experimentation to continue while scaling up raises the issue of governance, namely, how TIP can be governed in a way to balance these tensions and allow experimentation to continue without impeding the scaling-up process or vice versa. To address this gap, we develop a framework that contrasts agency-led, ecosystem-led, and hybrid governance solutions and investigate the extent to which these solutions support (or not) this dual objective of continued experimentation while scaling up. These solutions are being discussed across different institutional contexts using four European cases: Slovenia’s Smart Specialization strategic partnerships, Sweden’s VINNVÄXT, the Dutch Innovation Performance Contracts, and Denmark’s Innovation Networks. Across institutionally different settings, these cases reveal common governance mechanisms: brokerage, diagnostic monitoring, tailored support, and mutually reinforcing top-down and bottom-up coordination. On this basis, we introduce transformative partnerships as an institutional form that embeds experimentation in governance rather than treating it as an isolated pilot. The paper contributes by specifying scaling as a governance issue in TIP and by identifying institutional design features that enable experimentation to become cumulative, adaptive, and durable.

title: Temporary technology and the maintenance of technological sovereignty
Why and How Do Street‐Level Managers Mobilise Informal Resources as a Routine Managerial Tool?
abstract: ABSTRACT Street‐level implementation work routinely involves navigating resource scarcity while still meeting policy demands. Recent literature suggests that frontline workers cope with these challenges through informal practices, including the use of personal resources. This study expands contemporary knowledge by examining the role of street‐level managers and the impact of organizational resources. Using a mixed‐methods design, we examine why and how primary school principals in two Brazilian municipalities with different education budgets utilise personal resources. The quantitative survey of 92 principals shows that these informal practices are routine. Principals fundraise, solicit donations from families and communities, mobilise contributions from teachers, and donate their own money and unpaid time. The qualitative phase, consisting of 26 in‐depth interviews, demonstrates that rather than mere resource scarcity, principals mobilise personal and informal resources and engage in legitimising the use of informal resources from others as a managerial tool for addressing imperatives associated with multiple public sector reforms. The study contributes by demonstrating that the mobilisation of informal resources has become institutionalised as part of street‐level managerial work regardless of the level of formal resources available, as it allows managers to respond to local needs and implementation challenges that cannot be adequately addressed through formal resources alone.

title: Protecting at Home or Providing Abroad: Refugee Policy in Civil Conflicts
abstract: Abstract When civilians flee conflict, concerned donors adopt policies intended to curb both violence and large refugee flows, viewing these objectives as complementary. Can such policies reduce the flow of refugees while safeguarding civilians? Using a model of refugee flight in civil conflict, I find donors who link aid and migration policies may fail to restrain government violence, risking increases in displacement and repression. Specifically, when donors lack leverage or have inconsistent priorities, their goals are undermined by strategic government violence. Policies aimed at reducing migration, like increasing humanitarian aid or reducing access to asylum, can yield more intense fighting because they leave a larger base of support for rebels. Threats to suspend aid similarly do not deter violence when it is clear donors’ primary concern is migration. I find if donors condition assistance on reducing both migration and violence against civilians, but prioritize curbing repression, they can achieve both goals.

title: Matterialising grassroots hydrosocial territories: Visualising and politically reframing what matters in the upper Yanuncay River, Ecuador
abstract: The Yanuncay River Basin, in Azuay Province, Southern Ecuador, is facing mounting pressures from extractive industries, particularly large-scale mining and hydropower projects, that seek to grab and control the river and related territories. This article presents the counter-mapping methodology that was used with impacted communities residing along the river's headwaters and páramos. It presents and discusses how through an engaged participatory discussion, negotiation and resulting visualisation process, a grassroots map of their territory was co-created. This map reflects the communities' ecological knowledge, their experienced emotional and lived relations as well as their socio-economic dependence on their territory. The map is now being used and discussed by these communities and their broader river defence networks to support their efforts to protect the river. Based on our analysis we argue that counter-mapping is not merely a technical practice of visualisation but a political process of resistance that allows communities to articulate, express and reframe what in their territory matters to them (‘ matterialise ’). This matterialisation enables them to visually represent and discursively manifest their spatial-political and onto-epistemological territorial visions and interests. These challenge prevailing development models that threaten their river and related livelihoods in name of socio-economic progress.

title: Benchmarking in public updating of economic perceptions
abstract: Abstract How do people respond to new information about social conditions? For example, does an improvement always lead people to say things are “better”? We argue that people update their views differently depending on whether preexisting perceptions are positive or negative, meaning equivalent changes in conditions can elicit different public reactions. To test this possibility, we update a classic model of aggregate public responsiveness to economic conditions by including recent public perceptions as a moderator variable. This reveals a substantial source of heterogeneity: changes in the economy matter either a great deal for public perceptions or not at all, depending on the prior levels of those perceptions. The results imply that updates of public perceptions are benchmarked to the recent past.

title: Atmospheres and Activism: Rethinking Solidarity Politics
abstract: Abstract How and why does left solidarity fail women of color? Given the rising tide of far right extremism, this is an urgent question for social movement actors who wish to build sustainable coalitions for progressive politics. In this paper, we examine the dynamics of solidarity via a novel approach to the study of “atmospheres.” While scholars of emotions have identified the importance of atmospheres in social and political life, they are unable to answer their own important question: What do atmospheres make possible politically? We bring together the concept of racialized solidarity with the sensuous inequalities of activist spaces. We identify visual, sonic, somatic, and emotional inequalities that work together to produce what we name as the racialized atmospherics of activist spaces, in which the mood is systematically mobilized against women of color.

title: Do social movements influence decision makers? Evidence from U.S. immigration courts
Does a Food Waste Tax Work? Evidence from Quasi-Experiments in South Korea
abstract: Abstract Globally, one-third of food is discarded, generating lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions comparable to those from road transport. Further, waste management is among the largest municipal budget items worldwide. Exploiting plausibly exogenous unit-based food waste tax expansions in South Korea, I find that the tax substantially reduces food waste by discouraging excessive grocery purchases. Households sustain food intake despite buying less, but at the cost of additional time spent on meal production. Nonpecuniary motivations appear central to the policy’s e!ectiveness, and the tax is likely welfare-improving because more e"cient food use not only reduces externalities but also offsets time costs.

title: Do Health Insurers Matter for Health Outcomes? Evidence from a Large Natural Experiment in Colombia
abstract: Abstract While the relationship between health insurance coverage and health outcomes has been extensively studied, there is limited evidence on which specific features of insurance matter. We address this gap by leveraging the abrupt termination of Colombia’s largest health insurer and examining the spillover effects on patients who were not enrolled with the terminated insurer. The termination caused a 10% decrease in the breadth of provider networks among incumbent insurers and a 20% increase in mortality rates. We show two mechanisms drove the change in mortality: increased congestion stemming from the surge of enrollees at incumbent insurers and reduced provider network breadth. Insurers narrowed their networks by excluding higher-quality providers that served sicker, more expensive patients, whoin turn died at much higher rates than their counterparts. Findings suggest insurers play a key role in patient health through their provider networks.

title: Synthetic Controls for Experimental Design
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how to design experiments when the experimental units are large aggregate entities (e.g., markets), and only one or a small number of units can be treated. We propose a class of non-randomized experimental designs using the synthetic control method, which jointly selects treated units and untreated units to serve as a comparison group. We analyze the properties of estimators under these synthetic control designs and develop new inferential techniques. We show that, in experiments with aggregate units, synthetic control designs can substantially reduce estimation bias relative to randomized experiments.
