title: Was Javert Right to Be Suspicious? Marginal Treatment Effects with Duration Outcomes
abstract: Abstract We identify the distributional and quantile marginal treatment effect functions when the outcome is right-censored. Our method requires a conditionally exogenous instrument and random censoring. We propose asymptotically consistent semi-parametric estimators and valid inferential procedures for the target functions . To illustrate, we evaluate the effect of alternative sentences (fines and community service vs. no punishment) on recidivism in Brazil. Our results highlight substantial treatment effect heterogeneity: we find that people whom most judges would punish take longer to recidivate, while people who would be punished only by strict judges recidivate at an earlier date than if they were not punished.

title: The Bronx Is Burning: Urban Disinvestment Effects of Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plans
abstract: Abstract We study the unintended effects of Fair Access to Insurance Requirements (FAIR) plans developed by 26 states in the 1960s to address insurance redlining in urban neighborhoods. FAIR plans’ problematic features included prohibitions on considering environmental hazards in underwriting, mandatory insurer participation in pools that diluted underwriting incentives, and payouts exceeding market values in declining areas. Using a triple-difference design comparing pre/post-FAIR periods, neighborhoods with/without likely FAIR access, and participating/non-participating states, we find that FAIR inadvertently led to significant housing disinvestment and accelerated declines in neighborhood population, with simultaneous increases in the Black population share.

title: The Factor Bias of External Inputs: Implications for Substitution between Capital and Labor
Outside Income as a Signal: Evidence from Politicians and Voters
abstract: Abstract We study how public disclosure of politicians’ outside income affects their behavior. We exploit a disclosure reform targeting German federal MPs and tax-return data in a difference-indifferences setup using unaffected state MPs as controls. MPs increase their outside income by 24%, driven by likely right-leaning MPs. A representative survey experiment uncovers that right-leaning voters interpret outside income as a signal of competence and hard work, while left-leaning voters associate it with weaker representation. Consistent with this, we show that newspapers cover right-leaning MPs’ outside activities more favorably. Our findings suggest that politicians strategically use public disclosure as a signaling tool.

title: Fiscal Policy in Small Open Economies: The International Intertemporal Keynesian Cross
abstract: Abstract A recent literature studies fiscal policy with realistic intertemporal marginal propensities to consume and the absence of Ricardian equivalence. This literature shows that fiscal policy boosts consumption and is effective: (i) Cumulative fiscal multipliers are above one, and (ii) fiscal policy is fully self-financing. I show this does not extend to small open economies by providing conditions where (i) the cumulative fiscal multiplier is exactly one, and (ii) fiscal deficits are not fully self-financing. This is because the initial debt-fueled rise in consumption is offset by a drop to repay foreign debt. Finally, I provide conditions to overturn this result.

title: Firm Concentration and Job Design: The Case of Schedule Flexible Work Arrangements
abstract: Abstract We study how employer concentration affects job design, focusing on schedule flexibility as a non-wage job attribute. Using the full text of 46 million UK job vacancies from 2014–2019, we construct new measures of flexible work arrangements using supervised machine learning and large-language-model—assisted annotations. Adopting an instrumental variable strategy using a Bartik-style prediction of the change in employer concentration based on nationwide hiring trends, we show that higher concentration reduces the value of worker compensation partly through shifts toward “risky” flexibility that exposes workers to earnings volatility.

title: The Effects of Social Movements: Evidence from #MeToo
Excessive Pharmaceutical Marketing Expenditure: Policy Remedies from China
abstract: Abstract Developing countries face high pharmaceutical prices despite the presence of multiple generic producers. One key reason is excessive spending on sales and marketing by drug firms. This paper examines how centralized drug procurement can curb such marketing efforts and reduce prices, using a policy experiment in China where certain generics are procured through centralized auctions in pilot cities. Winning firms gain large market shares directly without high marketing costs. We find that the centralized auction significantly reduces both sales costs and prices, with winning firms experiencing notable decreases in marketing-related labor demand.

title: Property Rights and Market Frictions: Evidence from the Universe of Land Dispute Files in China
Determining Gender Differences in Education and Labor Market Outcomes
abstract: Abstract This paper studies gender differences in educational attainment and labor market outcomes. Across 21 OECD countries, though men are paid more than women, the college attainment rates and college premia are (mostly) higher for women. This paper explains these patterns through the quantitative analysis of a dynamic choice model of education and labor market outcomes. Using the estimated model, we decompose the observed gender gaps through a series of counterfactual exercises. One finding is that these gaps are driven mainly by gender differences in the average compensation at non-college jobs. The estimated lower compensation for non-college women generates for them larger college premia and higher incentives to attend college relative to men. A second finding, through the lens of the estimated model, is that observed gender wage gaps for college workers are largely driven by differences in the gender specific distributions across signals of ability rather than wage differences across genders given a signal.

title: Fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity
abstract: Abstract Different conceptions of inequality of opportunity have been developed in political philosophy. We focus on two competing conceptions: fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity. We develop an empirical framework to measure and compare these conceptions. Both fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity consider it unjust if ascribed characteristics such as social origin, gender, race, and ethnicity affect life outcomes. However, they differ in what they regard as just: fair inequality of opportunity considers it just if abilities and individual choices affect life outcomes, while luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity considers it just only if individual choices affect life outcomes. We measure fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity in education, occupation, income, and wealth using survey data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY). Our results show that conclusions about inequality of opportunity depend on the conception of inequality of opportunity employed. From the perspective of fair inequality of opportunity, the United States is a rather just society, while the nation’s degree of luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity is high. The difference between fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity is largest for education, followed by occupation, and finally income and wealth. There is no evidence that changes across cohorts differed between fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity.

title: Studying Propaganda as a Social Process
abstract: In recent scholarship on propaganda, no aspect has attracted more attention than the digitally mediated propagation of disinformation. In this intervention, we argue that focusing narrowly on disinformation risks missing the forest for all the trees: Only by considering disinformation’s embedding within broader propaganda strategies and processes, we can understand falsehoods’ distinctive rhetorical functions alongside other forms of (normative, motivational, etc.) propaganda messaging, comprehend their persuasive appeal, and theorize their capacity to gain discursive power within contemporary high-choice information environments. Advancing an approach that foregrounds propaganda’s inherent anti-democratic ambition over its manipulative means, we sketch a research agenda suitable to studying propaganda as a social process.

title: Affective Publics in the YouTube Live Chat: Multimodal Emotional Contagion During the 2024 U.S. Presidential Debate
abstract: Televised debates between political candidates have become dynamic, interactive events on live-streaming platforms where audiences form affective publics through real-time interactions and emotional expressions in live chat. In this study, we focused on real-time emotional contagion on a right-wing YouTube channel during the live-streamed 2024 U.S. presidential debate between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris. Examining how multimodal emotional expressions from candidates influence audience responses in live chats (N = 53,095), this study introduces a novel, multi-dimensional approach combining computational techniques, including face emotion recognition, speech emotion analysis, text emotion classification, and time series analysis, to analyze multimodal emotional cues across audio, video, and chat data. Results revealed that Harris’ vocal fear Granger-caused an increase in joy in the live chat, and that emotional contagion patterns varied by user engagement level and political leaning: low-engagement users were primarily influenced by the candidates, whereas higher-engagement users were more influenced by peer emotions. Pro-Trump audiences’ joy was amplified by Harris’s vocal sadness; among pro-Harris audiences, anger increased in response to Harris’s vocal sadness and the moderators’ facial sadness, while joy increased in response to Trump’s facial sadness. Negative public emotions including sadness and anger also reinforced joy in the live chat. These findings offer new insights into the role of emotional contagion in mobilizing online affective publics during live-streamed political events.

title: Pro-citizen rule-breaking among traffic police: the role of rule formalization and peer dynamics
abstract: Street-level bureaucrats (SLBs) often face a dilemma between complying with formal rules and helping citizens, especially in enforcement contexts. While prior research on public services has focused on prosocial rule-breaking (PSRB), this study conceptualizes pro-citizen rule-breaking (PCRB) as SLBs’ intentional violation of rules to benefit citizens within enforcement contexts where rule-breaking carries professional and institutional risks. Factors influencing PCRB were examined using a vignette-based survey experiment with 733 Chinese traffic police officers, who operate under a dual leadership system shaped by both formal bureaucratic rules and local responsiveness. The results reveal three main findings. First, formalized written rules significantly suppress PCRB compared to informal verbal directives. Second, PCRB cues from peers strongly increase officers’ willingness to break rules in order to help citizens. Third, these peer influences moderate the effect of rule formalization on PCRB, weakening its inhibitory influence. Robustness checks using alternative measures confirm these results. By introducing PCRB into the study of enforcement contexts, this study highlights factors shaping street-level bureaucrats’ decision-making.

title: Using generative AI to evaluate the leadership of emperors and presidents: psychometric validation and implications for public leadership research
How far can participatory governance models travel? Evidence from Jordan’s decentralization reforms
abstract: This article empirically critiques the mobility of participatory governance models when transferred to hybrid institutional contexts. In so doing, it critically examines Jordan’s 2017 decentralization reforms through elite interviews with 14 senior policymakers to unpack the structural conditions that impede reform. Through a blame avoidance lens, the study identifies three competing narratives on the reforms’ shortcomings, which are subsequently analyzed using the Institutional Analysis and Development framework to highlight the institutional incompatibilities that shaped reform outcomes. Despite its aims to strengthen local democracy through networked governance, the reforms produced a dysfunctional model that amplified centralization and patronage in Jordanian public administration. The study problematizes assumptions that Western governance frameworks can inherently enhance public sector performance, highlighting that successful policy transfer of participatory models in hybrid settings like Jordan is contingent on contextualization and co-design of transferred reform programs in order to synthesize external solutions with local institutional configurations.

title: Disentangling the notion of value in public services: evidence and future directions from a systematic literature review
abstract: “Value” is a popular yet contested construct in Public Administration and Management (PAM) research, and has gained increasing attention in relation to the value creation process in public services. Despite the close connection between value and public services, the field lacks a clear understanding of what value is actually about and, consequently, what is created within services. We contribute to this debate through a systematic literature review of 140 records across disciplines to detect how value is defined in the field of public services and the main features of the value creation process, with a specific focus on its beneficiaries, mechanisms, levels and stages, providing an unprecedented conceptual mapping of the intersection between the concept of value and public services. We conclude by outlining several research avenues to further advance the field, calling for a shift from a theory of value creation in public services to a theory of public value creation in services.

title: Beyond the hassle: how favorable outcomes reduce the subjective experience of administrative burden
abstract: A large body of research shows that compliance demands—administrative hassles and rules—impose learning, compliance, and psychological costs on individuals. Because costs are conceptualized as subjective, most studies rely on self-reported measures. This article examines that approach by asking: To what extent do factors beyond compliance demands shape the subjective experience of administrative burdens? We argue that one factor, distinct from compliance demands, is the favorability of outcomes allocated by public organizations. We integrate outcome favorability into the administrative burden framework, proposing that (1) favorable outcomes reduce administrative burdens, as subjectively experienced and (2) favorable outcomes moderate the effect of compliance demands on the experience of administrative burdens. We test these expectations in two studies: an analysis of real-world interactions from the German Life Events Survey (n ≈ 4,000) and a Danish survey experiment with randomized demands and outcomes (n = 1,624). Both studies show that favorable outcomes reduce administrative burdens, as subjectively experienced, raising questions about how much self-reported learning, compliance, and psychological costs reflect reactions to administrative requirements rather than other aspects of citizen-state interactions.

title: What drives perceived job crafting in the public sector? Evidence from a randomized COM-B-informed intervention study
abstract: Drawing on the Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation–Behavior (COM-B) framework, this study examines the impact of an intervention designed to help public employees develop the capability, motivation, and opportunity to reshape their work through job crafting strategies within highly rule-bound organizational contexts. Using a randomized longitudinal study from Italy, the findings show that a COM-B-informed job crafting intervention significantly enhanced social job resources and reduced hindering job demands. Although improvements in structural job resources and challenging job demands are more limited, the intervention promoted adaptive forms of job redesign that fit the constraints and dynamics of bureaucratic environments. Additionally, Public Service Motivation (PSM) helps sustain self-reported job crafting behaviors, and empowering leadership creates conditions that enable them. Overall, the study highlights the need for tailored job crafting interventions aligned with the structural and motivational dynamics of the public sector, fostering a more engaged and adaptable workforce. Moreover, the findings offer practical insights for public organizations seeking to enhance employee effectiveness and job satisfaction through structured job crafting initiatives.

title: Chainsaw or scalpel: which leads to more blame for a service failure when leaders downsize government?
abstract: The Trump administration’s DOGE attempted to radically downsize U.S. federal agencies. This study aims to clarify whether government leaders are blamed more for service failure when they employ either a DOGE-like (chainsaw) method or a more measured (scalpel) approach. A preregistered experiment was conducted in which respondents were randomly assigned to one of 6 vignettes that presented information about downsizing approaches, a public service failure, and the person or entity directly responsible for the failure. This study produced four main findings. First, people blamed city leaders more for the service failure when they knew a chainsaw approach was used to downsize government, compared to when they were given no information about the approach. Second, people blamed city leaders more when a chainsaw approach was used than when a scalpel approach was used. Third, simply knowing that city leaders had used a downsizing approach was not enough to shift blame away from the frontline employee toward city leaders. Fourth, blame shifted from the frontline employee to city leaders when people learned that a chainsaw approach—rather than a scalpel approach—had been used. The implications for research and practice are that a chainsaw approach is undesirable.

title: Prior beliefs and the biased interpretation of performance information: the mediating role of attention
Public service delivery under stress: The governance of funeral value-chain services during a pandemic
abstract: This study examines how city-level interorganizational networks managing the funeral value chain in Barcelona, Madrid, Paris, and New York maintained service continuity during the first wave of COVID-19. Using 38 semi-structured interviews and a comparative case design, we analyze process mechanisms—viewed as drivers (facilitators) and obstacles (impediments)—and evaluate how their function varied across governance modes (shared, lead-organization, hybrid). Results show that different governance models rely on distinct mechanisms to ensure service continuity. Shared governance benefits from trust, existing relationships, and active network management, while lead-organization modes depend more on clear authority lines and open communication channels. Hybrid arrangements perform well when preexisting plans are combined with listening arenas that preserve participant voice. These insights deepen our understanding of collaborative processes in high-pressure, service-critical settings.

title: How public managers view Sustainable Development Goals: a Q-study
Recruiting Street‐Level Bureaucrats Through Co‐Design: The Effects of Incorporating Citizen Insights Into Job Advertisements
abstract: ABSTRACT Street‐level bureaucrats (SLBs) directly affect citizens, making them central to public service delivery. Service success therefore hinges on public sector organizations' ability to recruit competent SLBs. We argue that citizens' perspectives should inform SLB recruitment, especially for contact‐intensive, relational frontline roles. Yet public administration research has not integrated citizens' perspectives into SLB recruitment, despite a broader shift toward a service‐user orientation. We test whether job advertisements co‐designed with citizens increase job seekers' application likelihood. Using a mixed‐method design, including a preregistered experiment, we find that co‐designed job advertisements (a) identify SLB competencies often overlooked in conventional recruitment (Study 1), (b) increase application likelihood regardless of applicants' awareness of citizen involvement (Study 2A), and (c) attract candidates whose values align with service‐user‐oriented organizations by improving person‐job fit (Study 2B). We advance public sector recruitment and SLB research by introducing co‐design as an innovative and effective approach to service‐user‐oriented SLB recruitment.

title: Tensions Between Client Satisfaction and Employee Motivation in Public Organizations, and Their Reconciliation Through Leadership
abstract: Public organizations widely use client satisfaction feedback to assess their employees, reflecting responsiveness and accountability to policy clients. Yet client satisfaction is inherently subjective and heterogeneous, and it often diverges from mission-relevant performance in ways that can compromise employees’ work motivation. This study conceptualizes this issue as a bottom-up democracy–bureaucracy dilemma and examines the role of leadership in mitigating it. Drawing on experimental evidence (n = 740) and open-ended qualitative responses (13,502 words) from frontline investigators in South Korea's National Police Agency, the study finds that low client (i.e., alleged victims) satisfaction despite high investigatory performance impairs officers’ work motivation. Notably, these demotivating effects are attenuated when the agency head explicitly acknowledges the weak link between performance and satisfaction and avoid treating low satisfaction as direct evidence of poor performance, even as client satisfaction remains a formal evaluative benchmark. This sensegiving approach appears to foster perceptions of interactional fairness, empathy, and understanding, thereby significantly improving officers’ experience ofsatisfaction feedback and their trust in the agency head. A broader implication of this study is that reconciling democratic impulses for policy clients and political stakeholders with administrative imperatives to empower the workforce is a unique challenge for public sector leadership.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Policy design for research and innovation: politics, institutions and interest intermediation practices
abstract: Claudia Acciai’s Policy Design for Research and Innovation: Politics, Institutions and Interest Intermediation Practices offers a rigorous and analytically grounded account of how research and inno...

title: Equity crowdfunding exemptions, industrial structure, and new venture creation
abstract: We investigate the impact of equity crowdfunding exemptions on new venture creation. We further explore whether the effect varies across industries with different levels of external finance dependence, and whether this heterogeneity is influenced by regional industrial structures. Empirical evidence shows that, while the average effect of crowdfunding exemptions on new venture entry is not statistically significant, the impact is positive and significant in industries with higher external finance dependence. Moreover, this positive effect is further amplified in regions characterized by greater related variety. Complementary analyses show that the increase in new venture creation does not appear to be accompanied by a decline in entry quality. These findings highlight the importance of firm-level financial constraints and regional industrial context in shaping the effectiveness of crowdfunding policies.

title: When stars hold power: The impact of returnee deans on academic publications in Chinese universities
Correcting measurement error bias in conjoint survey experiments
abstract: Abstract Conjoint survey designs are spreading across the social sciences due to their unusual capacity to estimate many causal effects from a single randomized experiment. Unfortunately, by their ability to mirror complicated real‐world choices, these designs often generate substantial measurement error and thus bias. We replicate both the data collection and analysis from eight prominent conjoint studies, all of which closely reproduce published results, and reveal high levels of measurement error in all. We then discover a common empirical pattern in how measurement error appears in conjoint studies and, with it, introduce an easy‐to‐use statistical method to correct the bias. Along the way, we provide a much simpler and simultaneously more powerful approach to designing, organizing, understanding, and analyzing conjoint data analyses.

title: Thinly Veiled: The Use of Femonationalist Speech in European Parliaments
For Everything There is a Season: Seasonality and Retrospective Voting in African Elections
abstract: Are African elections subject to seasonal effects? I argue that agricultural seasonality patterns election outcomes by influencing voters’ retrospective performance evaluations. When countries hold elections after harvests, voters reward incumbents. As the year continues and conditions worsen, voters begin to sour on incumbents. I construct a measure of agricultural seasons using satellite imagery and pair it with an original dataset of 145 executive-election results from 32 countries, as well as with over 100,000 Afrobarometer survey responses. I first show a curvilinear relationship between the time from harvest and support for incumbent executives. Initially, voter support for incumbents increases following a harvest, but this relationship eventually reverses before the next harvest. To account for endogenous election timing, I also examine quasi-experimental evidence from two Zambian by-elections triggered by the deaths of incumbents. Finally, I analyze survey responses to probe for causal mechanisms and find evidence of sociotropic rather than pocketbook voting.

title: “Don’t Know, Don’t Care?” How information and institutional reform affect voting in supranational elections: experimental evidence from the 2024 European Parliamentary elections
abstract: Abstract European elections consistently show lower turnout compared to national elections. Two types of explanations have been proposed. The first is the “don’t know” explanation: European citizens are not adequately informed about what the EU does, what the role of the European Parliament (EP) is, and what impact their vote can have. The second explanation is that they “don’t care”: voters do not care about European elections because they might think that EU policies do not affect them or that the European Parliament is not an important actor in EU politics. I use a between-subject survey experiment in 16 EU countries, with approximately 30,000 respondents, one month before the 2024 European elections, with a follow-up in the days after the vote, to see whether giving voters more information about what the European Parliament does and presenting respondents with hypothetical increases in the powers of the European Parliament, affects their intention to vote and eventual real-world vote. Results show that information increases likelihood to vote. Importantly, these effects last and increase actual voting propensity a month later. Surprisingly, hypothetical increases in the powers of the EP decrease the likelihood to vote among almost all groups of respondents. Among respondents that are skeptical of the EU or perceive a democratic deficit, this negative effect is more pronounced. Even among pro-EU respondents and among those that prefer to see a stronger role for the Commission, the backlash is strong. When considering increasing the powers of the EP, the European Union has little to gain and much to lose when it comes to civic participation. The EU needs to first improve its legitimacy before considering political reforms.

title: The Right to the Campus: Student Occupations, the University, and the Right to the City
abstract: While the 2024 Gaza solidarity encampments and campus occupations before them have been the objects of significant debate among academics and broader public audiences, the spatialized and radical democratic dimensions of these protests remain undertheorized. This article argues that turning to Henri Lefebvre provides valuable tools for better understanding campus occupations and answering the questions that universities face today. Grounded in Lefebvre’s comments about students, knowledge production, and campus life following May 1968, I argue that the university is a key site for demanding, clarifying, and expanding the “right to the city.” Extending Lefebvre’s analysis through a discussion of the spatial production activities of contemporary elite North American universities, I propose a novel “right to the campus” defined by radical democratization of university governance and use-driven spatial design. Finally, I draw lessons from the 1968 Columbia University occupations before applying the right to the campus to analyze the successes and disappointments of the more recent wave of encampments. Viewed through this framework, campus occupations posit control over university “property” as a mechanism for challenging the undemocratic management and market logic characterizing both campus spaces and university activities off campus.

title: The regime of bordering: Borderwork, mobility, and relational state power in the Greek–Turkish borderlands
abstract: The constitutive role of migration, mobilities and borders in state formation and the production of state power is well documented. Existing scholarship has largely focused on the politics and governance of migration, on encounters at and within state borders and often vis- à-vis a single type of cross-border mobility. Building on critical perspectives on everyday borderwork and state power as a relational topological force, this paper advances the regime of bordering as an analytical framework for a fine-grained and relational understanding of state power in postimperial borders, like the Greek-Turkish border. Epistemologically, this framework adopts a comprehensive mobility lens, rather than focusing on one type of mobility or borderwork, and combines a topological approach to power with a place-based analysis of cross-border mobilities and interactions in political, economic and social spheres. Empirically grounded in Greek-Turkish relations and the cross-border mobilities in the Thracian borderlands, the framework enables capturing the accumulated effects of mobility-related borderwork in the interrelated transnational geopolitical, geoeconomic and geosocial spaces. As such, it offers a spatially and temporally connected understanding of state-mobility relations.

title: Identity threat, personal values, and political attitudes: Evidence from a large‐scale survey across the European Union
abstract: Abstract In political contexts, identities are typically based on shared values. Populist rhetoric often utilizes real and perceived threats to evoke such identities, especially on the far right. Using dedicated items in a survey covering all 27 EU Member States ( N = 27,032), we present evidence on the understudied link between perceived identity threat and values, reflecting foundational motivations of people, as well as downstream political attitudes. At the EU level, personal values related to anxiety avoidance correlate positively with perceived identity threat, whereas growth‐focused values correlate negatively. The positive relationship between identity threat and values focusing on increasing one's self‐efficacy and status is especially pronounced, suggesting compensatory motivational processes. National‐level analysis reveals a more nuanced picture. Perceived identity threat correlates strongly with lower support for liberal policies. This result is relatively homogenous across the EU‐27 and holds when controlling for personal values. Overall, the findings resonate with populist rhetoric focusing on in‐groups and status while attacking liberal policies and universalist values. Conversely, the findings offer hope that policies and communication reducing identity threat may reinforce support for liberal policies and aligned values.

title: Baby Slump: The Political Consequences of Pregnancy for Candidates
abstract: Abstract Do women candidate’s parental status, whether childfree, pregnant, or a mother, influence how U.S. voters evaluate their leadership, commitment, and policy expertise at the state executive and legislative levels? Using data from a nationally representative survey experiment, I assess how voters rate these candidates’ competencies. Regardless of partisanship, I find voters reduce support for pregnant candidates, particularly at the executive level, due to concerns about time availability. I also discover a parenthood timing gap effect — while pregnancy is perceived as a limitation to do the job as an elected official, having young children as a mother enhances leadership evaluations, at least among Democrats. A partisan divide emerges, with Democrats rating maternal-cuing candidates higher on leadership competencies compared to Republicans. This research has important implications for how candidates need to strategize their presentation as we see more women and (expecting) mothers run for all types of office.

title: The Green Gender Gap in Adolescence: A Case Study of Norway
abstract: Abstract Previous research from predominantly Western contexts finds that men consistently show less concern for climate change and the environment than women, a pattern known as the Green Gender Gap. This article investigates whether political gender socialization contributes to this phenomenon. Drawing on two unique data sources from Norway, I find that among adolescents aged 15 to 18, girls are more supportive of the Green Party, consider environmental protection more important, and are more likely to prioritize the environment over oil production and industrial development. I also find that girls express greater concern about climate change than boys from as early as age 13, the earliest age at which data are available. The findings are consistent with the hypothesis that early-life political gender socialization plays a key role in shaping the Green Gender Gap. The gap emerges before structural gender sorting into different educational and occupational trajectories, and while most adolescents still live at home and share the same formative environment. These findings are particularly striking given the Norwegian context, which is characterized by minimal structural gender segregation among adolescents. The findings in this article point to gendered socialization, rather than structural differences between women and men, as one of the driving forces behind the Green Gender Gap.

title: Voting the Same, Feeling Differently: Sister Circles, Black Feminist Epistemologies, and Black Women’s Political Emotions During the Harris Campaign
abstract: Kamala Harris, a first multi-racial Black woman, became the official Democratic presidential nominee on August 5, 2025. This historic achievement only amplified the intensity of discussions about Black women’s politics in the United States. As Black feminist political scientists studying Black women’s politics, we knew we needed to document the nuance, dynamism, and historical nature of Harris’s campaign. We were keenly aware that we needed to capture the narratives of Black women voters to fully make sense of this historic moment. The media narrative that Black women were excited about Harris’s nomination (Jones 2024; Walker 2024) and scholarly findings that Black women voters preferred Black women candidates (Brown et al. 2019; Philpot and Walton, Jr. 2007) seemed superficial. We believed that beneath Black women’s support for Harris lay a particularized set of emotions and wide variation in candidate evaluations, which are underexplored because Black women consistently vote Democratic and are the demographic group most likely to support Black women candidates. These varied emotive responses lead to the same political behavior: a vote for Harris. Our research examines how Black women feel about politics and how these emotions translate into political action.

title: Entering the Inner Core of Cabinets: Electoral Causes and Consequences of Holding Salient Ministerial Offices
abstract: ABSTRACT Can electoral success be an asset for being appointed to more prominent ministerial posts in cabinets? Are ministers punished or rewarded by voters according to the importance of their post? These questions are explored in this article. Portfolio allocation as well as electoral consequences of participating in governments is usually studied at the party level and not for individual politicians. The novel approach in this article is to focus on individual ministers rather than parties. We approach importance of ministerial posts according to membership of certain cabinet committees, which can mark a clear demarcation line of which ministers have more and less influence on cabinet policies within parties in governments. By using a dataset on Danish ministers from 1977 to 2022 we find a complex relationship between personal votes and policy influence in cabinet, providing important nuances to the existing literature on cabinet governance, ministerial selection and cost of ruling.

title: Is inflation relief passed-through? Evidence from excise taxes
Disclosure in Insurance Markets with Limited Screening
Capital reallocation under climate policy uncertainty
Energy prices, inflation, and the ECB’s monetary policy during the 2021-22 energy crisis
ROBUST BAYES TREATMENT CHOICE WITH PARTIAL IDENTIFICATION
abstract: We study a class of binary treatment choice problems with partial identification through the lens of robust (multiple prior) Bayesian analysis. We use a convenient set of prior distributions to derive ex-ante and ex-post robust Bayes decision rules, both for decision makers who can randomize and for decision makers who cannot. Our main messages are as follows: First, ex-ante and ex-post robust Bayes decision rules do not agree in general, whether or not randomized rules are allowed. Second, randomized treatment assignment for some data realizations can be optimal in both ex-ante and, perhaps more surprisingly, ex-post problems. Therefore, it is usually with loss of generality to exclude randomized rules from consideration, even when regret is evaluated ex post. We apply our results to a stylized problem where a policy maker uses experimental data to choose whether to implement a new policy in a population of interest, but is concerned about the external validity of the experiment at hand, and to aggregation of data generated by multiple randomized control trials in different sites to make a policy choice in a population for which no experimental data are available.

title: SELF-WEIGHTED ESTIMATION FOR LOCAL UNIT ROOT REGRESSIONS WITH APPLICATIONS
abstract: A new self-weighted (SW) least squares (LS) estimation approach is developed for local unit root (LUR) autoregression with conditionally heteroskedastic innovations. Asymptotically controlled trimming of the most extreme observations in LS regression is shown to lead to mixed Gaussian limit theory and studentization produces standard normality free of the unknown LUR parameter. The estimator is super consistent with a convergence rate slightly below the <mml:math xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xmlns:mnf="http://cambridge.org/core/manifest" xmlns:cup="http://contentservices.cambridge.org" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:m="http://cambridge.org/core/metadata" xmlns:core="http://cambridge.org/core" xmlns:c="http://cambridge.org/core/content" display="inline"> <mml:msub> <mml:mi>O</mml:mi> <mml:mi>P</mml:mi> </mml:msub> <mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo> <mml:mi>n</mml:mi> <mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo> </mml:math> $O_P(n)$ upper O Subscript upper P Baseline left parenthesis n right parenthesis rate of LS estimation. The asymptotic theory relies on a new framework of convergence to the local time of a Gaussian process, allowing for the sample moments generated from martingales and many other integrated dependent sequences. A new LUR test in augmented autoregression is developed using SW estimation, providing an alternative approach that employs Gaussian limit theory in contrast to the augmented Dickey–Fuller and other tests. Simulation results show that the test has good size control and power performance against mildly integrated alternatives. An empirical illustration is conducted evaluating the persistence of several market fundamentals as predictors of S&P 500 excess returns.

title: ROBUST INFERENCE FOR CONVEX PAIRWISE DIFFERENCE ESTIMATORS
abstract: This article develops distribution theory and bootstrap-based inference methods for a broad class of convex pairwise difference estimators. These estimators minimize a kernel-weighted convex-in-parameter function over observation pairs with similar covariates, where the similarity is governed by a localization (bandwidth) parameter. While classical results establish asymptotic normality under restrictive bandwidth conditions, we show that valid Gaussian and bootstrap-based inference remains possible under substantially weaker assumptions. First, we extend the theory of small-bandwidth asymptotics to convex pairwise difference estimation settings, deriving robust Gaussian approximations even when a smaller-than-standard bandwidth is used. Second, we employ a debiasing procedure based on generalized jackknifing to enable inference with larger bandwidths, while preserving convexity of the objective function. Third, we construct a novel bootstrap method that adjusts for bandwidth-induced variance distortions, yielding valid inference across a wide range of bandwidth choices. Our proposed inference method enjoys demonstrably greater robustness, while retaining the practical appeal of convex pairwise difference estimators.

title: Social Security Reforms, Retirement, and Sectoral Decisions
Rational inattention: The interplay of stakes and prior beliefs in a laboratory study
Connectivity justice: A new concept for the post-digital society
abstract: This theoretical commentary introduces the concept of connectivity justice and discusses how it can be utilized in research on mobile, digitally reliant lives. Connectivity justice reframes questions of mobility and data justice for a post-digital world in which digital connections have become both indispensable and intrusive. The concept extends recent work on digital disconnection by examining the institutional and sociotechnical drivers of connectivity (in)justice, such as state actors, tech industry, labor conditions, and cultural norms, rather than individual-level correlates alone. By combining the capabilities approach with a feminist ethics of care, connectivity justice highlights that justice today involves not only equitable access to infrastructures but also the relational capacity to connect well, to engage, withdraw, and sustain digital life responsibly. This lens opens new directions for mobilities research, and beyond, inviting analyses of how digital infrastructures, labor platforms, and everyday practices shape people’s freedoms to move, communicate, and care. In doing so, it bridges normative and empirical inquiry, providing a vocabulary for understanding justice as an evolving balance between autonomy and interdependence within networked societies.

title: The nation’s third body: Shein’s paradox between performed nationhood and transnational operations
abstract: The intensifying global tariff tensions are reshaping the operations of cross-border e-commerce platforms. This study examines Shein, a Chinese-origin e-commerce platform with global reach, to explore nationhood and transnational operations amid emerging tensions through a communication lens. Conducting Shein as a case study, this paper draws on the nation’s two bodies to conceptualize the third body as a distinct form of nationhood in the platform age. Findings reveal that Shein enacted a deterritorialized yet embedded nationhood, performing through logistical sovereignty, digital infrastructure, and transnational governance. These dimensions indicate that the third body provides insight into how state power can remain invisible yet operate through platforms. This paper concludes with implications for future research on the infrastructural turn of platforms in today’s global ambivalent moment.

title: Ideology and organization in post-communist China: The case of university student party branches
abstract: This research examines how variations in the orientation of student party members toward party membership interact with types of activities organized by university student party branches in China. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork at two universities in Beijing, I identify four types of branch organizational culture and three ideal types of student party members. I find that student party members differ not only in why they join the party but also in how they understand party membership, what they seek from branch life, and how they engage in party activities after admission. I also demonstrate that branches vary in how they organize procedural, instructive, and outreach activities, and that these variations shape participation and interpretation in different ways.

title: Individualization, Relationships and Collective Action Among Migrants in China: Evidence from Rent Strikes
abstract: Abstract Based on a field study of the COVID-19 rent reduction actions of a group of self-employed migrants in Zhengzhou, China, this study examines how individualization shaped the relational networks of the migrants, which in turn dynamically influenced the trajectory and outcome of their collective action. The group’s collective action was shaped not by a single relationship but by an instrumental relational network woven from fragmented intra-group ties, fragile local connections, unstable market relations and arms-length government–migrant interactions. The “relational duality” framework proposed here reveals this network’s dual role in contention: shared experiences of external exclusion catalysed internal solidarity and short-term mobilization; however, the network’s inherent instrumentality and vulnerability rendered it highly susceptible to adversaries’ strategic activation of latent competitive boundaries through tactics like co-optation and relational repression, thus triggering a rapid dissolution of solidarity that resulted in the protest fragmenting. These findings enrich an understanding of the micro-dynamics of contentious politics in China and offer a fresh lens for analysing collective action among similar groups that undergo individualization.

title: Fostering Citizen Trust in Local Government Through Coproduction of Crisis Response: Does It Really Work?
abstract: Does citizen coproduction of crisis response foster trust in local government? This study addresses this question by developing and testing a framework proposing that participation in community coproduction of crisis response (CCCR) enhances citizen trust through sense of control over daily life and perceived social capital generated during CCCR, and these processes are further conditioned by citizens’ pandemic risk perception. Using survey data collected from 1,106 urban residents during the 2022 COVID-19 lockdown in Shanghai, China, we find that participation in CCCR generally strengthens trust in municipal government. The results show that this effect occurs primarily because participation in CCCR increases perceived social capital, whereas no evidence is found for the proposed role of sense of control. Moreover, the trust-enhancing effect disappears when risk perception is high, because elevated risk perception reduces the extent to which CCCR generates perceived social capital. These findings contribute evidence from a crisis context to the longstanding debate on whether coproduction enhances trust and provide explanations on how participatory arrangements can sustain governance legitimacy.

title: Mapping Institutional Hybridity and State Capacity in Polycentric Governance: Modes of Coordination and Performance in Polycentric Governance: Disentangling Complexity. By AndreasThiel, ElizabethBaldwin, MarkStephan, and SergioVillamayor‐Tomas (eds.), Oxford University Press, 2025. 206 pp
abstract: Data sharing not applicable to this article as no datasets were generated or analyzed during the current study.

title: Visualizing & strategizing public value: an unexpected path to invisibilizing
abstract: Whereas public value has become a central concern in public management, its visibility within strategic decision-making remains a major challenge. This article examines how visual tools contribute to visualizing and strategizing public value. Drawing on an action research conducted in a French municipality, we show that issue maps shape strategizing by making public value visible, discussable, and strategically actionable. We demonstrate that these tools direct attention, support deliberation and structure meaning, creating public value. Surprisingly, they also generate resistance and processes of invisibilizing: some values become unseen. These findings highlight the inherently selective and political nature of visualizing.

title: New development: Cultural impacts on unethical practices in public management—Are individualism and femininity a golden combination?
abstract: IMPACTThis study reveals that, in addition to directly addressing unethical practices through integrity codes and more specific measures, politicians and public managers should also consider the cultural factors underlying these practices. Public sector organizations are advised to integrate measures to ensure that employees show desirable moral behaviour in their human resources repertoire, including recruitment procedures and training programmes.ABSTRACTThis article explores the impacts of country-specific cultural dimensions on unethical practices in public management. The focus is on four unethical practices: corruption, manipulation of accounting information, bullying behaviour by managers towards their subordinates, and the acceptance of gifts by public servants. Each of these practices is examined in relation to Hofstede's country-cultural dimensions. The study suggests that individualism and femininity may reduce the likelihood of corruption and the manipulation of accounting information, offering a theoretical proposition for future empirical research.

title: Populist-inflected governance in a mature democracy: Bureaucratic de-legitimation and executive control in the United Kingdom (2019–2024)
abstract: IMPACTThis article is of direct practical relevance to UK policy-makers and officials, including elected politicians, senior civil servants, regulators, parliamentary staff and practitioners working in relevant accountability institutions. It shows how populist and anti-democratic forces can influence governance, even in a mature democracy like the UK: attacks on professional advice, pressure on formally independent bodies, and attempts to force policy through legal or administrative obstacles. By examining anti-civil service ‘blob’ rhetoric, reforms to regulators, and the Rwanda asylum scheme, the article offers practitioners a framework for recognizing these dynamics as they emerge. For politicians and policy-makers, it highlights the risks of treating bureaucratic resistance, legal constraint, or regulatory independence as politically motivated obstruction. For officials and campaigners, it identifies where safeguards may be weakest. Its real-world value lies in helping actors who support democratic governance preserve and strengthen mediating democratic institutions, including in other national and sub-national contexts.

title: Social learning rules and the effectiveness of behavioural policy: an agent-based model
abstract: Abstract Behaviour-change interventions unfold in social systems where people learn from others. We develop a stylised agent-based model to examine how four canonical social learning rules – conformist transmission, informational prestige-biased copying, payoff-biased copying and random copying – shape the impact of a simple seeding intervention. Two arms evolve under identical conditions and learning rules, differing only in initial adoption: both start with exactly 5% baseline adopters and the treatment arm additionally seeds 20% of the remaining non-adopters, yielding an exact 25% vs 5% contrast at t equals 0 $t = 0$ <mml:math xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xmlns:mnf="http://cambridge.org/core/manifest" xmlns:cup="http://contentservices.cambridge.org" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:m="http://cambridge.org/core/metadata" xmlns:core="http://cambridge.org/core" xmlns:c="http://cambridge.org/core/content" display="inline"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>t</mml:mi> <mml:mo>=</mml:mo> <mml:mn>0</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> . Across homogeneous populations, 70/30 mixed ecologies and sweeps over the share of payoff-biased learners, we track adoption trajectories and treatment–control lift; we also vary payoff parameters, prestige informativeness and conformist thresholds in robustness analyses. We find that the same seeding intervention can stall, drift or cascade depending on the learning ecology. In the baseline specification, conformist dynamics exhibit threshold effects that erase treatment gains, prestige-biased and random copying can preserve positive final lift when diffusion remains incomplete and payoff-biased copying mainly changes the diffusion regime rather than preserving large end-point gaps. Robustness checks show that negative payoff premia suppress diffusion, weak or noisy payoff signals can generate treatment advantages, prestige effects depend on how informative prestige is and conformist treatment effects are concentrated in narrow threshold-boundary regions. These results motivate policy heuristics that evaluate interventions relative to local diffusion potential, make successful outcomes visible when payoff cues matter and tailor seeding to the prevailing mix of learning rules.

title: Governance networks in public administration and public policy
abstract: Reading this book will certainly attract our attention to re-study shifts in public administration, starting from classical public administration, new public management, and collaborative public ma...

title: What is wrong with positivist policy process theories? Controversies over empirically grasping policy complexity
abstract: Debates between positivist and interpretivist Policy Process Theories are typically framed as either irreconcilable or easily combinable. Rather than addressing the underlying ontological and epistemological differences between the two approaches, this essay singles out one dimension relative to the debate: how the two approaches empirically grasp policy complexity differently and what this means for policy process theory. Toward this end, I examine two controversies: identifying ‘collective entities’ (coalitions, networks, beliefs) and delineating ‘policy subsystems’ versus ‘policy micro-arenas.’ Through shale gas and urban infrastructure cases, I show how positivist approaches simplify reality by constructing stable entities and unified subsystems for causal inference, while interpretive approaches observe micro-level interactions and emergent configurations to capture complexity and uncertainty. I then show how interpretive approaches observe actors’ multipositionality and emergent configurations to capture complexity and uncertainty. Interpretive inquiry reveals unstable coalitions, fragmented configurations, multiple circulations, and unpredictable pathways that simplified concepts necessarily obscure. These empirical controversies demonstrate that grasping policy complexity requires approaches capable of observing details that reveal how policies actually unfold, rather than imposing stable, bounded entities and systems that obscure this complexity.

title: Medicalization, deservingness, and policy feedback: survey evidence on public support for gendered-reproductive health care in Canada
abstract: Abstract Public policies are shaped not only by institutions and interests but also by interactions between policy construction and ideology, which define social problems, determine who is deserving, and set the boundaries of legitimate public provision. This study examines how these dynamics shape support for contested health services, asking how medicalization and social constructions of deservingness influence public attitudes. Using a survey experiment with 2,000 respondents in Canada, the analysis examines support for IVF, abortion, gender-affirming care, and HPV vaccination. Findings suggest that medicalization significantly increases support for public funding for select services, while constructions of deservingness mediate these effects. Policy feedback operates not only through institutional arrangements but also through how citizens perceive the boundaries of healthcare and the deservingness of recipients. The study advances research on policy feedback and health politics by showing how medicalization and social constructions shape public opinion and debates over medical necessity.

title: AI “nationality”, policy types, and public support for embedding AI in policymaking
Agenda exit and policy closure: defensive governability‑making and housing tax reform in Australia (2014–2021)
abstract: Abstract Why do some policy agendas disappear not merely as a matter of declining attention, but as a consequence of becoming politically unsayable? Scholarship on policy processes has devoted extensive attention to agenda‑setting and non‑decision, but far less to the mechanisms through which once‑contested policy options are actively withdrawn from the space of legitimate political action. This article develops the concept of agenda exit to explain how policy contestation is stabilised when proposals become non‑viable to articulate and are subsequently constrained against return. Drawing on a process‑tracing analysis of housing tax reform in Australia from 2014 to 2021, the article shows how a coordinated field of property‑sector actors transformed electoral defeat into a durable agenda constraint through practices of reputational risk construction, substitution, and boundary‑policing. The core contribution is to theorise agenda exit as a condition of structured absence: an interregnum in which a policy remains technically conceivable but is rendered politically unsponsor‑able within ordinary arenas of contestation. This clarifies a distinct mode of policy stability, in which governability is secured not through consensus or resolution, but through the defensive narrowing of political possibility. By specifying how policy options become absent without formal decision, the analysis extends existing work on agenda control, blame avoidance, and policy continuity, and highlights the importance of studying the conditions under which policies can no longer be credibly proposed.

title: Corporate Quasi‐Sovereignty: Big Tech and the Politics of Sovereign Authority in the Digital Age
abstract: ABSTRACT As private technology firms expand their control over critical infrastructures, questions of sovereignty and governance are increasingly displaced from states to corporate actors. Existing scholarship on sovereignty assumes that authority is either monopolized by states or shared through institutionalized public–private arrangements. Yet, recent events, including SpaceX's control of wartime communications in Ukraine, Meta's confrontation with the Australian government, and OpenAI's attempts to shape global AI regulation, demonstrate that firms can exercise discretionary authority without formal delegation, legal accountability, or democratic oversight. This study introduces the concept of Corporate Quasi‐Sovereignty (CQS) to theorize how certain technology firms function as de facto sovereign actors. CQS is defined by the convergence of three enabling dimensions: infrastructural command, executive autonomy, and normative or geopolitical assertion. Drawing on Kingdon's Multiple Streams Framework (MSF), this paper theorizes ‘sovereignty windows’ as the mechanism through which firms internally collapse the problem, policy, and politics streams, enabling unilateral interventions with geopolitical consequences. ‘Stream collapse,’ the internalization of all three MSF streams within a single corporate hierarchy, is operationalized as a boundary condition of MSF, distinct from conventional stream coupling. The ‘conditional policy entrepreneur’ is introduced as the corporate analogue to Kingdon's entrepreneur: a founder‐CEO who exercises this role only when all three CQS enabling conditions simultaneously converge. Drawing on comparative case analyses of Meta, SpaceX, and OpenAI, the article shows how CQS captures both reactive and anticipatory modes of corporate authority, showing that firms now operate as both market actors and quasi‐sovereign agents capable of substituting, bypassing, or preempting state power.

title: Individual militant democracy in EU institutions
abstract: The literature on whether militant democracy can be used to justify EU sanctions against Member States due to their democratic backsliding has so far focused on EU institutions and Member States as (potential) agents of militant democratic sanctions. Yet, militant democratic measures, in some circumstances, may also be imposed by individual agents on individuals who pose a threat to democracy. At the same time, new work in political ethics explores the duties and opportunities of individual political actors, such as Members of the European Parliament, to respond to backsliding in their collegial relations. In this article, we explore whether a militant democratic framework can justify such individual responses to democratic backsliding. We argue that, in principle, individual political actors such as MEPs, members of the European Council, Member State delegates on the Council, and COREPER officials can justifiably apply militant measures against colleagues who hold mandates or offices in a shared decision-making or supportive body of the EU and are elected in or delegated by undemocratic Member States. Such measures, while they would need to pass a high bar of normative justification, require no institutional reform to be implemented.

title: Autocratization by dual aggrandizement: the civil–military coalition driving Mexico’s democratic backsliding
abstract: An unprecedented civil–military coalition is governing Mexico. This article examines the legacy of Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018–2024), a charismatic populist who successfully freed the Presidency of Mexico from checks and balances and expanded the military to tasks well beyond national defence. Both processes have shaped Mexico’s ongoing episode of autocratization. Now under President Claudia Sheinbaum (2024–2030), executive power has partially decompressed, yet the top brass has attained a legal role in “governability” through the Cabinet of Security, a rising organ reflecting the new civil–military relations in Mexico. As of 2026, Mexico’s militarization turned from a functional instrument of populist executive power into an independent driver of democratic backsliding. The Mexican case confirms the need to keep an eye on military aggrandizement as a mode of autocratization.

title: Is assembly-independent government good for democracy? Bhutan, Suriname and Switzerland in comparative perspective
abstract: Assembly-independent government (AIG) is a rare and understudied hybrid of parliamentarism and presidentialism. The political executive is indirectly authorised through the elected assembly, rather than through separate presidential elections, but cannot be removed from office through an ordinary majority vote of no confidence. The article defines this hybrid from the perspective of democratic theory and studies its consequences for executive dominance and legislative majority rule. It compares AIG in Bhutan, Suriname and Switzerland and argues that its causal effects depend on the party system and the details of executive design. In Switzerland, AIG is essential to a system of complex majoritarianism that deconcentrates and depersonalises executive power, avoids the creation of veto players and empowers shifting legislative coalitions around the political center in parliament. In Bhutan and Suriname, by contrast, it contributes to the concentration of power in the chief executive. It is part of simple majoritarianism in Bhutan and competitive clientelism in Suriname. The analysis has important implications for debates about constitutional reform in cases such as Togo and the United States.

title: Institutionalization of electoral authoritarianism in North Africa: the 2024 presidential elections in Mauritania
abstract: Over the past two decades, elections have become a central feature of authoritarian governance, increasingly serving regime stability rather than democratization. While earlier scholarship emphasized elections as moments of vulnerability, more recent research highlights their consolidating effects when competition becomes institutionalized. This article examines the 2024 presidential elections in Mauritania, addressing the puzzle of how procedurally credible and internationally validated elections can coexist with persistent authoritarian rule. It argues that Mauritanian authoritarianism has been strengthened through the institutionalization of electoral competition as a mechanism of regime reproduction, relying less on systematic fraud than on the interaction of formal institutions and informal practices that minimize uncertainty and contain opposition challenges. Drawing on qualitative evidence from field observation in Nouakchott, semi-structured interviews, and documentary analysis, the study analyses four stabilizing mechanisms: dominant-party organizational control, elite co-optation and opposition fragmentation, institutional management of competition, and international legitimation combined with selective post-electoral repression. The findings show that the 2024 election reinforced authoritarian consolidation by generating legitimacy and elite coordination while preventing meaningful prospects for alternation.

title: Who won the feed? TikTok campaigning of the alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left in Germany’s 2025 federal election
abstract: The 2025 German federal election marked a historic low for centrist parties among voters under 25, a demographic shift that coincided with TikTok becoming a primary news source. Integrating theories of political personalization with research on platformized communication, we argue that the digital resonance of the AfD and Die Linke is underpinned by their strategic alignment with TikTok’s specific logic, though they achieve success through divergent pathways. Analyzing a novel dataset of 3702 TikTok posts, we find that while structural personalization acts as a universal driver of engagement, the two parties mobilize different dimensions of the platform. The AfD excels at exploiting technical affordances like hashtags and duets to maximize visibility, while Die Linke secures engagement by adapting to participatory vernaculars such as humor and trending audio. We conclude that the platformized landscape accommodates distinct mobilization logics, where the radical right optimises for technical visibility to scale reach and the radical left secures engagement by aligning with the community’s participatory norms.

title: Balancing Act: Coercion, Terrorism, and Regime Stability
Response to a Critique
Irregularities in Perez Brower (2024), “Reframing Gendered Issues: Intersectional Identity Frames and Policy Agendas”
Editorial Expression of Concern: Reframing Gendered Issues: Intersectional Identity Frames and Policy Agendas
Partisanship and the Social Construction of Deservingness in the United States
Government Spending Shapes the Emergence of Women Candidates for Local Office
abstract: Women are underrepresented across all levels of government, yielding profound public policy consequences. Yet, policy outcomes may also shape who runs for office. To align research on women candidates and leaders, we consider both parts of the broader political ecosystem. Research shows women hesitate to run because politics do not fulfill their communal goals. But governments’ communal policy priorities vary, producing substantial differences in women’s entrance into politics. Analyzing over 70,000 Brazilian candidates and municipal spending patterns, we show that communal spending patterns at the local level and policy outputs predict women’s emergence. We provide consistent evidence that women’s interest in pursuing political office varies across place and time.

title: Inscribing the Dutch imperial geopolitical order: The colonial geography of Louis van Vuuren (1873-1951)
Public support for climate policies: costs, redistribution, and ideological divides
abstract: Securing public support for climate policies remains a major challenge. Citizens’ perceptions of the costs, benefits, and distributive consequences of these policies are key factors shaping their attitudes, yet how these dimensions interact remains insufficiently understood. This question is addressed through two experimental studies in Spain. Study 1 embeds a vignette experiment in two surveys to analyse how exposure to the costs or benefits of ten climate policies affects support. Cost framing significantly reduces support, whereas benefit framing has only a modest positive effect. Study 2 implements a conjoint experiment to examine how costs, benefits, and redistributive implications jointly influence preferences for climate policy packages. Results confirm previous evidence regarding costs and benefits and highlight the central role of redistribution: citizens strongly favour policies improving the situation of the poorest, while ideological divides reveal that left-wing voters are more supportive and sensitive to redistributive cues.

title: Effective tax rates, firm size and the global minimum tax
Do ultra-poor graduation programs build women’s resilience to weather shocks? Evidence from rural Ethiopia
abstract: We assess whether layering an ultra-poor graduation program on Ethiopia’s Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP) protects women and their households from localized weather shocks. Using panel data from a large cluster-randomized trial matched with detailed weather records, we identify community-level exposure to dryness shocks. Women who are exposed to dryness shocks experience deteriorating nutritional status (in conjunction with declining household food security and assets) and a significant increase in the risk of intimate partner violence. However, access to the graduation program fully buffers women from any increase in intimate partner violence, and partially buffers women and their households against other adverse effects. Further analysis suggests that improved household savings likely drives the program’s protective impact.

title: Women’s labor subsidy: Evidence from Chile
The stalled gender housework revolution in the United States
abstract: Abstract Prior studies document a declining but persistent gender housework gap since the 1960s, with declines in women’s housework time far exceeding increases in men’s. Yet scholars differ in their assessment of what these trends mean about the pace and extent of gendered change in family life. Using individual-level longitudinal data from the 1976–2023 waves of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, this study addresses this theoretical impasse by asking whether housework has become fundamentally degendered over time. I assess degendering using two novel indicators: the residual gender housework gap relative to the total gap and gender symmetry in associations between key predictors and housework. Results show that although the overall gender housework gap has declined substantially, the share of the total gap accounted for by theoretically relevant observed predictors remains small and has not increased over time. Individual fixed-effects models further show that cohabitation, marriage, and children remain much more strongly associated with increases in women’s housework than men’s across periods. Associations of paid work hours and earnings with housework, in contrast, attenuate over time, with less consistent evidence of gender asymmetry. Overall, these findings indicate limited progress in degendering housework and are more consistent with a stalled gender housework revolution.

title: Review of “Unequal Worlds of Care: The Politics of Global Health in Malawi”
abstract: Unequal Worlds of Care analyzes healthcare in Malawi, where private and public foreign health aid focus overwhelmingly on HIV/AIDS care. Amy Zhou finds that contemporary assistance programs tend to be targeted and temporary. Certain problems, like mother-to-infant transmission of AIDS, receive considerable resources, while other serious problems, like neonatal mortality, do not. This type of dichotomy characterizes the "two worlds" of care. Zhou argues that each aid project in this piecemeal approach may do some good, but overall, the projects tend to have few lasting impacts because they do not invest in the overall healthcare system. She calls for a reimaging of healthcare and donor aid globally to create a broader and more integrated system. Zhou begins with a preface that places the study in the current context of substantially reduced US funding for global health concerns. If anything, the recent retrenchment in foreign aid to combat HIV makes the core themes of Unequal Worlds of Care even more relevant—the hypothetical situation Zhou uses as a foil throughout the book is now much closer to reality. Aid cuts could reignite a new AIDS crisis, a situation that was unimaginable to most healthcare workers while the study was being conducted. And in the pattern of cuts, the two worlds persist: experts estimate that, while funding for HIV has been cut about 20 percent, funding for maternal and child health, family planning, and reproductive health has been cut 90 percent (p. xv). The uncertain future underscores the problems that arise when every donor creates their own temporary structures of care, typically separate from the central health system.

title: Review of "Insecurity Politics: How Unstable Lives Lead to Populist Support"
Review of “Living Diaper to Diaper: The Hidden Crisis of Poverty and Motherhood”
Review of "Governing the Excluded: Rural Livelihoods Beyond Coca in Colombia's Peace Laboratory"
abstract: In May 2017, Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos arrived in Briceño to officially launch Colombia’s coca substitution program, one of the key initiatives of the recently signed peace agreement with the leftist guerrilla Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). In his speech, Santos promised to expand the presence of the state through the construction of roads and schools, and to provide economic help “so that you [farmers] can permanently substitute coca for licit crops… Most people want to leave coca behind because they know it brings violence… [t]hey want a better future for their children, they want the state to come.” (p. 76). Has the landmark agreement lived up to these promises? How have the lives and livelihoods of Colombian farmers been impacted, and how has it transformed the relationships between rural communities and both state and non-state actors? Alex Diamond’s outstanding book, Governing the Excluded, is among the first book-length studies to answer these critical questions by foregrounding rural farmers’ perspectives and experiences.

title: Survival First: How Citizens Prioritize Competing Climate‐Health Risk Countermeasures Under Fiscal Constraints
abstract: When governments must allocate limited resources among competing climate-health countermeasures, citizen risk priorities determine political feasibility-yet whether those priorities translate into fiscal support remains poorly understood. This study develops a hybrid best-worst scaling and contingent valuation framework that integrates individual-level priority parameters into an acceptance model, enabling direct testing of whether preference intensity predicts willingness to pay. Applied to a large-sample survey of residents in Yokohama, Japan-a rapidly aging metropolis facing escalating heat emergencies-the analysis reveals three findings. First, citizens exhibit a survival-first hierarchy, decisively prioritizing immediate protective measures over long-term structural interventions, with consensus varying sharply across countermeasure types. Second, a systematic priority-WTP disconnect emerges: The priority parameters for the most valued measures show no statistically detectable association with acceptance of the proposed payment, consistent with a possible entitlement interpretation in which life-saving services are perceived as government obligations rather than goods warranting additional taxation, while a group of lower-ranked supplementary measures is jointly associated with greater fiscal support. Third, chronic quality-of-life burdens-particularly sleep disruption-are more consistently associated with willingness to pay than are acute health symptoms, while private cooling costs are negatively associated with support for public adaptation, consistent with a crowding-out mechanism that may pose a regressive barrier to equitable financing. These findings suggest that preference intensity and fiscal support may operate through partially distinct evaluative pathways, implying that standard valuation methods relying on willingness to pay alone can systematically misrepresent the structure of public risk priorities.

title: Robust Solar Radiation Modification Strategy for Achieving Temperature Targets
abstract: Solar radiation modification (SRM) provides an additional cooling option for limiting warming, but uncertainties about its realized cooling outcomes challenge the robustness of temperature-target strategies. This study develops an SRM decision framework that is robust in achieving the temperature target by embedding the min-max regret (MMR) rule into an integrated assessment model. We evaluate SRM strategies under uncertainty in cooling efficiency, SRM-related damages, and climate sensitivity. The results show that policies designed for adverse cooling-response states can better avoid temperature-target failure but generate great welfare losses from over-deployment. The MMR-based strategy exhibits distinct phasing, with restrained deployment before mid-century and accelerated deployment thereafter. Sensitivity analyses show that this two-phase pattern remains robust across alternative uncertainty sets.
