Overall, the robust framework balances the risk of temperature-target failure against the welfare cost of over-deployment under persistent uncertainties.

title: Making Words Count: Computational Linguistics in Management Research
abstract: In recent years, a rapidly growing number of management scholars are using computational linguistics (CL) to analyze vast corpora of naturally occurring organizational language. Yet the rapid adoption of CL methods has outpaced the development of shared standards for linking theoretical constructs, linguistic data, and computational measurement. We synthesize 353 articles published in leading management journals for 2013–2025, identifying four recurring challenges shaping the credibility of CL-based research: misalignment between constructs and textual corpora, unnecessary model complexity, the opacity of large language model workflows, and insufficient transparency in reporting. Building on these patterns, we develop four integrative design principles—construct-language fit, minimal sufficient complexity, LLM sensitivity and auditability, and disclosure-as-assessability—and identify key research implications that reposition CL as a theoretically consequential lens for management scholarship.

title: Make the Alliance Personal: A Dependence Framework of Managerial Personal Tie Activation in Alliance Management
abstract: In this study, we explore an intriguing yet understudied question: Would top managers decide to activate personal ties to manage their firms’ alliances? We address this question by synthesizing the insights of the research on personal tie activation and resource dependence theory to develop a nuanced theoretical framework on the mechanisms underlying top managers’ personal tie activation decisions in alliance management. We highlight that the interdependence features between two alliance partner firms (i.e., mutual dependence, power imbalance, interpartner competition, and the interactions thereof) together shape the partner firms’ relational dynamics in the value creation and value appropriation in their alliance. Accordingly, these features determine the potential benefits and costs for top managers of the partner firms to activate their personal ties to manage this alliance, both for their firms and for themselves. We draw empirical evidence from a field study with 244 alliances between Chinese firms and an experimental vignette study with 212 real-world managers in China. Results of our analyses support our predictions, with a few intriguing exceptions. We derive valuable implications for theory and practice.

title: Common Identities and Political Talk: Evaluating Cross-Cutting Political Discussions in Sports Communities on Reddit
abstract: Research suggests that online nonpolitical communities may facilitate better cross-cutting political discussions than explicitly political communities as users’ shared nonpolitical identities can offset partisan bias, in line with the Common Ingroup Identity Model. This study tests this idea through a large-scale computational analysis comparing the quantity, tone, and substance of political discussions on the same topics in political and sports communities on Reddit. Overall, we find that sports communities facilitate more cross-cutting political discussions than political communities, with the exception of soccer communities. These discussions use similar proportions of credible sources but use significantly fewer sources that are not credible compared to discussions in political communities. On the flip side, we do not find evidence of a meaningful difference in toxicity levels of cross-cutting political discussions in sports and political communities. Further, we find that political discussions in sports communities use fewer sources overall. These results advance a nuanced understanding of the promise of nonpolitical spaces for deliberative democracy and the role of common identities in political discussions.

title: When the Mass Line Encounters the Ground: Public-Oriented Accountability and Frontline Coping in China
abstract: While the consolidation of state control in China is well-documented, less attention has been given to the reinforcement of public-oriented accountability, which emphasizes citizen satisfaction with complaint resolution in government performance assessments. Drawing on statistical data and fieldwork interviews, this study finds that while public-oriented accountability can partially promote substantive government responsiveness by imposing institutional pressure on frontline officials, it also fosters a public perception of an omnipotent government and exacerbates the predicament of grassroots incapacity. This not only traps frontline bureaucrats in administrative burden caused by blame-avoidance strategies, but may also fuel frustration among mobilized citizens with heightened expectations. The findings reveal the institutional sources and constraints of government responsiveness and highlight the potential challenges of operationalizing the mass line to consolidate legitimacy.

title: How digital technologies reshape traditional governance: clan networks and family migration in China
abstract: This study investigates the impact of local clan networks at migration destinations on migrant settlement patterns and the role of digital technologies in this process. The results indicate that destinations with strong clan influence tend to discourage family migration, a finding supported by robustness checks. Moreover, this effect is observed primarily among migrant families who have resided in the destination for more than three years and those located in small- and medium-sized cities. Further analysis of the underlying mechanisms reveals that clan effects operate primarily by shaping social identity. Meanwhile, the diffusion of digital technology weakens the inhibitory effect of local clan networks on family migration, underscoring the moderating role of technological advancement in reshaping the influence of traditional informal institutions on migrant settlement decisions.

title: Mapping Organized Crime as a Stakeholder: A Risk‐Based and Responsive Governance Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Organized crime (OC) can influence firms through coercion, collusion, financial ties, and supply‐chain relationships, yet these interactions remain underexamined in stakeholder theory. This article conceptualizes organized crime as an analytically relevant but non‐normatively legitimate stakeholder and develops a risk‐based framework combining stakeholder salience, interface channel, interest level, and influence strategy. The framework specifies when OC is likely to command managerial attention and which configurations are expected to pose the greatest risks of value destruction and escalation. Three illustrative Italian cases involving preventive anti‐mafia measures show variation from latent relational exposure, through indirect supply‐chain contamination, to embedded ownership and financial control. By linking these configurations to graduated governance responses, the framework helps managers and regulators calibrate proportionate, revisable, and auditable interventions. It extends stakeholder theory to adversarial actors while clarifying institutional conditions that shape the credibility of prevention and remediation.

title: Economic sanctions and income inequality: the Russian experience in the aftermath of the Crimean crisis
abstract: Although the causal effect of economic sanctions on macroeconomic variables has been widely studied, there remains a significant research gap in understanding their causal effect on income inequality in targeted countries. This study aims to fill that gap by examining the sanctions imposed on Russia following its annexation of Crimea and assessing how these sanctions affected income inequality in the country. To this end, we construct a counterfactual scenario using the synthetic difference-in-differences method to estimate Russia's income inequality trajectory in the absence of sanctions. Comparing the actual trajectory of income inequality in Russia after the sanctions with that of synthetic Russia without sanctions, we find that income inequality in Russia declined as a consequence of sanctions. Additionally, we conduct a series of robustness tests and demonstrate that our findings are reliable. Furthermore, we observe that the share of the highest income group fell during the sanction period, while the middle-income group's share in national income rose notably, further strengthening the evidence that sanctions reduced income inequality in Russia.

title: From Policy Reform to Strategic Governance Reconfiguration: Pathways to Sustainable Development in Africa
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable development remains a central objective of public policy. However, governance reforms in Africa have achieved limited results due to fragmented policies, weak institutions, and low adaptive capacity. These challenges are compounded by overlapping governance frameworks operating across continental, regional, and national levels. This study re‐examines governance frameworks and introduces the Sustainable Development Governance Model (SDGM) to align public policy and governance with sustainability goals. Guided by the research question (how can governance frameworks be strategically re‐evaluated to improve public policy effectiveness and sustainable development?), the study employs qualitative content analysis to examine key governance frameworks across policy scales. The findings reveal persistent structural and coordination gaps despite emerging institutional innovations and adaptive governance practices. The analysis shows that incremental reforms are ineffective without coordinated policies, adaptable institutions, and multilevel governance integration. The study contributes to governance and policy studies by offering a framework that moves beyond reform‐oriented approaches. Related Articles Ben Brik, Anis. 2025. “Deconstructing Policy Evaluation in the Global South: Historical, Political, and Transnational Influences.” Politics & Policy 53, no. 5: e70061. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70061 . Villanueva Ulfgard, Rebecka. 2019. “Mexico's Struggle with Development between Global Compromises and National Development Plans.” Politics & Policy 47, no. 1: 50–78. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12288 . Adegboye, Alex, Kofo Adegboye, Uwalomwa Uwuigbe, Stephen Ojeka, and Eyitemi Fasanu. 2023. “Taxation, Democracy, and Inequality in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Relevant Linkages for Sustainable Development Goals.” Politics & Policy 51, no. 4: 696‐722. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12547 .

title: Public support for democracy and different patterns of democratic backsliding
abstract: This paper examines whether public support for democracy helps constrain two common patterns of democratic backsliding: executive aggrandizement and strategic electoral manipulation. Previous studies often rely on aggregate democracy indices, but such measures may mask the specific ways backsliding occurs by collapsing multiple dimensions into a single score. This paper argues that while public support may not improve the overall quality of democracy, it can nonetheless help constrain executive aggrandizement and electoral manipulation. Drawing on panel data covering more than 30 years of public support for democracy across 141 countries, combined with data from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project, we focus on three measures of democratic quality: clean elections and judicial and legislative constraints on executive power. The results show that public support is not significantly associated with the Liberal Democracy Index, but in democracies it is positively associated with electoral integrity and institutional checks on executive power. These findings offer a more nuanced understanding of democratic resilience, showing that while public support may not improve democracy overall, it can still matter for constraining backsliding in targeted institutional domains.

title: Bringing War Back In: victory, defeat, and the state in nineteenth-century Latin America
abstract: It is surely better to win a war than to lose one. But whether it is better in the long run to have avoided a war or fought it depends on its uncertain outcome. In the simplest sense, those are the...

title: Fostering refugee receptivity through perspective taking: Evidence from Thailand
abstract: This paper investigates how perspective taking influences attitudes toward refugees in Thailand, a Global South country affected by Myanmar’s 2021 military coup and ensuing civil unrest. Despite Thailand’s long history of hosting refugees, public support for refugee reception remains underexplored. Drawing on a pre-registered survey experiment, we find that Thai participants who completed a simple perspective-taking exercise—imagining themselves as refugees—expressed significantly greater support for hosting Myanmar refugees and for Thailand signing the UN Refugee Convention. In contrast, treatments emphasizing financial burden-sharing, international reputation, or humanitarian sympathy had no discernible effect. A follow-up survey two months later suggests that the impact of perspective-taking may persist over time. These findings highlight the role of psychological mechanisms such as empathy in shaping attitudes toward refugees and offer insights into the potential for perspective-taking interventions in Southeast Asia and other Global South contexts.

title: Beyond prejudice reduction: Personal and civic effects of intergroup contact among marginalized youth in Northern Ireland
abstract: Abstract Intergroup contact reduces prejudice, but its potential to foster broader personal and societal change remains understudied. We address these gaps by examining a large‐scale peacebuilding intervention (PEACE4Youth) among marginalized youth in post‐conflict Northern Ireland. Using latent growth curve modeling across three waves, we demonstrate that increased intergroup contact is associated with improvements not only in youth's outgroup attitudes but also in their self‐esteem, leadership skills, and civic engagement. Youth with steeper contact gains showed the strongest growth across all domains, supporting intergroup contact as a mechanism for multidimensional change. While effects emerged across Catholic and Protestant youth, baseline differences underscore the role of pre‐existing disparities. These findings extend contact theory by empirically linking contact to personal and societal development, redefining it as a tool not only for harmony but also for empowering individuals to transform divided societies.

title: War propaganda without misinformation? Normative framing and side-taking in war
Gun policy and the steel paradox
Implicit land taxes and their effect on the real economy
Mental Models of the Stock Market
abstract: Abstract Investors’ return expectations are pivotal in stock markets, but the reasoning behind these expectations is not well understood. This paper explores economic agents’ mental models of what drives returns. We survey the general population, retail investors, financial professionals, and academic experts to investigate how they forecast and explain future returns in scenarios with stale news about future company earnings. We find that investors strongly disagree in their forecasts and reasoning. Most academic experts view markets as efficient. By contrast, most households express a perspective we call “expected earnings reasoning”: they directly equate higher expected earnings with higher expected returns. Professionals are split between market efficiency, mispricing, and expected earnings reasoning. In detailed experiments, we dissect why households adopt expected earnings reasoning. We show that it arises from inattention to how stock-price changes affect investor costs — that is, how much investors must pay to acquire a claim to future cash flows — because the typical format and context of investment problems obscure these cost implications. Our results help connect a series of previously documented anomalies in expectation and trading data and highlight the importance of selective attention and context in shaping reasoning and belief formation.

title: The Transmission of Reliable and Unreliable Information
abstract: Abstract Information often spreads and influences beliefs regardless of its reliability. We show that this occurs in part because indicators of reliability tend to be lost in the process of word-of-mouth transmission. We conduct controlled experiments where participants listen to economic forecasts and pass them on through voice messages. Other participants listen either to original or transmitted audio recordings and report incentivized beliefs. Across various transmitter incentive schemes, a claim’s reliability is lost in transmission much more than the claim itself. Reliable and unreliable information, once filtered through transmission, impact listener beliefs similarly. Mechanism experiments show that reliability is lost not because it is perceived as less relevant or harder to transmit, but because it is less likely to come to mind during transmission. Evidence from our experiments, a large corpus of everyday conversations, and economic TV news shows that contextual cues can bring reliability to mind and induce its transmission, but situations in which people share information seldom contain such cues.

title: The Lock-In Effect and the Corporate Payout Puzzle,

title: A small volume reduction that melts down the market: Auctions with endogenous rationing
Cross‐Prudence and Optimal Prevention
abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we study optimal prevention in the presence of a correlated nonfinancial background risk. Under positive correlation, cross‐prudence in the nonfinancial attribute reduces optimal prevention. We establish this result in the most direct extension of the standard prevention problem with binary marginal distributions and show that it extends to richer settings. Our analysis highlights a broader implication: in economically relevant cases with loss probabilities below one‐half and positive correlation, cross‐prudence emerges as an additional force that discourages prevention. As a result, optimal prevention can fall below the expected‐cost minimizing level, even when agents are risk‐averse.

title: Rethinking platform vernaculars: Collective practices and power dynamics in platform environments
abstract: In 2015, Gibbs et al. introduced the concept of platform vernaculars to describe how communicative genres emerge through interactions between platform affordances and user practices. Although widely adopted in media research, the concept has not been systematically refined in light of recent developments in affordance theory and platform studies. Drawing on an integrative literature review, this paper revisits platform vernaculars as plural, recognizable, repeatable, temporarily stabilized, and contested formations emerging through collective negotiations of affordances within platform environments. The paper further introduces four heuristic categories–intended vernaculars, dominant vernaculars, community vernaculars, and counter-public vernaculars–to discuss how communicative norms, genres, and modes of participation become normalized, marginalized, contested, or transformed across platforms. By rethinking platform vernaculars, the paper offers a systematic analytical framework for studying platform practices and norms. Furthermore, it positions vernaculars as a lens for analyzing platform power and user agency, opening avenues for future research.

title: Why does distant suffering matter? Discursive domestication in Chinese mainstream media and social media on the Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum
abstract: This study examines how distant suffering is domesticated across Chinese mainstream media and social media through the case of the Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum. Existing research has largely focused on media representations and audience responses to mediated suffering events, paying less attention to commemorative spaces and users’ digital participation in non-Western contexts. Drawing on critical discourse analysis of mainstream media texts and Xiaohongshu posts, this study identifies three institutional domestication strategies, namely emotional, familiarizing and moral domestication, and shows how social media users re-domesticate commemorative meaning through affective resonance, geopolitical reframing and everyday spatial practices. The findings reveal that social media participation neither simply accepts nor rejects institutional narratives but produces a negotiated field of meaning shaped by platformed affect, contemporary geopolitical imagination and urban spatial consumption. By conceptualizing this process as participatory re-domestication, the article extends the study of distant suffering from media events to commemorative spaces, showing that spatial encounters with distant suffering do not automatically generate cosmopolitan empathy but are filtered through local platform practices and ideological structures.

title: What Shapes Subnational Policy Implementation in the Global South? A 17‐year Study of Implementing India's Forest Rights Act
abstract: ABSTRACT Over the past two decades, global debates among policymakers and conservationist organizations have recognized the existence of Indigenous and local communities' rights to their customary forests. However, emerging forest tenure reforms have been severely criticized by scholars and practitioners for their slow implementation. Moreover, the literature resolving this puzzle and identifying how rights have been recognized is sparse. Responding to this neglect, I study India's federally enacted Forest Rights Act. Using public documents and informal interviews, I analyze subnational action prescriptions to recognize community forest resource rights in India's Maharashtra state for 17 years. Contributing to practice, I show that subnational action prescriptions setting claim recognition targets, providing supporting human resources, and directing field‐level mission‐mode approaches are associated with better titling of customary forests. Contributing to debates on implementation theories, the study finds the key role of bottom‐up theory, arguing that the exercise of subnational discretion aimed at resolving communicated field‐level problems is likely to lead to better implementation.

title: Worthy of trust? AI governance and the role of (dis)trust
journal_name: Perspectives on Public Management and Governance

title: Policy Transfer and Lesson‐Drawing in Online Harms Regulation: From NetzDG to Online Safety
abstract: ABSTRACT Since Germany's passage of the Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG) in 2017, a growing number of countries have introduced online harms legislation requiring internet intermediaries to remove or address harmful or illegal content. Arguments about Germany's influence on other jurisdictions have relied on an undertheorized notion of policy transfer. We use a multiple streams framework to distinguish two mechanisms of policy transfer: emulation and lesson‐drawing. We then examine the policy processes behind online harms legislation in four liberal democracies (Germany, Australia, the United Kingdom, and Canada). Our findings reveal lesson‐drawing as the primary mechanism: cross‐jurisdictional influence shaped how policy problems and solutions were defined, whereas the politics stream was driven by domestic politics. Lesson‐drawing among liberal democracies should be distinguished from a form of emulation by illiberal states that we call policy camouflage . Understanding these mechanisms is critical for evaluating different approaches to online harms and internet regulation more generally. Manica, L., Damásio, B. and Mendonça, S. 2026. “Institutional Legacies and Governance Models: A Comparative Study of Broadband State Aid in Europe.” Politics & Policy 53, no. 5: e70069. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70069 .

title: Advancing Major Policy Change Analysis in the Advocacy Coalition Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT The Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF) has been used extensively to study policy processes globally. Existing research, however, fails to sequence the combination of factors that influence policy change. Using theory‐testing process tracing and a within‐case study design focused on Ghana and Nigeria, we address these knowledge gaps by answering the research question: How does the interaction between external and internal shocks, and the sequence of subsystem internal dynamics, lead to major policy change? The data were collected from 40 interviews and over 600 news media articles spanning 30 years. We find that initial triggers comprising the oil discovery in Ghana and regime change in Nigeria influenced dynamic factors, such as coalition formation and policy‐oriented learning, leading to policy change. We propose a tripartite scheme for analyzing policy change: initial triggers (external and internal shocks), sequence of factors (subsystem internal dynamics), and outcome (major policy change). Related Articles Nam, Aerang, & Christopher M. Weible. 2023. “Examining Experts' Discourse in South Korea's Nuclear Power Policy Making: An Advocacy Coalition Framework Approach to Policy Knowledge.” Politics & Policy 51(2): 201–221. 10.1111/polp.12522 . Nwalie, Martin Ike. 2019. “Advocacy Coalition Framework and Policy Changes in a Third‐World Country.” Politics & Policy 47(3): 545–568. 10.1111/polp.12302 . Bandelow, Nils C., Johanna Hornung, & Sofie Klingner. 2025. “A Multidimensional Operationalization of Policy Change.” Politics & Policy 53(5): e70073. 10.1111/polp.70073 .

title: Are AI Issues Wicked?
Confidently Wrong: Benefit Overuse Beliefs and Deservingness Among Adolescents
abstract: ABSTRACT Previous research shows that adults overestimate benefit overuse and that such misperceptions are associated with lower perceived deservingness, a crucial dimension through which welfare attitudes relate to broader welfare state legitimacy. Yet, the origins and malleability of benefit overuse beliefs remain poorly understood. This study addresses this gap by using original survey data from 1527 Swiss secondary school students (ages 13–18) and a follow‐up survey experiment pilot ( N = 130). We first demonstrate that adolescents severely overestimate unemployment benefit overuse: more than 60% believe that overuse is at least ten times higher than the most recent government‐issued rate of approximately 1% in Switzerland. Moreover, over one‐third are misinformed, holding incorrect beliefs with confidence. Notably, male and right‐leaning students are more likely to be misinformed than female and centre/left‐leaning students, but for different reasons: male students tend to be confident whether right or wrong, while right‐leaning students are more confident mainly when wrong, suggesting early traces of motivated reasoning. Crucially, it is the misinformed, not the uninformed, who perceive the unemployed as less deserving. However, the results of the experimental pilot study show that false beliefs are malleable. Providing students with proportional information about benefit overuse substantially improves accuracy and reduces the share of misinformed participants. Moreover, changes in overuse beliefs partly show in the higher perceived deservingness of the unemployed. Overall, the findings demonstrate that welfare misconceptions are widespread but not fixed among adolescents, suggesting that the impressionable years are an important window for investigating the informational foundations of welfare attitudes.

title: Street-Level Discretion in the Implementation of Healthcare and Immigration Policies for Migrants in Johannesburg, South Africa
abstract: The paper examined how street-level bureaucrats (SLBs) interpreted and exercised discretion when implementing healthcare and immigration policies affecting migrants in the City of Johannesburg (CoJ), Gauteng, South Africa. Drawing on interviews with 30 frontline workers and guided by Street-Level Bureaucracy theory and the 7-C policy implementation model, the paper identified a persistent disconnect between progressive legal provisions and frontline practice. While most SLBs understood core health policies, limited knowledge of migration legislation, conflicting policy prescripts, and resource constraints shaped highly variable decision-making. Discretion produced mixed outcomes: some frontline workers used flexibility to facilitate access for vulnerable migrants, while others engaged in discriminatory practices, including overcharging, delayed treatment, and refusal of care. Analysis through the 7-C framework showed that context, capacity, communication, and coordination most consistently shaped discretionary decision-making. Implementation challenges stemmed from policy ambiguity, weak oversight, socio-political pressures, and uneven institutional support, pointing to the need for clearer policy guidance, targeted training, and stronger intergovernmental coordination.

title: Institutional Resilience in South Asia: The Role of Governance, Preparedness, and Accountability
abstract: Governments in South Asia remain vulnerable to recurrent shocks, exposing institutional, fiscal, and demographic weaknesses. This study develops an accounting-oriented framework to assess resilience across eight countries using a Composite Resilience Index (CRI) and advanced econometric techniques, including fixed-effects, 2SLS, and Structural Equation Modeling. Results show governance capacity, crisis preparedness, digital government, and performance auditing as the strongest driver of resilience, while health and emergency expenditure also contribute positively. Demographic pressures, however, significantly erode resilience and weaken other investments. Findings underscore the need for stronger accountability, strategic fiscal planning, and institutionalized resilience accounting to enhance adaptive capacity. JEL Codes : C38; H11; H61; H83; O20

title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place: Social Policy and Political Regime Change in Central America
abstract: ABSTRACT Does democracy deliver more inclusive and transparent social policy in low‐capacity states? And how does democratic backsliding reshape social policy? Drawing on a comparative analysis of El Salvador, Guatemala and Nicaragua, we examine how regime change and political ideology are associated with patterns of social policy access and transparency since the 1990s. We show that while both democratic and authoritarian governments expanded social spending modestly, democratic periods were consistently associated with greater transparency and public accountability. By contrast, democratic backsliding eroded access to information mechanisms and increased the opacity and politicisation of social programs, even when spending levels were maintained. These findings suggest that in weak states, the most significant contribution of democracy to social policy may lie less in spending and access expansion than in sustaining transparency and oversight.

title: Beyond the ideal type: Investigating ‘mixed preferences’ for who should govern in nine European countries
abstract: Abstract Noting widespread disenchantment with representative actors and institutions, a growing field of research has investigated public support for decision-making by alternative actors, such as ordinary citizens and independent experts. However, previous research has mainly focused on ideal-type models of government centred on a single actor, rather than considering that citizens may hold ‘mixed preferences’ for multiple actors. Through a latent profile analysis of survey responses to an established battery measuring preferences for who should govern, we identify six preference types that exist across nine European countries, though their prevalence varies from country to country. The results show that only a small minority of respondents support an ideal-type model, i.e., the representative democrats, while most favour a combination of actors. A sizeable share of respondents continues to support politicians but would like to see greater involvement from either citizens or experts. Finally, we identify three profiles that lack strong theoretical or empirical grounding in previous research but emerge across multiple countries and therefore merit further attention: stealth populists, responsible democrats, and moderates.

title: “Nothing else matters?” Salience differences between young and old
abstract: Abstract Younger generations’ attitudes and behavior increasingly diverge from those of older individuals. To better understand these political differences, it is relevant to analyze whether younger citizens also disagree about “what matters” in politics. However, this assumption of younger voters’ different salience perceptions has rarely been tested for a large range of issues. Thus, this paper argues that younger and older citizens differ in issue salience and specifically suggests that younger generations perceive cultural issues as more salient. To test this, I use novel survey data collected in Germany ( N = 2,509) and Switzerland ( N = 2,494) and apply rating tasks and a pairwise choice experiment, looking at young and older respondents’ salience regarding six political issue areas and a selection of 42 political issues derived from widely used voting advice applications in the respective countries. The results show that issues related to gender equality and certain age-related socioeconomic policies, such as rent prices, are more salient for younger than older respondents, whereas immigration is more important for older generations. This points to both value change and self-interest that divides salience assessments. Overall, these findings can help understand diverging political perceptions and the resulting electoral differences between younger and older generations.

title: The politics of self-imposed term limits
abstract: This article considers how "self-imposed term limits," voluntary pledges by candidates for elected office to step down at the end of their term if elected or reelected, can arise endogenously within a formal model of electoral accountability. To this end, I extend a standard two-period political agency model with adverse selection by appending an election campaign during which two candidates compete with the option to commit not to seek reelection. I show that term limit pledges can emerge in equilibrium without commitment power, revealing their relationship with informative cheap talk. The subsequent analysis considers scenarios where commitment power is necessary for upholding term limit pledges. In these cases, self-imposed term limits allow strong candidates to signal their private type to voters, giving them an electoral advantage over those seeking reelection. However, these candidates' appeal comes not from the informational content of their pledges but from their ability to make policy decisions free from career considerations. I characterize the equilibria of a model specification in which politicians have differing policy preferences, identifying conditions under which term limit pledges are simultaneously informative and improve voter welfare.

title: Controlling for Oversight in Studies of Oversight
abstract: ABSTRACT In honor of the creation of the Congressional Oversight Research Database (CORD), we explore some of the selection effects that observable measures of oversight may be subject to. We present a model in which Congress endogenously chooses whether to hold a hearing or to preempt the need for one by overturning an agency's policy in advance. These endogenous oversight choices imply that observable outcomes arise through two pathways: Congress may overturn a policy immediately or only after acquiring additional information through a hearing. Failing to account for this information‐gathering stage can obscure the underlying mechanisms that drive these outcomes. Using data from ProQuest and CORD, we test two implications of the model, finding evidence that Congress selects into conducting oversight hearings and implementing subsequent policy reversals more often when in opposition to the President, with no impact of the information gathered during a hearing on subsequent policy reversals. This implies that Congress uses committee hearings primarily as a mechanism for sharing information about the executive branch when it is politically convenient, rather than as a mechanism for gathering information on policy alternatives. We then conclude with broader implications for empirical research on oversight, including the importance of distinguishing between information gathering and information sharing in oversight.

title: Refuturing in the ruins: Higher education after resilience targeting
Probabilistic spaces: Terrains of resilience targeting in an age of generative AI
Joyful education: Care-fully resisting resilience targeting
Digital marronage in the neoliberal university: Building a liberatory stack
Resilience targeting and the war on pluralist democracy
Between markets and regimes: Minority urban entrepreneurs' political voice in gentrifying neighborhoods across diverse political-geographic contexts
abstract: Studies on ethnic entrepreneurship and political agency often highlight how minority business owners leverage commercial spaces for cultural visibility and political voice. However, the mechanisms transforming these spaces into sites of representation remain under-theorized. This study challenges the liberal-democratic normativity in Global North scholarship, which normalizes political voice as a desirable and viable branding choice. Instead, I introduce the concept of Situated Entrepreneurial Activism to argue that entrepreneurial agency is geopolitically contingent, where the regime dictates whether politicization functions as a marketable asset or a financial liability. Using commercial gentrification as a critical backdrop, positioning ethnic entrepreneurs at the intersection of competing class and ethnic interests, I analyze how different political environments shape this agency. Through a Critical Juxtaposition of Latino entrepreneurs in the US (Barrio Logan) and Arab entrepreneurs in Israel (Old Acre), the research reveals two distinct patterns: In the liberal-democratic context of California’s Barrio Logan, notwithstanding its structural challenges and rising political polarization, diversity functions as a market asset; consequently, Latino entrepreneurs engage in Cooperative and Separatist Entrepreneurial Activism, transforming political slogans into 'consumer products.' Conversely, in Israel’s ethnocratic and conflict-driven setting, Arab entrepreneurs perceive politicization as a liability, prioritizing class identity or adopting Covert Entrepreneurial Activism. This pragmatic "Resistance through Presence" prioritizes asset preservation and physical rootedness over overt politicization. By framing commercial spaces as geopolitical indicators, this study shows how regime type and political tolerance shapes the shifting value of minority entrepreneurial activism.

title: More than a partisan pandemic: Worldview and COVID ‐19 response in the United States
Measuring affective polarization: Matching concepts to measures
Procedural Change in the Danish Parliament, 1850–2025
abstract: ABSTRACT There is much recent interest in the politics of procedural change in European legislatures. In this article, we advance existing research by examining the evolution of legislative procedures in the Danish parliament. Our contribution is threefold. First, we introduce a novel, complete and machine‐readable dataset of all rules of procedure of the Folketing between 1850 and 2025, creating a free resource for scholars of parliamentary politics. Second, we use the new data to explore patterns of procedural change in the Folketing, revealing a sharp increase in parliamentary regulation alongside elements of continuity. Third, we provide two illustrative applications of our data: revisiting the measurement of agenda‐setting powers in the Folketing and examining the impact of constitutional revisions on the dynamics of procedural change. Taken together, our data and analysis deepen understanding of legislative developments in Denmark and beyond.

title: Correction to: A Further Augmentation of the Solow Model and the Empirics of Economic Growth for OECD Countries
Kinky Europe: Evidence from the regional Phillips curve in the euro area
Political Accountability During Crises: Evidence From 40 Years of Financial Policies
abstract: ABSTRACT We show that politicians facing a binding term limit are more likely to engage in financial deliberalization than those facing reelection, but only in the wake of a financial crisis. In particular, they implement policies that tend to favor incumbent financial institutions over the general population, such as increasing barriers to entry in the banking sector. We propose a conceptual framework and several mechanisms to rationalize this behavior and show that revolving doors between the government and the financial sector play a key role in encouraging bank‐friendly policies after crises.

title: Sex and the City: Demographics, Spatial Sorting, and the Marriage Market
abstract: ABSTRACT We study how the interaction between demographic changes and spatial sorting affects marriage matching across space. Using data from China, we first present stylized facts on the diverging spatial distribution of singlehood characterized by a high singles rate for females (males) in more (less) developed cities. We then build a quantitative spatial equilibrium model. It reveals that more highly educated women sort into the service sector in more developed cities than men. With persistent social norms of hypergamy, this results in more failed marriage matches for females (males) in more (less) developed cities, thereby lowering the national marriage rate.

title: Agentic Loafing: An AI Decision Delegation Risk
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly making decisions in healthcare, not just supporting them. This research introduces "agentic loafing" to describe the intentional yet unexamined delegation of decision-making authority from clinicians to AI systems. Using netnography of professional podcasts and secondary analysis of gray literature, this study uncovers three institutional drivers that normalize AI delegation: performance culture conformity, structural isolation of responsibility, and legitimization through quantification. These drivers invert classical delegation theory. Where traditional delegation assumes monitoring, punishment, and shared objectives, AI delegation thrives in their absence. This inversion produces what this research terms "risk evaporation": the systematic disappearance of accountability when AI-assisted decisions fail, leaving no single party responsible. To help organizations manage this risk, this research also develops a "preliminary" diagnostic tool, with its intersectional interventions, that transforms "agentic loafing" from an unmanaged bet into a measurable risk score. From this, a critical implication follows for risk analysis: the most dangerous AI systems are not those that fail unpredictably but those that function just reliably enough to quietly erode human judgment without ever triggering an alarm.

title: The Impact of Strategic Leaders’ International Experience on Organizations: An Integrative Review and Multilevel Framework
abstract: Internationally experienced business leaders bring distinct human capital, social capital, and cognitive schemas into organizations, influence strategic orientation through their decision-making, and in turn shape organizations’ strategies and performance. The impact of the international experience (IE) of an organization’s upper echelon has been studied in various bodies of management literature, varying in terms of the theoretical perspectives, conceptualizations of the IE construct, and outcomes considered. However, the effects are not straightforward with regard to which elements of IE affect which aspects of organizational dynamics, and how. This review integrates separate streams of organizational research to develop a more holistic understanding of the role of the IE held by strategic leaders such as chief executive officers, entrepreneurial founders, top management teams, and boards of directors, and its impact on organizational strategies and performance. We refine the conceptualization of the IE construct at multiple levels of analysis and explore cross-level mechanisms suggested by multiple theories to develop an integrative framework that links strategic leaders’ IE to organizational decisions, strategies, and performance. On this basis, we propose an agenda for future research.

title: Care Under Strain: Caregiver Mental Health and Early Childhood Development in Rural China
abstract: Drawing on quantitative and qualitative data collected in 2024 and 2025 in a relatively well-off rural area of China, this study examines the mental health of primary caregivers of young children and its correlates. The quantitative data show high prevalence of cognitive (40%), language (42%), and motor (20%) developmental delays among the children. Caregiver mental health problems may be one possible contributing factor given that approximately 17% of caregivers exhibit at least one mental health issue (i.e. stress, anxiety, or depression). The qualitative analysis identifies several risk factors of caregiver mental health problems: limited awareness of mental health concepts; heavy burden of caregiving; insufficient public services; and a lack of awareness of caregiver mental health’s impact on child development.

title: The Family We Created: The Sense of Family Among Chinese Co-Living Youth
abstract: This article, based on ethnographic fieldwork conducted in two co-living houses in Shanghai, examines the sense of familial belonging among young Chinese adults residing in co-living arrangements. These youth frequently conceptualize their co-living environments as familial units, designating their roommates as family members ( jiaren 家人). Co-living, characterized by collective funding of communal goods, close interpersonal relationships, and egalitarian decision-making, aligns with the idealized familial values held by contemporary youth. However, this shared sense of family coexists with divergent and occasionally conflicting perspectives on family-related matters. This paradox highlights evolving conceptualizations of family that prioritize affective and supportive ties while deemphasizing blood relations and marital obligations. These shifting perceptions are shaped by the rise of neo-familism, state-endorsed family values, and processes of individualization. Consequently, co-living youth are expanding their understanding of family beyond kinship-based structures to include peer networks, signaling potential transformations to conventional conceptions of family among younger generations.

title: Linking Decision Roles to Knowledge Utilization in US State Governments: A Mixed‐Method Study
abstract: ABSTRACT The current movement for evidence‐based policymaking advocates the use of scientific knowledge in government. However, in practice, civil servants often prioritize different types of knowledge depending on their decision‐making roles and the context. Using survey responses from 259 civil servants across three US state governments and 36 semistructured interviews, we employ a mixed‐method approach to understand how civil servants strategically utilize various types of knowledge to meet different role requirements and decision‐making responsibilities. Consistent with our hypotheses, our findings indicate that civil servants involved in policy and legislative roles value political knowledge more, while those in contracting roles place greater importance on experiential knowledge. Contrary to our hypothesis, while civil servants in budgeting roles value political knowledge more than their counterparts in other decision roles, they show no such preference for scientific knowledge. Our qualitative interviews provide possible mechanisms for this unexpected finding.

title: The Supply of Collaboration Assets During co-Response to Overlapping and Concurrent Community Problems
abstract: Communities increasingly face complex problems that demand coordinated public responses. While collaboration has been an operational mainstay of local governments for several decades, attention to how communities approach and manage multiple demands from the same set of resources has been underexamined. This study examines ten communities navigating the opioid crisis and the onset of COVID-19 in early 2020. Using two waves of survey data, we assess the evolution of collaborative capacity and explore how pandemic response efforts interacted with existing opioid initiatives. Findings reveal that communities mobilized existing collaborative assets without degrading prior efforts. Notably, these assets were predominantly intangible—such as trust, norms, and shared understanding—rather than material resources. This distinction is critical for understanding resilience in public systems. We apply a common pool resource framing to conceptualize the supply and deployment of collaborative assets across concurrent challenges, offering insights into sustaining effective governance under pressure.

title: It's A Matter of Perspective: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Civil Servants’ Appraisal and Coping with Negative Civil Servant Stereotypes
abstract: Negative civil servant stereotypes are often described as problematic in public administration research. In this study, we investigate municipal employees’ own ideas on whether and how these stereotypes form a problem for public sector work and public services. Using semi-structured interviewing and reflexive thematic analysis and building on psychological literature on appraisal and coping with stereotypes, we identify two themes. First, respondents use different perspectives to understand and explain the stereotypes: They view stereotypes as (1) undeserved and untrue, (2) inevitable and part of the work, (3) understandable misunderstandings, and/or (4) reflections of truth. While these external attributions help respondents cope with the negative stereotypes, they also come with blind spots that could affect their work. Second, respondents think the stereotypes have a bigger impact on the citizen-government relationship, trust, and citizen-state interactions than on civil servants themselves. We discuss the implications for service delivery in the public sector and directions for future research.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: The Plurinational State in the Chilean constitutional process: an analysis of discursive positions
abstract: The plurinational state (PS) became one of the most contested elements in Chile’s 2022 constitutional proposal, despite being framed by its proponents as a project of recognition, coexistence, and historical repair. We examined how Indigenous demands were translated, reframed, and contested as the PS entered formal constitutional politics. Drawing on Situational Analysis, we analyzed the discourses regarding the PS during the constitutional process. We used a positional map framed on two larger axes of concern: whether the PS was understood as consistent with the diversity of Chilean society, and the extent to which it was perceived as producing social unsettledness. The PS was simultaneously constituted as historical repair, unfair privilege, legal and social threat, and elite political imposition. We also focused on a meaningful discursive silence regarding how Indigenous communities themselves envisioned the PS. The article provides a contemporary analysis of how discourse shaped the intelligibility of constitutional change, Indigenous rights, and political legitimacy during Chile’s constitutional process.

title: “Hard” and “soft” signals: Bounded rationality and weighing performance versus compliance in multi-level governance
abstract: Principal-agent models often simplify how principals integrate heterogeneous signals from multiple subnational agents. We theorize that, under information overload, hard performance signals may condition the relevance of softer rhetorical alignment signals. Using a panel of annual Government Work Reports from 267 Chinese prefecture-level cities, linked to subsequent earmarked transfers over the 2005–2009 study window, we compare a simple additive account with the observable implications of a lexicographical heuristic. Textual policy compliance has no independent association with transfer allocation. In continuous interaction models, however, its association with transfers becomes positive within empirically favourable regions of economic vitality and social stability. This conditional pattern is consistent with the proposed informational hierarchy, although percentile-based dichotomizations are sensitive to the selected cut-off and do not identify a unique institutional threshold or a literal two-stage decision process. The findings extend bounded-rationality perspectives on multi-signal evaluation in China’s province – prefecture setting.

title: Designing a teaching-oriented policy in a research-centric system: procedural bypass and institutional mimicry in Taiwan’s higher education
abstract: This study examines the formation of Taiwan’s Teaching Practice Research Programme (TPRP), a national policy instrument designed across 2017 and 2018 to institutionalize the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) within a higher education system strongly oriented towards research. Drawing on an extended multiple streams analysis and a process-tracing study of nine elite interviews, it asks how a teaching-oriented instrument was designed, legitimated, and consolidated in an environment structurally unfavourable to it. The analysis finds that the TPRP was not the product of a fortuitous policy window but the outcome of deliberate design work by a reform coalition. The coalition layered a new funding channel alongside the established one, routing grants directly to individual academics, and modelled the new instrument on the national research-grant system in order to borrow its academic legitimacy. The study’s contribution is empirical: it shows how mechanisms of institutional layering, mimetic isomorphism, and policy feedback were consciously combined in the work of policy design, and it identifies the procedural and instrument-design strategies through which a teaching-oriented reform secured an institutional foothold. The case also illustrates the limits of such a strategy, since borrowing the legitimacy of research may leave the underlying prestige hierarchy intact.

title: Rolling out the red carpet but finding no guests: administrative burden and settlement intentions in talent housing policy
abstract: Amidst intensifying inter-city competition for human capital, talent housing policies serve as essential tools for local governments to attract talent. However, procedural burdens during the implementation phase of talent housing policies often undermine their appeal. Drawing on administrative burden theory, this paper employs a mixed-methods design that combines a 2 × 2 between-subjects survey experiment with semi-structured interviews to examine how administrative burdens within talent housing policies affect talent settlement intentions and to further explore the underlying mechanisms. The results indicate that high learning and compliance costs both significantly reduce settlement intentions, with compliance costs exerting a stronger negative effect. A significant interaction exists between the two dimensions, as high compliance costs amplify the negative impact of high learning costs, creating a non-linear cumulative burden. Procedural satisfaction partially mediates the relationship between administrative burdens and settlement intentions. Subsequent qualitative interviews provide process-oriented evidence for these findings and reveal the sources and potential consequences of psychological costs. This paper offers practical implications for optimizing policy implementation and demonstrates the strategic value of reducing administrative burdens to gain a competitive edge in talent acquisition across East Asia and the Global South.

title: Digital Futures Between Participatory Digital Democracy and Participatory Digital Fascism
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper explores one of the defining political questions of the twenty‐first century: will digital technologies strengthen democracy or accelerate new forms of authoritarianism and fascism? Against the backdrop of platform capitalism, AI‐driven communication, surveillance infrastructures, disinformation and democratic crisis, the study asks how experts in digital democracy assess the present condition and possible futures of digital society. To address this question, the paper draws on the Futures of Digital Democracy Survey (FDDS), a two‐round international expert survey involving researchers, practitioners and civil society actors working in the fields of digital democracy, media, Internet governance and digital society. Combining futures research, scenario analysis, and qualitative and quantitative content analysis, the study investigates competing trajectories of digital development ranging from participatory digital democracy to corporate and state‐controlled digital fascism. The findings reveal a profound tension at the heart of contemporary digital society: while respondents overwhelmingly imagine an ideal future democracy in participatory and deliberative terms—centred on citizens’ assemblies, digital participation, public‐service Internet platforms and democratic AI—they simultaneously express deep pessimism about the actual direction of digital capitalism and platform power. Experts consider authoritarian and fascistic digital futures significantly more likely than democratic ones. The paper analyses these contradictions by examining the relationship between deliberative democracy, constitutional rights, platform governance, digital commons, public service media, AI, surveillance and the political economy of Big Tech. It argues that democracy in the digital age can only survive if participatory and deliberative digital structures are institutionally combined with constitutional safeguards, public ownership, democratic regulation and the defence of human rights. By bringing together debates on digital democracy, authoritarianism, political economy and digital futures, the paper offers both a critical diagnosis of the contemporary digital condition and a normative vision of democratic alternatives in the age of AI and platform capitalism.

title: How experience moderates the impact of AI suggestions on researchers' perceptions of their ideas
abstract: At the heart of scientific discovery are researchers who identify ideas worthy of inquiry. In performing research tasks, researchers increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. While this technology offers the promise of increased efficiency across the research process, little is known about how generative AI assists researchers with the generation of initial research ideas—one of the most fundamental tasks in science—and their willingness to adopt it for such purpose. In a pre-registered randomized online experiment with 310 researchers and a follow-up ideation study with 28 researchers, we show how one's research experience plays a role in receiving generative AI suggestions when formulating new research ideas. Experience negatively moderates both the incorporation of generative AI suggestions as well as its effect on perceived novelty and impact of the researcher's idea. We also find that generative AI may be reshaping research ideation by adding a layer of non-human exchange that precedes feedback from human experts. By focusing on the critical moment at which research ideas spark, we provide an initial understanding of how researchers respond to generative AI at a time when the paradigm of human knowledge production may be shifting from a human-only to a joint human-AI model.

title: Beyond institutional age and size: what drives innovation-related performance in Brazilian Federal Universities
The overhead paradox: full-cost recovery and the competitiveness of university–industry research collaboration
Still Instrumentally Inclusive
abstract: Do individuals in Western democracies shift their views on LGBT+ inclusion when exposed to opposition from Muslim out-groups? And is this “homonationalist” responsiveness stronger among anti-immigration individuals? Our article “Instrumentally inclusive […]” addressed these questions using representative data from Britain (Study 1) and crowd-sourced data from Spain (Study 2). We revisit Study 2 in response to concerns about post-stratification weighting a convenience sample and erroneously inconsistent use of robust standard errors. Varying population reference parameters, weight caps, variance estimators, subgroup definitions, and covariate adjustments, we find strong support for the original findings. Neither reasonable alternative weighting schemes nor corrected variance estimators substantively change the results. In fact, the originally published point estimates are equal to or smaller than the median across alternative specifications. Consistent with the Article, we find that treatment increases support for LGBT+ inclusion in Spain, without consistent identifiable variation by immigration attitudes.

title: Bonding, bridging, & bypassing: understanding ethnic politics in diverse societies
