title: Bold Claims, Low Wages: Why Voluntary Sustainability Standards ( VSS ) Struggle to Implement Living Wages
abstract: ABSTRACT Voluntary sustainability standards (VSS)—such as Fairtrade International and the Forest Stewardship Council—aim to improve sustainability in global supply chains by setting high social and environmental standards and certifying businesses that adopt them. This article examines why some VSS adopt ambitious goals for living wages or living incomes yet continue to certify businesses that only pay a minimum wage. Drawing on previous literature, it offers a typology of five ways that VSS can decouple. Drawing on documents, interviews, and participant observation, it offers detailed case studies of how five VSS have engaged in the coupling and decoupling of wage standards. The research identifies four drivers of decoupling: priorities that complete, costs of coupling, low risk of decoupling, and anticipation that coupling will be easier in the future. It also describes several factors that influence these drivers. Finally, it shows how decoupling may paradoxically facilitate progress, while pressure to fully couple may inhibit transformative change, and concludes with recommendations for avoiding empty claims while harnessing aspirational standards.

title: Public trust and crisis governance: evidence from rural Thailand during COVID-19
abstract: This study reconceptualizes public satisfaction during the COVID-19 pandemic as a governance signal rather than a performance metric. Using household-level data from 2,135 rural households in three provinces of Thailand drawn from the TVSEP Covid-19 Special Survey 2020/21, the analysis examines satisfaction with the national government, provincial government, and overall life through a descriptive and associative approach within an interpretive, non-causal design. The findings show consistently higher reported satisfaction with provincial than national government, despite widespread income decline. Economic disruption is associated with satisfaction in ways that appear to depend on how governance is perceived and interpreted, rather than through material hardship alone. These findings underscore the importance of multi-level and place-based governance in shaping public evaluations during crises and position public satisfaction as an observable indicator through which broader judgements about trust and legitimacy may be interpreted, rather than as a simple measure of policy approval. The interpretive significance of multi-level governance lies in showing how national authority and provincial proximity jointly structure citizens’ evaluations of institutional responsiveness, trust, and legitimacy during crisis conditions.

title: Tinkering at the margins? Korea’s reform strategies to close the gap between labour market insiders and outsiders
abstract: Over a relatively short period, Korea has developed a comprehensive welfare state centred on eight social insurance schemes. However, its heavy reliance on contributory social insurance has become increasingly inadequate for protecting atypical and non-regular workers, an expanding segment of the labour market. This article argues that recent reforms have largely expanded protection through institutional layering while leaving the structural limitations of Korea’s contribution-based welfare intact. Drawing on recent policy developments and labour market trends, it shows how contribution-dependent eligibility rules and insufficiently coordinated non-contributory programmes can reinforce labour market dualization. The article proposes reforms that adapt contributory institutions to fragmented employment by broadening contribution arrangements, revising eligibility rules, and ensuring that minimum protection complements rather than competes with social insurance. The Korean case demonstrates that sustainable welfare reform requires modernizing contributory systems so they remain inclusive, equitable, and compatible with increasingly diverse employment patterns.

title: From procedural reforms to structural gaps: a qualitative legislative analysis of eviction laws in Maryland
abstract: Abstract Advanced welfare states have come to consider housing displacement and eviction among their most pressing policy concerns; this is especially true since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. In the United States, state governments have enacted new protections for renters with the aim of protecting rental markets from destabilisation and reducing displacement. This article provides a qualitative legislative analysis of Maryland’s eviction-related legislation passed from 2020 to 2024, using more than twenty-five legislative documents, hearing transcripts and stakeholder testimonies to conduct the analysis. In doing so, we employed racial capitalism and slow violence as analytical frameworks to explore how legislation that is technically race-neutral may recreate ongoing structural inequities, specifically for Black women and low-income renters. The analysis shows that although legislative measures in Maryland, such as HB 18 and HB 200, improve procedural protections, they fail to disrupt ongoing dynamics of racialised housing precarity. This analysis contends that procedural justice alone, without material redistribution or enforcement, does not necessarily change the racial inequalities we seek to address but instead runs the risk of reproducing them. This paper illustrates the implications of technocratic eviction laws and distinguishes the significance of differentiating between procedural reform and structural change in housing policies.

title: The crowding in effect: how technical assistance expands advisory systems and builds policy capacity
abstract: This article examines how the expansion of policy advisory systems (PAS) affects governments’ analytical policy capacity in developing countries. More specifically, it explores whether European Union (EU)-funded technical assistance “hollows out” or “crowds in” analytical capacity in Turkey, a country that experienced rapid PAS expansion through the EU’s Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance (IPA). This question is significant because the evidence on PAS externalization effects remains concentrated in Western democracies, leaving the consequences for developing and middle-income countries underexplored. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with civil servants, international organization experts, and consultants, alongside legislative and programming documents, the article demonstrates that EU-IPA technical assistance produced a crowding-in effect across individual, organizational, and systemic levels of analytical capacity in combating child labor in seasonal agriculture. Individual-level gains were the most pronounced. Civil servants evolved from having weak domain-specific knowledge to possessing autonomous analytical competence, while organizational information systems and a broader knowledge ecosystem expanded substantially. Risks stem from the external origin of demand for rigorous analysis, over-corporatization of training, and declining meritocratic recruitment standards. We recommend domestic policymakers to prioritize institutionalizing capacity gains within organizational structures and international organizations to calibrate programming by taking risks into account.

title: The Evolution of UAE's Africa Foreign Policy: Motivations, Strategies and Challenges
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent studies on the foreign policies of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries attribute their increasing involvement in Africa to security and economic considerations. However, only a few studies have investigated the foreign policies of the individual GCC countries in more detail for confirmation. Hence, using a neorealist perspective on small states, this article enriches this debate by examining the United Arab Emirates' (UAE) foreign policy in Africa. This task is accomplished via a qualitative case study design to analyze the UAE's transition from its limited humanitarian approach in Africa to a holistic involvement encompassing diplomatic, economic, and security engagement. The UAE's foreign policy in the Horn of Africa and West Africa is analyzed to show how the country has used its power to achieve influence despite its small state status. The findings suggest that the UAE's approach embodies neorealist principles of small‐state behavior with structural limitations in the international system. Related Articles Kinyondo, A. Salim Al Jaberi. 2022. “The Post‐Oil Strategy of the UAE: An Examination of Diversification Strategies and Challenges.” Politics & Policy 50, no. 2: 380–407. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12457 . title: Preferences or principles? The ‘noncompliance penalty’ and the limits of public support for the rule of law
abstract: Abstract When will individuals support government noncompliance with the written law? A bedrock principle of the rule of law is that politicians who fail to comply with written law will face political consequences. Drawing on survey experiments fielded in two consolidated democracies, we introduce the noncompliance penalty , the loss of public support for a government action that contravenes the law. The results show that citizens do penalize governmental noncompliance with the law. However, we find that this penalty decreases if government noncompliance advances the policy interests of favored protest groups, and mixed evidence that this penalty increases with professed support for the rule of law. Perhaps surprisingly, our results suggest that citizens with the strongest commitment to the rule of law can become the most accepting of noncompliance if it advances their policy goals. These findings have important implications for understanding whether the public will punish politicians who disregard the formal letter of the law.

title: Online gendered violence and visibility in electoral autocracies: Evidence from multi-level elections in Türkiye
abstract: Abstract Online platforms have become indispensable tools for political candidates to gain visibility, particularly for female candidates in electoral autocracies who often lack access to traditional networks, party hierarchies, and media platforms. We argue that online visibility, while a resource for female candidates, disproportionately exposes them to online violence that functions as a mechanism of political control, reinforcing patriarchal exclusion from the political sphere. Our analysis draws on more than three million tweets directed at 1,834 candidates across the 2023 parliamentary and 2024 local election campaigns in Türkiye, providing a rare opportunity to observe how these dynamics unfold at both the national and subnational levels. We find that while online visibility increases abuse for all candidates, the effect is markedly stronger for female candidates, who are disproportionately targeted across diverse forms of violence, including profanity, demeaning and ridiculing language, physical threats, and ethnic and religious hate speech. Moreover, our results suggest that in local elections, where candidates rely more heavily on personalized campaigns, increases in visibility are more strongly associated with female candidates’ exposure to online violence.

title: Who cares about politics under authoritarian rule? Evidence from China
abstract: Abstract Departing from mainstream research on political interest in democratic contexts, this study investigates its evolution in an authoritarian setting. To disentangle temporal dynamics, it applies the age–period–cohort interaction model to repeated cross-sectional data from five waves of nationally representative surveys conducted in China. The results demonstrate distinct effects across age, period, and cohort dimensions. Age effects indicate that younger individuals consistently exhibit lower levels of political interest than older adults. Period effects reveal a downward trend in political interest among the Chinese public between 2002 and 2019. Importantly, cohort effects suggest that, contrary to the linear evolutionary predictions of modernization theory, individuals who underwent political socialization during critical historical periods—such as the Great Famine and its aftermath (1959–1963) and the late Cultural Revolution (1974–1978)—as well as those born in the late 1970s and throughout the 1980s, exhibit heightened political interest. These findings contribute to theoretical reflections on the evolution of political interest.

title: Revolutionizing Time, Reforging Social Orders: State-Building Success and the Enforcement of Symbolic Programs in Revolutionary France
Reproductive Rights, Reframed: Federalism and Vote Choice in the 2024 Election
abstract: ABSTRACT The overturning of Roe v. Wade sent shockwaves through the American political system. Running on women’s reproductive health care rights, Democrats vastly outperformed expectations in the 2022 midterm elections. The 2024 US presidential election provided a test of whether broad public support for reproductive health care access would continue to translate into electoral gains for Democrats. Using a novel set of survey questions, this article examines attitudes toward abortion and the abortion pill (i.e., mifepristone) as well as preferences over whether policy should be decided federally or by individual states (i.e., locus of authority). Our findings provide partial support for the expectation that locus-of-authority preferences shape vote choice. Whereas support for a constitutional protection for abortion remained strongly associated with voting against Trump regardless of locus-of-authority preferences, the pattern for mifepristone access more closely matched our expectations. Among voters who supported mifepristone access, those who were comfortable leaving the issue to the states were significantly more likely to support Donald Trump. His emphasis on state control may have functioned as strategic ambiguity, especially on a less-polarized reproductive health issue such as mifepristone access.

title: Democracy for Whom? Herrenvolk Democracy and the American Founding
abstract: ABSTRACT As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence amid democratic erosion, this article asks why 250 years of democratic development have not produced a multiracial democracy. It argues that the United States is a herrenvolk democracy—a regime in which democracy coexists with racialized limits on political membership and governing power. By examining colonial law, the Declaration, the Constitution, and the Naturalization Act of 1790, I show how the founding joined popular sovereignty to racial exclusion in ways that continue to shape struggles over belonging, representation, and coercive power. The legacy of 1776 includes both the Declaration’s democratic promise and a durable model for how democracy can coexist with exclusion.

title: Teaching Election Inversions in the Electoral College: Two Simple Models
abstract: ABSTRACT The Electoral College is an important concept in many undergraduate American politics courses. Although students often understand the basics of the “House-seats-plus-two” rule and the “winner-take-all” system, many struggle to understand election inversions, in which the winner of the popular vote loses the Electoral College vote and therefore loses the presidency. This article presents two models using only foundational arithmetic to explain election inversions, including an example illustrating how a Republican candidate could also win the popular vote but lose the Electoral College vote. A survey of student-learning experiences showed positive results: students found the models accessible and helpful, and they reported greater confidence in the integrity of US presidential elections and in American democracy after working with the materials. These models can be incorporated into a range of American politics courses to help even first-year undergraduate students make sense of the US presidential election system.

title: Trump, the International Criminal Court, and the Future of Global Impunity
abstract: The US has traditionally played a key role in fighting global impunity for atrocity crimes, but the policies of Donald Trump’s administration suggest that a dramatic shift in American priorities may be underway. This article examines America’s commitment to addressing impunity in the context of US relations with the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump presidency, I argue, showcases a curious mix of continuity and change in America’s relationship with one of the world’s most prominent international institutions. In particular, Trump’s general strategic approach to the ICC represents continuity with past American presidents, but the brazenness of the specific tactics Trump has used to oppose the ICC represents a notable change. The reverberations of recent American attacks on the ICC raise implications for the future of global impunity that will be felt in three distinct areas: in the US–ICC relationship, among ICC adversaries, and among ICC allies.

title: Let Them Eat Pie: Addressing Sample Selection in Multiparty Elections
abstract: Abstract Elections are central to the study of politics. When studying parties’ vote shares across districts, scholars are encouraged to use compositional-outcome models in order to test their theories about what factors shape the dynamics of electoral support. Existing compositional modeling approaches incorrectly deal with scenarios in which not all parties compete in every electoral district. Because unobserved factors that affect a party’s decisions to contest a district are likely correlated with its performance in districts where the party fielded candidates, failing to account for partial contestation is likely to result in sample selection bias. Addressing sample selection in a compositional setting is challenging because the outcomes are in log-ratio form, and thus the errors often deviate from normality. To deal with these issues, we introduce a novel maximum likelihood approach which accounts for this type of sample selection and demonstrate through simulations that our method outperforms commonly used solutions, including the conventional Heckman correction. We illustrate the utility of our approach by analyzing the 2017 and 2019 U.K. parliamentary elections in English constituencies.

title: Benefit-based taxation can include substantial redistribution
Optimal Age-based Policies for Pandemics: An Economic Analysis of Covid-19 and Beyond
When It Hurts the Most: Timing of Parental Job Loss and a Child’s Education,
abstract: Abstract We estimate how the timing of parental job loss shapes children’s human capital by exploiting plant closures in Danish administrative data. We match treated children to observably similar untreated peers and difference out age-invariant selection using children whose parents are displaced after school completion. Job loss during infancy (ages 0–1) reduces ninth-grade mathematics achievement by 0.04 standard deviations and raises non-completion by one percentage point. Effects are smaller in later childhood. Treated infants are 1.4 percentage points less likely to enrol in general upper-secondary programs. We find that liquidity-constrained families drive these results, suggesting that transient income shocks create permanent educational scars.

title: Productivity and Entry Regulation in the Service Sector: Evidence from the Universe of Firms in Italy
abstract: Abstract Burdensome entry regulations can hinder productivity growth, particularly in services where competitive pressures are weaker. We construct a novel measure of entry regulation, varying across narrowly defined sectors, and combine it with firm-level data for the universe of Italian firms. Exploiting reforms that generate variation across sectors and over time, we find that deregulation (reductions in red tape) raises productivity. The effect is driven by incumbent firms, with a smaller role for reallocation and selection. Effects are larger in the lower-middle of the productivity distribution and in sectors with higher entry rates and tighter initial regulation.

title: Courts, contracts, and international trade: judicial enforcement and global value chain participation
Minority Protection in Voting Mechanisms – Experimental Evidence
abstract: Under simple majority voting an absolute majority of voters may choose policies that are harmful to minorities. It is the purpose of sub- and super-majority rules to protect legitimate minority interests. We study how voting rules are chosen under the veil of ignorance. In our experiment, individuals choose voting rules for given distributions of gains and losses that can arise from a policy, but before learning their own valuation of the policy. We find that subjects on average adjust the voting rule in line with the skewness of the distribution. As a result, a higher share of the achievable surplus can be extracted with the suggested rules than with exogenously given simple majority voting. While the rule choices are not significantly biased towards underor overprotection of the minority, towards majority voting or towards status-quo preserving rules, they only imperfectly reflect the distributions of benefits and costs.

title: Co-exportation of products by multi-product firms
IDENTIFICATION AND ESTIMATION OF A NONPARAMETRIC TIME-VARYING PANEL DATA MODEL WITH COMPLETELY MISSING REGRESSORS IN SOME PERIODS
abstract: This article considers a nonparametric time-varying panel data model in which the primary regressor of interest is completely missing in some periods. Under standard assumptions, identification results are established for the unknown functions and the distributions of the missing regressor. Specifically, one period of completely observed data suffices to identify the random effects model, whereas two periods are required for the fixed effects model. Following identification, conditional deconvolution kernel estimators are developed, and their convergence rates are derived. Simulation results show that these estimators perform well in small samples, and an empirical exercise demonstrates the relevance and practical potential of the proposed method.

title: MINIMAX REGRET TREATMENT RULES WITH FINITE SAMPLES WHEN A QUANTILE IS THE OBJECT OF INTEREST
abstract: Consider a setup in which a decision maker is informed about the population by a finite sample and, based on that sample, has to decide whether or not to apply a certain treatment. We work out finite sample minimax regret treatment rules under various sampling schemes when potential outcomes are restricted onto the unit interval. In contrast to Stoye (2009, Journal of Econometrics 151, 70–81), where the focus is on the maximization of expected utility, the focus here is instead on a particular quantile of the outcome distribution. We find that in the case where the sample consists of a fixed number of untreated and a fixed number of treated units, any treatment rule is minimax regret optimal. The same is true in the case of random treatment assignment in the sample with any assignment probability and in the case of testing an innovation when the known quantile of the untreated population equals 1/2. However, if the known quantile exceeds 1/2, then never treating is the unique optimal rule, and if it is smaller than 1/2, always treating is optimal. We also consider the case where a covariate is included.

title: Measuring the Stringency of Building Height Regulations
abstract: ABSTRACT This study proposes a novel methodology to measure the stringency of building height regulations. This measure gauges the difference in building heights with and without regulations. The primary challenge is to recover unobserved building heights in the absence of regulations. I develop a dynamic discrete choice model of building height decision‐making by parcel owners and conduct a counterfactual experiment that removes height regulations. An application to residential buildings in central Tokyo presents three findings. Without height restrictions, the number of stories would increase by 2.7%, and housing prices would change by 3.7%. Regulatory stringency is stronger near the central area, while the static model tends to overestimate it.

title: Climate Change and Economic Dynamics: Temperature‐Dependent Shock Propagation
abstract: ABSTRACT The gradual rise in temperatures motivates conceptualizing climate change as a phenomenon shaping the propagation of macroeconomic shocks, rather than as an independent shock. We formalize this in a theoretical model, showing that climate change induces a structural shift by steepening the aggregate supply curve, exacerbating the price effects of demand shocks while dampening the output response. Our empirical evidence is consistent with this prediction: higher temperatures raise the share of inflation variation attributable to demand shocks by up to 10 percentage points, underscoring the role of climate change in intensifying stagflationary dynamics rather than independently driving business cycles.

title: Techies and Firm‐Level Productivity
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the impact of techies—engineers and other technically trained workers—on firm‐level productivity. We first report new facts on techies in the firm using French administrative data. Techies are STEM‐skill intensive and associated with innovation, technology adoption, management, and diffusion within firms. Using structural econometric methods, we estimate the effect of techies on firm‐level Hicks‐neutral productivity in manufacturing and nonmanufacturing. We find that techies raise productivity, and that this effect goes beyond R&D workers, extending to ICT and other techies. In nonmanufacturing firms, the impact operates mostly through ICT and other techies, not R&D workers.

title: Mapping Human–AI Teaming in Risk Analysis: Role Evolution, Thematic Landscape, and Governance Mechanisms From News Media
abstract: Human-artificial intelligence (AI) teams are increasingly embedded in risk analysis, yet news reports repeatedly portray meaningful oversight as fragile when review conditions are poorly designed. This study examines how public discourse has portrayed the roles, failure modes, and governance mechanisms of human-AI teaming in risk analysis. Drawing on 184,282 AI-related Factiva news articles (1956-2025), we use a funnel-shaped mixed-methods design to identify 3571 articles describing human-AI interaction in risk-analytic contexts. Structural topic modeling identifies 20 thematic clusters and their temporal and cross-domain dynamics, whereas LLM-assisted inductive thematic analysis produces five mirror-mapped pairs of failure modes and governance mechanisms: opacity and explainability, bias and auditing, agency erosion and cognitive friction, systemic fragility and oversight and liability, and accountability vacuums and institutional governance. The analysis shows that media discourse often follows an AI-predicts-human-decides paradigm and portrays formal human-in-the-loop requirements as insufficient without deliberate interaction design.

title: Bittersweet Symphony: A Music Theory Approach to Stakeholder Dissonance and Value Creation
abstract: Stakeholder theory emphasizes value creation for diverse stakeholders, yet it offers limited guidance for understanding how value is created when a firm’s and a stakeholder’s values differ. We reconceptualize firm–stakeholder relationships as dynamic processes in which value accumulates through the engagement and resolution of value dissonance. Drawing on tonal harmony from music theory, we develop a framework that treats dissonance not as a defect to be eliminated but as generative pressure for value creation. The framework evaluates value dissonance at the issue level and aggregates tension at the relationship level, enabling systematic assessment of where firms can productively intervene. We then theorize three mechanisms through which firms convert dissonance into value: managerial intervention, structural resolution, and timing. Our central insight is that value emerges from the sequenced movement between tension and release. This dynamic perspective advances stakeholder theory by explaining how value can be created across the full stakeholder portfolio, including relationships that firms might otherwise avoid, suppress, or attempt to force into alignment.

title: Algorithmic muteness: How algorithmic management obstructs platform content operators’ resonance with their labor
abstract: Workers who plan, curate, and promote content fuel platforms’ traffic success, yet frequently experience their labor as leaving no meaningful trace. While critical scholarship links this estrangement to algorithmic management, how it reshapes the quality of workers’ relationship with their own labor remains underexplored. Drawing on Rosa’s Resonance Theory and 27 interviews with platform content operators at China’s leading internet companies, this study reveals how algorithmic management obstructs resonance across content production, distribution, and feedback. Quantification hollows out labor’s normative worth; black-boxing forecloses self-efficacy through the (un)controllability paradox; amplification and acceleration suspend the possibility of self-transformation, even amid measurable success. We conceptualize ‘algorithmic muteness’, which captures a relational state—workers maintain high-intensity, data-mediated contact with their labor, yet this contact rarely yields genuine responsiveness. Algorithmic muteness moves beyond documenting the static, structural consequences of algorithmic management (e.g. alienation, meaninglessness) to tracing the relational process producing them, while critically revealing algorithms’ deep entanglement with platform capital.

title: “Communicating in the Air Force”: the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication , and U.S. military education, 1950–1962
Through their eyes: neural and behavioral evidence for enhanced immersion via point-of-view editing
Pulling Strings at the Margins: Blind Storytellers and the Politics of Survival in Socialist China, 1938–1977
abstract: This article examines the mobilization and governance of blind storytellers in Southeast Shanxi from 1938 to 1977, arguing that disabled bodies occupied a structurally ambivalent position within the Chinese Communist Party’s revolutionary project. Their mobility, endurance, and bodily labor enabled the extension of state power into rural society and were endowed with political value. However, these same qualities proved increasingly incompatible with socialist labor regimes organized around standardized productivity and administrative control. As a result, blind storytellers were progressively reclassified from effective propagandists into marginal or welfare-dependent subjects. Drawing on local archives and oral histories, this article shows how revolutionary inclusion did not resolve social difference but reorganized it, producing new forms of differentiated value and exclusion. The case of blind storytellers thus reveals a fundamental tension within socialist governance between incorporation and control.

title: Rising Engagement and Substantive Responsiveness: 13 Years of Online Petitioning in China
abstract: Abstract The Chinese government has invested heavily in online petition platforms to channel public grievances, yet systematic longitudinal evidence on citizen–state interactions within these venues remains limited. This research report presents nationwide evidence showing that both public participation and government responsiveness through e-petition institutions have increased markedly since Xi Jinping took office. Analysing more than four million citizen appeals submitted to the country’s largest online petition portal, Message Board for Leaders, from January 2011 to January 2024, we find a twelvefold rise in petition volume and a fivefold increase in users, largely driven by urban residents in eastern provinces. Appeals have also diversified, with notable growth in housing-related issues and more strategic appeals directed at Party secretaries. Meanwhile, local governments have raised response rates from 50 per cent to 98 per cent, shortened average wait times from 176 to 19 days, and increased the substantive resolution rate from 17 per cent to 31 per cent over the past decade.

title: Institutional Pressures or Organizational Capacity? Antecedents of Digital Maturity in Local Governments
abstract: ABSTRACT Public administration research has identified institutional pressures and organizational capacity as digital maturity (DM) antecedents, yet these are typically considered in isolation. Taking the proverbial next step, this study draws on primary survey data to explain the variation of DM among local governments in Flanders (the northern region of Belgium) by juxtaposing the explanatory power of institutional pressures on the one hand, and political and administrative capacity on the other hand. Using multiple regression analyses, our findings highlight the critical role of administrative capacity in advancing DM among local governments. In contrast, and somewhat surprisingly, political capacity and institutional pressures appear to play a more limited role. These findings challenge conventional assumptions in existing literature, indicating that institutional pressures may catalyze the initial stages of DT, whereas organizational capacity seems to be more influential in sustaining and advancing DM.

title: Transforming a Poaching Hotspot: Embedded NGO Governance Between State and Community in Southern China
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how a local environmental NGO in southern China transformed Guantouling Hill, once a prominent poaching hotspot along the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, into a recognised model of community‐based biodiversity conservation. Drawing on 6 months of ethnographic fieldwork, including participant observation, semi‐structured interviews, and documentary analysis, this study analyses governance practices that have emerged through the sixteen‐year conservation efforts of the Guangxi Biodiversity Research and Conservation Association (BRC). At the macro level, the analysis situates NGO action within polycentric governance, public value governance, and state‐reinforced self‐governance frameworks that shape state–society relations. At the meso level, it conceptualizes ‘two‐way embeddedness’ as NGOs' simultaneous integration within state institutions and local communities, enabling them to translate policy priorities into context‐specific interventions. At the micro level, it explores collaborative governance practices grounded in trust, relational authority, and everyday participation. The case of BRC illustrates how sustained ecological monitoring, joint enforcement with state actors, and community trust‐building can produce gradually stabilized governance practices without formal delegation of authority. The findings contribute to debates on non‐state actor roles in development‐oriented environmental governance and demonstrate how NGOs can extend state capacity, institutionalize local participation, and generate new governance spaces within fragmented institutional landscapes.

title: Mechanisms of Social Enterprise: Pathways to Building Capacity, Enhancing Capability, and Creating Sustainable Public Value
abstract: ABSTRACT Social enterprise can be seen as citizen's active participation in the pursuit of public value in a financially sustainable manner. Despite a burgeoning interest in social enterprise in the public administration and policy fields, the marketing capabilities of social enterprises for sustainable public value creation have received little attention. While the literature has developed theoretical linkages between marketing capabilities and public value, the ability to partner with other organizations and to absorb and create knowledge as essential antecedents of marketing capabilities remain understudied. Using a capacity‐capability‐outcome framework, we investigated whether and how social capital influences social enterprise's marketing capabilities via the mediating mechanism of absorptive capacity in the context of East Asia. Our study extends current discourse in ‘ social enterprise as a means for public value creation ’ by testing several alternative pathways that explain capacity‐capability‐outcome as mechanisms that simultaneously contribute to financial performance and sustainable public value creation. Our study offers practical implications to social enterprise operators and policymakers.

title: The rural versus urban voting preferences using liquid and solid modernity as a framing device
abstract: IMPACTThis article is relevant for national and regional policy-makers, local government leaders, public managers, regional development agencies, and practitioners working in territorial governance, and public policy design. Using comprehensive commuting and election data from Slovakia, it demonstrates that strong economic integration between rural and urban areas does not necessarily translate into convergence in political preferences. Although based on the Slovak case, the findings have broader international relevance for countries experiencing growing urban–rural political divides, as they suggest that functional economic integration alone is insufficient to reshape place-based political identities. The findings challenge a common policy assumption that improved connectivity, labour market integration or regional development alone will reduce social and political divides. Instead, they highlight the continuing importance of local identity, community attachment and place-based governance. For practitioners, this means that investments in infrastructure and economic development should be complemented by targeted civic engagement, public communication and locally responsive policy approaches. The proposed liquid–solid modernity framework also offers an accessible lens for understanding citizen responses to change, helping policy-makers design interventions that are better aligned with the values and expectations of different communities.

title: From horizontal transfer to upward diffusion: the logic of innovation borrowing
abstract: Policy innovation involves two stages: local innovation and national scaling-up. Existing studies often conceptualize this process as a linear ‘pilot-to-scale’ trajectory, thereby overlooking potential discontinuities in the underlying logic when local innovations are elevated to national policy. The specific pathways through which local innovations, particularly borrowed innovations, achieve upward diffusion remain insufficiently explored. Drawing on policy transfer theory while incorporating policy attributes and the institutional features of hierarchical experimental governance, this article uses the ‘X-Chief Systems’ (XCS) derived from the River Chief System (RCS) as its empirical case and employs fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to systematically examine the configurational pathways through which innovation borrowing leads to upward diffusion. The findings identify two pathways: the Policy Reproduction-Driven Pathway and the Diffusion Effect-Driven Pathway. The former features policy reproduction and provincial government support as core conditions, whereas the latter features cross-contextual characteristics and provincial government support as core conditions, with the scale of prior upward diffusion serving as a peripheral condition. This study extends the explanatory scope of policy transfer theory, provides a configurational explanation of how innovation borrowing leads to upward diffusion, and offers policy insights for mitigating excessive and repetitive policy innovation.

title: Two decades of public service motivation research in China: a systematic review and research agenda
abstract: As public service motivation (PSM) scholarship expands beyond Western settings, a systematic understanding of how this construct has been studied within specific non-Western contexts remains underdeveloped. This systematic review provides the first dedicated longitudinal mapping of English-language PSM research in China, synthesizing two decades (2006–2025) of scholarship across 96 peer-reviewed publications. Our analysis documents China’s structural landscape of PSM research, including publication trajectories, sample profiles, methodological choices, measurement practices, antecedent clusters, and outcome patterns. Distinctive empirical patterns emerge, such as the dominance of leadership as the central antecedent, PSM’s robust buffering function against burnout and defensive behaviours, and the predominance of Western measurement instruments applied without cross-cultural validation in 51.0% of studies. These patterns are consistent with China’s Confucian relational governance traditions and party-state institutional context. We propose a research agenda that positions Chinese scholarship to extend PSM theory through relational conceptualizations, multilevel designs, and subnational comparative research, contributing distinctive theoretical perspectives rather than merely replicating Western frameworks in Eastern settings.

title: Access to social services – how refugees navigate through fragmented local worlds
abstract: Abstract Regarding refugees’ social protection studies in social policy and migration, research emphasises the importance of different local framework conditions as well as individual strategies of refugees. While the debates in these disciplines have so far been largely separate, this article sheds light on the interplay between strategies and local framework conditions in the context of flight. Based on qualitative interviews with refugees and local actors in twelve municipalities in Germany, we illustrate the practices of refugees in accessing and utilising social rights and services against the backdrop of fragmented local worlds. The municipalities analysed differ in terms of local policies, migration-related narratives and space. Firstly, we show that refugees pursue diverse strategies of access and participation in education, healthcare and the labour market, which are initially independent of municipal framework conditions. Secondly, we illustrate the extent to which these strategies are associated with different consequences for access to and utilisation of educational, healthcare and employment opportunities for refugees depending on local conditions. Based on our findings, we argue that social protection of refugees must be understood as an interplay between local conditions and individual practices.

title: Transparency and Responsibility Attribution: A Field Experiment in Western Uganda
abstract: ABSTRACT The implementation of public policy is increasingly diffuse with responsibilities divided among several levels of government administration, the private sector, and nonprofits. In the face of such diffusion, many advocate for transparency initiatives to inform the public about policymaking. However, it remains unclear whether transparency initiatives clarify the blame and credit for policy, or what this means for collective action and accountability. Such concerns are especially pressing in complex settings like the non‐renewable extractives sector (oil, mining, and natural gas). We assess policy attributions of blame and credit using data from a field experiment that randomizes stakeholder engagement in Western Uganda's oil sector, building on our prior work showing that this intervention increased collective action. While participating in multistakeholder forums improved transparency for communities, we find that it did not change their attributions. In other words, improving transparency does not ensure that citizens will update their opinions about who is to blame for the problems they face. Yet, this did not preclude greater collective action. Evidence from this intervention highlights the need for more exploration of pathways linking transparency, collective action, and accountability.

title: Scientific Collaboration in the Age of AI Geopolitics: Governing Openness Under Strategic Competition
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying geopolitical competition while deepening scientific interdependence. Amid the global AI race, governments increasingly restrict technological exchange to protect national security and strategic advantage. Yet, AI innovation depends on transnational flows of knowledge, talent, data, computing resources, and open‐source tools. This essay argues that science policy should navigate this tension through “managed openness,” an approach that rejects both unrestricted interdependence and wholesale technological decoupling. Drawing on the coexistence of scientific collaboration and strategic rivalry, it proposes distinguishing among forms of research risk; applying transparent, proportionate safeguards rather than broad restrictions; preserving cooperation on shared AI safety and governance challenges; and supporting scientific intermediaries that sustain communication across political divides. Managed openness also enables states to strengthen resilience in strategic areas while maintaining international collaboration. It thus offers a pragmatic framework for reconciling legitimate security concerns with the openness essential to scientific innovation and global AI governance.

title: The Politics of Subjective Well‐Being: How Social Capital Operates in Different Regime Types
abstract: ABSTRACT To what extent does regime type condition the association between social capital and subjective well‐being (SWB)? While social capital is widely recognized as a correlate of SWB, little is known about how this association varies across political contexts. Using data from the World Values Survey and Our World in Data, we analyze 262,945 observations from 95 countries to examine how three dimensions of social capital—in‐group trust, out‐group trust, and informal social networks—are associated with life satisfaction, happiness, and financial satisfaction. In‐group trust and informal social networks are positively associated with all three SWB dimensions across political regimes. More importantly, the results reveal that regime type consistently moderates the association between out‐group trust and all three SWB outcomes, with the relationship between out‐group trust and well‐being being more favorable in democratic contexts. By contrast, the associations of in‐group trust and informal social networks with well‐being are largely regime‐invariant, suggesting that the well‐being benefits of close social ties operate independently of political regime type. These findings highlight the nuanced role of political context in shaping the social capital–SWB relationship, with regime type mattering most for how out‐group trust translates into well‐being. Related Articles Flavin, P., A. C. Pacek, and B. Radcliff. 2011. “State Intervention and Subjective Well‐Being in Advanced Industrial Democracies.” Politics & Policy 39, no. 2: 251–269. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1747‐1346.2011.00290.x . Ramírez Herrera, M. 2019. “The Measurement of Well‐Being Caught between Tradition and Modernity in Mexico's Poverty Reduction Strategy.” Politics & Policy 47, no. 1: 79–104. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12283 . Jakubow, A. 2014. “State Intervention and Life Satisfaction Reconsidered: The Role of Governance Quality and Resource Misallocation.” Politics & Policy 42, no. 1: 3–36. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12057 .

title: Role Clarification and Organizational Performance in a Multi‐Goal Context: Evidence From Water Quality Management in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the widely acknowledged costs of role ambiguity and the growing consensus on the crucial roles of local leaders in public management, few studies examine whether role clarification for local leaders, as an effective approach for reducing ambiguity, can enhance organizational performance. In China, the appointment of river chiefs, which assigns the responsibilities and tasks of managing each river to specific local leaders, serves as a policy intervention of role clarification. This study uses the difference‐in‐differences method with annual water quality data from 102 prefectural‐level cities to assess the effectiveness of role clarification for local leaders in a multi‐goal context. The results show that role clarification for local leaders significantly improves the performance of local government in water quality management. However, higher economic growth targets significantly weaken this positive effect, whereas higher air pollution reduction targets slightly strengthen the relationship. These findings offer crucial policy implications for improving organizational performance by clarifying roles for local leaders in a multi‐goal context.

title: Ethnic and Gender Disparities in Pension Receipts and Savings in Later Life
abstract: ABSTRACT Pension incomes in later life are determined by the combination of eligibility rules and an individual's life‐course trajectory, including their contributions to pension schemes. Existing research documented that older individuals from minority ethnic communities have a lower likelihood of receiving pension benefits compared to White British persons. However, the current literature lacks comprehensive research in addressing disparities in pension receipts and nonpension savings by ethnicity, migration status and gender in the current pension policy context. Using UK Household Longitudinal Study data from 2009 to 2024, this paper addresses these gaps and adds to our understanding of trends and patterns of pension receipts by ethnicity, migration status and gender. Using the latest wave, we assess the role of ethnicity, migration status, demographic, socioeconomic, health and subjective well‐being factors in explaining older individuals' propensity to receive state, workplace and private pensions, and pension credit and the expectation to use nonpension savings/investments for retirement. Our findings indicate persistent ethnic and gender gaps in receipts of state, workplace and private pensions, and Pension Credit receipt and in expectations to use nonpension savings in retirement, with older individuals from Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and Other White communities faring worse than other ethnic groups, while first‐generation migrants and those in difficult financial situations are less likely to receive workplace pensions. The findings point to the need for more inclusive pension policies for future generations of retirees from diverse backgrounds.

title: Democratic erosion and its international implications: how governments in eroding democracies shift their foreign policy behaviour
abstract: Democratic erosion constitutes the most relevant path of democratic regression since 1990. In this gradual process, legally elected incumbents follow an illiberal and antidemocratic agenda, dismantling democratic institutions and norms. While most studies so far concentrate on the domestic conditions, the implications of democratic erosion on the international level only recently attracted academic interest. This paper contributes to this emerging field by capturing how governments of eroding democracies translate their domestic transformative agenda to international politics. For doing so, I examine the voting behavior in the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), which is particularly adequate for observing governments' foreign policy preferences. I conduct a difference-in-differences analysis relying on the Episodes of Regime Transformation dataset and the UNGA Voting dataset. Two illustrative cases (Venezuela and Hungary) offer an additional in-depth perspective. The study shows that governments of eroding democracies differ in their foreign policy behavior from non-eroding democracies, and that they deviate in two regards: from the country's previous international alignment and from the “Western” consensus regarding the liberal international order. These findings make an important contribution to the understanding of the internal-external nexus of democratic erosion and for policymakers who need to deal with the emerging challengers in eroding democracies.

title: Losing elections, losing trust? A quasi-experimental investigation of the winner-loser gap on political trust
abstract: Abstract Voters’ experiences of winning or losing elections significantly influence their attitudes, particularly satisfaction with democracy, while other outcomes such as trust are less studied. Additionally, studies often rely on observational data, limiting causal conclusions about effects. We make three key contributions to this literature. First, we use a quasi-experimental design based on the implementation of the European Quality of Government Index Survey during elections across several European countries and regions to demonstrate causal effects of elections on trust. Second, we introduce a novel theoretical argument that voters of populist parties are especially sensitive to electoral outcomes. Third, we explore three ways to define ‘winners’ and ‘losers’: government/opposition status, vote margin changes, and results relative to recent polling. Our findings show that elections generally boost trust, with a pronounced winner-loser gap driven by winners, particularly when measured as entering government. Additionally, populist party voters exhibit greater sensitivity to these effects.

title: Representation of environmental issues: Is there a link between campaign and legislative behaviour in the European Parliament?
abstract: This article assesses the link between Members of the European Parliament's campaign salience and legislative behaviour, focusing on environmental issues. Environmental issues were discussed by several MEP candidates during the 2019 campaign and they were important for voters. Nonetheless, it is unclear whether MEPs were consistent with their campaign commitments in their parliamentary votes. MEPs’ environmental salience is computed by coding 50,393 campaign tweets and their legislative behaviour is assessed by examining roll-call votes on amendments related to emissions reduction. Results indicate that MEPs who focused more on environmental issues during the campaign cast more pro-environmental votes. This indicates that the European Parliament can exercise its representative role in domains relevant for EU policy.

title: Differences in EU citizen voter registration: Evidence from French local elections
abstract: The 1992 Maastricht Treaty guarantees European Union citizens the right to vote in local and European elections held in their country of residence. Yet, few mobile European Union citizens actually exercise this right. In France, which hosts the second-largest number of EU immigrants, only 26.2% of this population were registered to vote for the 2020 local elections. This article uses traditional explanations of immigrant electoral participation to understand the low electoral participation of foreign EU citizens. We combine census, electoral and local data to examine the determinants of registration rates for the nine largest EU nationalities in France. Our findings suggest that existing theories of resistance, transferability and exposure account for differences in electoral registration, while also suggesting that municipality size is an important factor.

title: The Leadership Premium: Committee Leadership Status and Political Donations to Incumbent Legislators in South Korea
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the effect of committee leadership positions on political fundraising in the South Korean National Assembly from 2004 to 2019. Drawing upon theories of legislative power and campaign finance, we examine whether acquiring standing committee chairmanships significantly increases political contributions received by legislators, even within Korea's highly restrictive regulatory regime that prohibits corporate donations. Utilizing OLS regression and difference‐in‐differences with Panel Matching methodology, we find compelling evidence of a substantial leadership premium. OLS estimates reveal that committee chairs consistently outraise non‐chairs by 16%–21%; Panel Matching estimates confirm an immediate increase of approximately 1.15 log‐points (a 216% increase) following chair appointment. Event study analysis validates our identification strategy by demonstrating parallel pre‐trends and sharp treatment effects at the moment of leadership transition, with effects dissipating after chairs leave their positions. Split‐sample OLS estimates reveal a cross‐over pattern: the premium is significant for Targeted and Mixed committees in the first half of the legislative term but shifts to Universal committees in the second half, suggesting that the relevant dimension of heterogeneity may be whether a committee holds jurisdictional authority over concentrated regulatory or budgetary stakes. These findings demonstrate that the link between institutional power and political money persists even under highly restrictive campaign finance regimes—reflecting structural features of legislative organization that transcend specific regulatory designs. The individual‐as‐proxy mechanism we identify, whereby organized interest groups circumvent the corporate donation ban through coordinated individual‐level contributions, suggests that regulation reshapes the channels of strategic giving without eliminating its underlying demand.

title: Pandemic (Im)mobilities: How humanitarian workers navigated evacuation and COVID-19
Social dominance orientation
abstract: Abstract Social dominance orientation (SDO) refers to how much a person generally opposes group‐based equality and supports group‐based dominance. SDO is measured as an individual difference and pertains very broadly to people's socio‐political attitudes and perceptions, to endorsement or rejection of political parties and candidates, and to behaviors that enforce organizational hierarchies. This paper reviews empirical evidence published from 2010 to 2024 concerning social dominance orientation, first presenting evidence of its stability over time and measurement integrity, next showing that, across numerous cultures and languages and ways of measuring group prejudice and stereotypes, SDO correlates with prejudice favoring people in dominant groups rather than people in subordinate groups, and that this effect is stronger within dominant groups than subordinate groups. Similarly, we review evidence that people higher on SDO are more anti‐social and tend to take hierarchy‐enhancing rather than hierarchy‐attenuating roles. We then delve into the psychology of SDO and summarize the evidence for the relation of SDO and closed cognitive styles, low scores on humility‐honesty, and low concern for other people rather than the self. Using existing adult and child development studies, we outline two processes by which higher SDO may develop: one based on learning to categorize and to rank categories as superior/inferior, and one based on parents' emphasis on obtaining high status to gain approval. We conclude by outlining the next questions that might be pursued.

title: How patronage communicates: information campaigns and government responsiveness in China
abstract: Abstract How do social relationships among government officials shape information flows within bureaucratic hierarchies? Classic principal–agent theories emphasize information asymmetries as a source of inefficiency, yet we know far less about the actual nature of communication within bureaucracies. We argue that patron–client ties embedded within formal hierarchies play a central role in structuring internal information flows. Lower-level officials with patronage ties to higher-level leaders have incentives to conduct informal information campaigns that signal diligence and competence as a way to compete for political favors. Using newly assembled data from China—including a rare corpus of internal emails between city-level patrons and county-level clients, as well as original datasets on county governments’ public responses to citizen complaints—we find that client counties communicate more frequently with higher-level officials, more often highlight their diligence in addressing complaints, and more actively defend themselves against accusations. However, client and non-client counties perform similarly in how they respond publicly to citizen complaints. These findings reveal how patronage relations can increase upward information flows without impacting public-facing performance. More broadly, these results suggest that communication in nondemocratic settings may serve to strengthen informal political ties.

title: Minimum wage laws and job search
Basic income versus fairness: redistribution with inactive agents
Foreign Exchange Intervention with UIP and CIP Deviations
abstract: Abstract We examine the welfare-based opportunity cost of foreign exchange (FX) intervention when both CIP and UIP deviations are present. We consider a small open economy that receives international capital flows through constrained international financial intermediaries. Deviations from CIP come from limited arbitrage or through a convenience yield, while UIP deviations are also affected by global risk. We show that the sign of CIP and UIP deviations may differ for safe haven countries. We find that FX reserves may provide a net benefit, rather than a cost, when international intermediaries value the safe-haven properties of a currency more than domestic households. We show that this has been the case for the Swiss franc and the Japanese Yen. We examine the optimal policy of a constrained central bank planner in this context.

title: Marriage, Assortative Mating and Wealth Inequality
abstract: Abstract We use population data on capital income and wealth holdings for Norway to measure asset positions and wealth returns before individuals marry and after the household is formed. These data allow us to establish a number of novel facts. First, individuals sort on personal wealth rather than parental wealth. Second, people match also on their personal returns to wealth and assortative mating on returns is as strong as that on wealth. Third, post-marriage returns on family wealth reflect in equal part the pre-marriage returns of the two spouses. However, for households at the top of the wealth distribution at marriage, family wealth is largely managed by the spouse with the highest potential to grow it, providing a microfoundation for the scale dependence in wealth returns documented in several empirical papers. Fourth, marriage lowers the degree of wealth inequality as well as the heterogeneity in returns relative to the counterfactual case of no marriages. We use a simple framework to illustrate how the inequality-attenuating role of marriage is affected by assortative mating on wealth and returns and by wealth management task allocation between spouses.

title: The effect of disaster relief on climate adaptation: Evidence from floods in Pakistan
Influencer Cartels
abstract: Abstract Social media influencers account for a growing share of marketing worldwide. We demonstrate the existence of a novel form of market failure in the advertising market: influencer cartels, where groups of influencers collude to increase their advertising revenue by inflating their engagement. Our theoretical model shows that influencer cartels can improve consumer welfare if they expand social media engagement to the target audience, or reduce welfare if they divert engagement to less relevant audiences. Drawing on the model’s insights, we empirically examine influencer cartels using novel datasets and machine learning tools, and derive policy implications.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Loosen the ties that bind: interprovincial circuit tribunals, political interference, and judicial independence
Going separate ways: spatial sorting by education, work, and real income in the USA since 1970
Having a child through medically assisted reproduction: a social stratification perspective
Age‐Specific Monte Carlo Simulation‐Based Microbial Risk Assessment of Drinking Water Contamination in Islamabad: Integrating Hydrochemical Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Microbial contamination of drinking water poses a significant public health concern, yet age‐specific risks in Islamabad, Pakistan, remain poorly characterized. This study applied a Monte Carlo simulation‐based quantitative microbial risk assessment to estimate the annual probability of infection (P (a)inf ) and disease burden (DB) associated with indicator organisms Escherichia coli ( E. coli ) and total coliforms across four age groups and one overall population category at three microbiologically contaminated drinking‐water locations in Islamabad. Hydrochemical analysis, including principal component analysis, was conducted to characterize groundwater chemistry and explore links between physicochemical conditions and contamination vulnerability. Estimated risks were evaluated against U.S. EPA and WHO health‐based benchmarks, and sensitivity analysis was used to identify the main drivers of DB. The results showed that estimated P(a)inf exceeded the U.S. EPA benchmark (1E‐4 pppy) and DB exceeded the WHO benchmark (1E‐6 DALYs pppy) across all modeled age groups at the three microbiologically contaminated drinking‐water locations. Risk estimates were highest among middle‐aged adults and elderly individuals and lowest among children, primarily due to differences in assumed drinking‐water intake volumes. The total coliforms‐associated risks were generally higher than those associated with E. coli. Sensitivity analysis identified exposure concentration as the dominant contributor to DB variability, accounting for 73%–75% of total variance. Some microbiologically unsafe locations showed hydrochemical characteristics associated with higher mineralization, including elevated EC, TDS, and HCO 3 − concentrations; however, these associations represent statistical patterns rather than evidence of direct causal relationships between hydrochemical conditions and microbial contamination. These findings suggest that routinely measured physicochemical parameters may serve as practical screening indicators for identifying contamination‐prone zones and support targeted drinking water monitoring and intervention in Islamabad.

title: The Knowledge Gap in a High-Choice Media Environment: Experimental Evidence from Online Search
The Hollowing Out of Nonprofit News: An Ethnographic Investigation into the Implications of Exploited News Workers
abstract: This work examines the practices of news workers within the unique funding structures of nonprofit news organizations using qualitative interviews and ethnographic methods. From a political economy perspective, my findings show that organizational concerns are prioritized over journalism by news workers in nonprofit news contexts. I argue this exploits public-service oriented journalists to do unpaid labor. I suggest that dependence on external funders reduces the power of nonprofit news organizations to do journalism.

title: Entangled political institutions and forms: From corporatisation to treaty
abstract: Abstract The lands and waters now called Australia have been home to diverse political ordering and institutions for thousands of generations. The comparatively very recent arrival of settlers and the violent imposition of their political structures and institutions have forced First Nations to respond to, adapt to, resist, and refuse colonial authority. While the settler state generally operates in ignorance of or indifference to Indigenous laws and culture, First Nations are burdened with a far more difficult task: to navigate the settler order while also honouring their obligations to Country and people. At this interface, First Nations organisations and institutions operate around and through a complex entanglement of cultural ideas, norms, and values, where the reality of contested jurisdiction and authority is made visible. This article foregrounds these entangled relations to explore the possibilities and limitations presented by Indigenous political formations of diverse kinds—from Aboriginal community‐controlled organisations to Indigenous corporations to new representative bodies such as the First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria. Rather than ‘failing’, as mainstream political discourse often suggests, these Indigenous governance institutions have adapted, responded, innovated, and evolved, pushing towards greater autonomy and self‐determination. This article focuses on the experience, challenges, and innovations of Indigenous communities as they seek to navigate complex relationships with the state using a variety of organisational vehicles. Points for practitioners First Nations governance requires Indigenous people to manage both the demands of the settler state and their own responsibilities to culture and Country. This is complex and difficult work that receives little recognition. Public administration practitioners working in this domain would benefit from recognising that they are also in a governance relationship that has been shaped by the politics of colonialism, rather than being authoritative and neutral practitioners of governance. Indigenous efforts would achieve greater success if governments and policymakers were able to relinquish control and become more responsive to Indigenous forms of governance.

title: The future of regional airports in Australia: Policy challenges
abstract: Abstract Council‐owned regional airports in Australia face governance challenges that have caused significant financial unsustainability across the sector. Federal policy frameworks fail to address these challenges and risk exacerbating existing pressures by outlining ambitious visions for the adoption of new technologies and achieving net zero. The current Aviation White Paper rests on overly optimistic assumptions about council capacity and ignores the gap between federal‐level policy design and the realities of implementation at the local level. This study uses a scenario planning approach. Data gathered from stakeholder interviews and desktop research were used to underpin the development of future‐oriented narratives describing how these regional airports might evolve over the next 25 years, with these narratives then being subjected to expert validation. Regardless of whether demand for regional passenger services grows or stagnates, sustaining regional airports requires rethinking the distribution of responsibility across government levels and developing governance frameworks flexible enough to support the heterogeneity of regional airport contexts. Such challenges extend beyond aviation as the distribution of infrastructure responsibilities across multiple government tiers without adequate institutional support creates conditions for policy failure that compound over time and resist resolution through incremental policy adjustment. Points for practitioners Top‐down policy formulation in the field of public infrastructure provision could lead to uneven implementation outcomes, especially in heterogeneous regional contexts. Federal and state governments need to move beyond ad hoc grant programmes and develop coordinated governance frameworks that actively support councils in managing complex infrastructure assets. Alternative governance arrangements offer pathways to address the financial and operational constraints that the prevailing model of sole council ownership and operation has been unable to resolve.

title: Is limited regulation supporting policy inaction? International student housing in Australia
abstract: Abstract The international education sector in Australia is subject to significant government policy and regulation, but the effectiveness of interventions in providing for international student well‐being is continually questioned. Housing insecurity is one of the most pressing well‐being issues among students. This paper analyses the effectiveness of existing policy and regulatory instruments in the arena of international student housing, specifically in terms of if, where, and how instruments provide for students’ well‐being. In doing so, we utilise ‘regulation theory’ and ‘policy inaction’ theory, merging consideration of traditional command‐and‐control methods; more persuasive and individualised forms of government oversight; and instances where governments ‘do nothing’ in the face of important societal problems. Interrogating government strategies, policies, and both traditional and softer regulatory instruments at the federal, state, and local government levels, the article finds that, despite extensive apparent policy activity, international student housing is an area of policy inaction. The utility of combining the two central theoretical perspectives stems from: its capacity to expose ‘buck‐passing’ in federal systems such as Australia's, both between levels of government and between the policy domains of international education and housing; its illustration of the need for evidence to inform policy; and its allowance for the identification of neoliberal tendencies towards the ideologically inspired use of markets to usurp and replace government action. Points for practitioners Assessing government commitment to a policy area can be facilitated by considering regulatory action/inaction and policy action/inaction together. Analysing the effectiveness of both policy and regulation in international student housing is important to understanding the well‐being of this group of temporary migrants. Considering regulation in all of its forms, alongside policy inaction, provides unique lenses through which to view policy coordination in a federal political system. In considering the coverage of legislation, it is important to examine its likely effects and not just its wording.

title: Decoupling sustainability and performance: How government infrastructure projects in Australia fare on strategic environmental commitments
abstract: Abstract Australian government organisations are pivotal in helping to meet the United Nations sustainable development goals. Yet while these organisations promote sustainability in their strategic plans, they struggle to embed these same commitments into their own infrastructure and construction projects. This study examines this persistent disconnect using the lens of strategic decoupling, which explains how organisations symbolically align with external expectations while internal practices remain unchanged. Using a two‐stage qualitative design, we conducted a positivist discourse analysis of strategic artefacts from six government organisations and a theoretically informed interpretivist analysis of 30 interviews with project professionals, framed by strong structuration theory. We identify widespread policy–practice decoupling, reinforced by institutional inertia and the flawed success logic in project management's iron triangle. Our findings reveal the moral burden experienced by middle managers who, as reflexively knowledgeable actors, find their professional identities in conflict with organisational mandates. We extend strategic decoupling theory by introducing the interpretive authority of middle managers and the concept of strategic recoupling. These are intentional efforts by agents to bridge the gap between rhetoric and practice. We call for systemic reform, including strengthened accountability and targeted support for managers to shift sustainability from a ceremonial commitment to an operational reality. Points for practitioners Government sustainability policies often decouple from project reality, creating persistent gaps between rhetoric and practice. Middle managers act as pivotal agents for recoupling but lack sufficient institutional authority and support. Middle managers strengthen accountability by embedding measurable sustainability targets and post‐project impact reviews into governance frameworks. Middle managers integrate sustainability ratings into design‐phase documents to avoid procurements locking in high‐emission materials.

title: Navigating the digital transformation: unravelling the dynamic evolution of smart city collaborative governance networks
abstract: Smart city initiatives, as public service innovation, represent a major evolution within state-led meta-governance, requiring complex inter-participant collaboration. Yet scholarship often treats these networks as static, missing how governance structures adapt to digital uncertainties. To fill this gap, this study employs stochastic actor-oriented models and collaborative governance theory to examine the evolution of network structures and participant attributes across 3482 smart city projects in China. Results reveal three governance patterns: government-dominated, government-SOE hybrid, and multi-stakeholder. Transitive triads, age similarity, geographic proximity, and size heterogeneity promote evolution, while outdegree constrains it. Findings guide optimizing partner selection and strengthening adaptive governance.

title: Navigating the Battlefield: How Social Media Platforms Respond to Governance Demands From Legitimacy Communities in Geopolitical Conflicts
abstract: ABSTRACT Social media platforms have become central actors in governing online speech during geopolitical conflicts, navigating complex governance demands from diverse stake‐holding communities including states, civil society, and users. This paper explores these dynamics through an analysis of Meta, X (formerly Twitter), and TikTokduring the recent Russia–Ukraine war and Israel–Palestine conflict. We develop a framework categorizing platform strategies along two dimensions: activeness and alignment, leading to five response types: proactive, accommodation, avoidance, defiance, and disregard. Through analysis of 126 interaction events, we found three platforms’ distinct strategic approaches. Meta adopted the most proactive measures with clear inclinations to the Western states and calculated defiance against others. X's strategy shifted dramatically after Musk's takeover: from accommodation to defiance and disregard, though it made pragmatic accommodations under severe pressure. TikTok, risk‐averse, and geopolitically vulnerable, frequently employs cautious and ambivalent avoidance and disregard strategies. The findings shed light on how corporate strategy, institutional background, and geopolitical positioning shape how platforms construct their legitimacy in content governance.

title: Supply‐Side Policy Feedback
abstract: ABSTRACT The scholarship on policy feedback has been among the most plentiful and successful of the policy sciences. Much of it has focused on the demand‐side, or on the political relationship between a public policy and its recipients. Less attention has been paid to the supply‐side: the political relationship between a public policy and its providers. Parents may care about education, patients about health care, and prisoners about criminal justice—but an emerging literature shows that teachers, hospital employees, and the police care just as, if not more, about these areas. This article builds on new work to introduce a theory of supply‐side policy feedback and outline a research agenda for its further investigation.
