Using process tracing of Thailand’s 2006 military coup, 2008 judicial-political deadlock, and 2010 street confrontations, the article shows how crisis responses repeatedly achieved operational settlement without political resolution, fragmenting elected political capacity and weakening civilian analytical autonomy. The findings challenge complementarity assumptions in policy capacity theory: in hybrid regimes, governance failure may arise less from aggregate capacity scarcity than from how capacities are distributed across rival centres of authority.

title: Contested Rule Formation Under Institutional Mismatch: A Framework for Early‐Phase Governance of Disruptive Innovations
Searching together: Human–AI complementarities in innovation search
Attitudes Toward Energy Across European Union Member States (2006–2024)
The long shadow of typhoons: Prenatal exposure and adult mental health
Access to Essential Services: A Critical Factor for Predicting Recovery and Quantifying Resilience
Hospital Capacity Pooling in Pandemics: Simulation‐Based Mortality Impacts and Diversification Mechanisms
From Structural Inequalities to Labor Precarity: Adoption of Digital and AI Tools in Latin American Journalism
abstract: While inequalities in technological access and use have been widely documented, few studies have examined their link to labor precarity and social inequality in journalism in the Global South. This article analyzes this relationship through a multilevel study of Worlds of Journalism Study data from 4,250 journalists in 11 Latin American countries. Results show that macro-level inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, is not associated with the use of advanced digital technologies, including AI, while micro-level precarity, expressed in contractual instability and excessive workloads, is. Working conditions, rather than national disparities, are key to explaining inequalities in technology adoption.

title: Generative Logic and the Mediatization of Politics: Deepfake Parodies and Political Reinterpretation in China
abstract: This study revisits the theory of the mediatization of politics in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), questioning its applicability beyond Western democracies and proposing an extension through the concept of generative logic. Drawing on the analysis of AI-generated parodies in China’s cyberspace, it examines a distinctive mode of political communication in which foreign political figures’ faces are superimposed onto characters from Chinese historical television dramas. These satirical videos construct five patterns of analogical displacement, enabling users to reinterpret international affairs through culturally familiar frameworks. Rather than merely destabilizing truth boundaries, this content reflects a locally embedded form of AI-mediated political expression shaped by the interplay of political logic , media logic , and generative logic . We conceptualize this configuration as a multi-logic communicative structure that sustains a stable yet dynamic mode of political discourse in authoritarian contexts. The findings contribute to a broader understanding of how generative technologies reshape political engagement, symbolic meaning-making, and mediated reality across diverse political systems.

title: Organizational Capacity to Implement Social Equity in Emergency Management: A Local Government Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT The emergency management profession and discipline is increasingly embracing social equity as a core value, yet limited attention has been paid to whether local emergency management organizations possess the capacity to implement equity‐focused practices. Drawing on the Capacity Building Framework, this exploratory study analyzes data from a national panel survey of US emergency managers to examine the organizational capacity to advance social equity through the lens of adaptive capacity. The findings reveal that while political, technical, financial, and managerial capacities matter, financial capacity is the most critical constraint. Respondents prioritized additional funding for personnel, community outreach and education, and the development of accessible public resources. The results highlight how resource scarcity shapes the pursuit of equity at the local level and underscores the need to align equity goals with investments in organizational capacity. This study contributes insight into the practical challenges emergency managers face in translating equity commitments into action.

title: From Social Equity Budgeting to Revenue Equity: Minority Leadership and Local Governments' Exploitative Revenues
abstract: ABSTRACT Social equity budgeting has gained increasing attention, yet research has largely focused on expenditures while neglecting revenue equity. This study contributes to the literature by examining the relationships between minority population size and local governments' reliance on exploitative revenues, and whether minority political representation moderates this relationship. Drawing on racial threat and political representation theories, we analyze data from 66 Florida counties between 2011 and 2019. Results show that counties with larger minority populations rely more heavily on exploitative revenues, but this relationship diminishes when minority political representation increases. These findings highlight how minority leadership could moderate fiscal practices that disproportionately burden minority communities. More broadly, this study advances the framework of social equity budgeting by shifting the focus from expenditure allocation to revenue generation.

title: Under Pressure: Analyzing LEO Turnover in America's Swing and Pivot Counties for 2016, 2020, 2024
abstract: ABSTRACT Post‐2024, the United States faces an acute labor crisis marked by accelerating Local Election Official (LEO) attrition. This study examines causal drivers of this exodus, focusing specifically on disproportionate turnover within volatile “swing” and “pivot” counties. Utilizing a mixed‐methods design, using longitudinal data from the Bipartisan Policy Center, US Census Bureau, Elections Voter Survey, MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MEDSL), and the Reed LEO survey, alongside an original dataset compiled from 74 competitive counties and 25 “super landslide” counties. Using Geographic Information Systems, we connect a detailed county profile to spatial mapping of the legal and political environment across the 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections. LEOs in highly competitive jurisdictions face an erosion of institutional trust, serving as a primary catalyst for departure. These volatile jurisdictions highlight where democratic machinery is vulnerable, offering evidence‐based insights for state‐level policy interventions designed to stabilize the public administrative workforce amidst unprecedented hyperpolarization.

title: Multiracial young adults’ experiences of Whiteness as a wage and tax
Explaining gendered language through embedding approximation: how “stupid” became a man’s word
Festivalized marriage as a Time Threshold: Spring Festival bottlenecks, Qualification Audits, and escalating entry standards in rural China
More Than the Sum of Its Parts? Bridging Research-to-Practice Gaps to Explain Local Nonprofit Sector Health
abstract: This study examines nonprofit sector capacity by integrating economic concepts of supply and demand with practitioner perspectives. Focusing on health and human services nonprofits in a midsize southeastern U.S. city, it combines community indicators with survey and interview data. Findings suggest that sector capacity depends not only on resource availability and organizational density but also on the strength of local networks and community context. Well-established nonprofits embedded in local networks differ from more loosely connected organizations, demonstrating how network position shapes perceptions of capacity and the ability to meet community needs. These findings advance research on nonprofit carrying capacity.

title: Debate: Credibility, not expansion, is the foundation of effective public audit

title: Theoretical and Practical Frontiers in Urban Governance from a Global Comparative Perspective
Responding or responsiveness? How politicisation influences the European Commission's policy formulation
abstract: Does politicisation have an impact on how the European Commission puts forward policy proposals? A large body of research has addressed this question from a responsiveness angle, assessing the degree to which the EU’s policy outputs align with public opinion. We complement this with a procedural approach that assesses how politicisation affects the input, throughput, and output stages of Commission policy formulation. We distinguish between responding – adapting processes to societal pressures – and responsiveness – substantive adjustment of proposals in response to public opinion. Empirically, we combine computational text analysis methods to develop a novel, media-based measurement of politicisation with qualitative, in-depth case analysis of Commission proposals in the realm of agricultural policy (between 2014 and 2024). We analyse three such proposals (with low, moderate, high politicisation respectively) to trace public input across policy-making stages. Our findings indicate that responding and responsiveness vary independently: low politicisation produces narrow responding, moderate politicisation produces broad responding with selective responsiveness, and high politicisation produces narrow responding alongside high responsiveness. Our paper contributes to theory development on how the Commission navigates politicisation by relying on different registers of procedural responding and responsiveness.

title: The landscape of trust diversity in wildfire collaboratives and impacts on environmental, social and process outcomes
Citations in 280 characters: Is social media presence worth it for elite journals?
The Power of Words: Adult Literacy Campaign and Intergenerational Transmission of Human Capital
Value of Information in Social Learning
A Hybrid Optimization Model for Shelter Location and Materials Assignment in Earthquakes Based on Evacuation Behavior
abstract: A critical gap in disaster response persists between optimized logistical plans and the complex, often unpredictable evacuation behaviors of affected populations. Traditional location-allocation models often prove insufficient in practice, as they typically treat evacuees as homogeneous, rational actors, thereby overlooking the dynamic, hierarchical needs that govern decision-making on the ground. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hybrid optimization framework that systematically translates data-driven behavioral insights into a multi-objective model for shelter location and material assignment. Rather than modeling microscopic routing behaviors, our methodological innovation lies in a two-stage pipeline. First, we integrate thematic analysis of large-scale social media data (3400 relevant posts) from recent earthquakes to extract and quantify time-varying demand patterns for three core needs: essential survival, medical treatment, and psychological needs. Second, these empirically derived priority dynamics are embedded as dynamic parameters within the optimization model. Validated against the 2013 Ya'an earthquake case study and compared with classical baselines (e.g., the p-median model), the framework reduces the average evacuation distance while ensuring feasible access for heterogeneous vulnerable groups. Concurrently, it enhances resource equity by dynamically prioritizing material allocation based on the evolving urgency of evacuee needs. This research thus contributes not only a specific decision-support tool but also a generalizable paradigm for bridging descriptive behavioral data with prescriptive operations models, offering a more realistic foundation for risk analysis in humanitarian logistics.

title: Reclaiming Place Through Symbolic Geographies: Visual Resistance on Palestinian Instagram
abstract: Palestinians use Instagram to construct symbolic geographies that resist displacement and assert cultural presence. Analyzing 9,126 posts from 834 users posted between October 2023-March 2024, we identify three recurring visual themes that serve as anchors of digital placemaking. The sharing of images depicting everyday routines and familiar spaces functions as an act of asserting belonging in the face of cartographic erasure. Resilience is conveyed through motifs of joy, family, and faith, symbolizing continuity under siege. Knowledge cultivation emerges through practices of naming places, traditions, and environmental markers, reinforcing cultural memory. Comparing Instagram content with 7,448 international news headlines, we find that user-generated posts often offer alternative framings that are absent in mainstream narratives. We close with a discussion of how Palestinian Instagram users created a networked archive that resists material destruction and algorithmic suppression, mapping threatened spaces and producing narrative coherence through everyday digital acts of documentation and resistance.

title: Enemies Abroad, Animosity at Home: Media Influence on U.S.-China Policy and Anti-Asian Sentiment
abstract: How do portrayals of foreign nations as threats shape public opinion on foreign policy and domestic racial attitudes? This study examines how portrayals of China as a threat influence Americans’ support for U.S. policy toward China and attitudes toward Asian Americans. A content analysis of CNN and Fox News transcripts from 2010 to 2020 shows that both outlets increasingly portrayed China as a threat, although Fox News more often emphasized threats to the United States, whereas CNN focused more on threats affecting other countries, international institutions, and populations. A national survey and a preregistered survey experiment further demonstrate that exposure to China threat narratives, regardless of whether the threat targets the United States or another country, increases support for hawkish U.S. foreign policy and heightens anti-Asian resentment, especially among Republicans. These findings show how portrayals of foreign threats shape public opinion and spill over into racial attitudes at home.

title: Agile Digital Transformation and the Rule of Law: Perks and Perils in a Belgian and a Dutch Public Sector Organization
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the interplay between agile digital transformation and the rule of law within the public sector, focusing on case studies from a semi‐large municipal government in the Netherlands and a department of the Flemish regional government in Belgium. Drawing on expert interviews, the paper explores how agile methods, championed for flexibility, interact with existing administrative routines and affect rule of law principles that prioritize consistency. Theoretically, the paper builds on public administration scholarship concerning administrative routines and the rule of law. Empirically, the paper shows that agile methods align well with administrative routines that prioritize decentralized leadership and collaboration. Moreover, it shows that agile approaches can foster, rather than threaten, the rule of law: many legal uncertainties arise not from agile practices themselves but from existing complexities in laws and policies, highlighting a need for stronger technical precision in lawmaking and administrative awareness in digital implementation.

title: Governing Before the State: Indigenous Javanese Administrative Theory
abstract: ABSTRACT Public administration scholarship often treats the Weberian ideal type as a universal model of bureaucracy, making governance arrangements that differ from it appear deficient rather than different. A decolonizing approach instead asks whether non‐Western historical records can offer alternative ways of theorizing governance. This study explores that possibility through the Nagarakretagama, a 14th‐century Javanese court eulogy composed by Mpu Prapanca in 1365, which predates Machiavelli's The Prince by 148 years. Qualitative content analysis of all 98 cantos identifies five governance domains: bureaucratic hierarchy, mandala‐based territorial administration, conditional fiscal exemptions, a legal order combining written law and custom, and ceremonial practices integrated with administration. These dimensions show how the Javanese empire organized authority, territory, revenue, law, and legitimacy through institutional arrangements that differ from the Weberian model. Reading this governance system as theory reveals an alternative conceptualization of administration and advances a decolonizing, pluriversal approach to public administration.

title: Giving in or giving out: what U.S. universities may expect from private foundations in the new political climate
Reform Begets Reform: Reform Memory and the Dynamics of Pension Policy Change
abstract: ABSTRACT Building on theories of path dependence and policy feedback, this paper examines whether pension reform exhibits Reform Memory, the tendency for recent reform history to influence the probability of subsequent policy change. While existing research highlights the importance of historical legacies in shaping public policy, little systematic evidence exists on whether pension reforms themselves exhibit a measurable and predictable temporal structure. Using a newly constructed global database of 790 pension reform events across 183 countries from 2000 to 2024, we analyse the dynamics of major structural and parametric pension reforms. Employing rare‐events logit models and a range of robustness exercises, we find strong evidence of a highly non‐linear form of reform memory in pension policymaking. Countries that experienced a major reform within the previous 2 years exhibit a major reform probability of 10.1%, compared with only 1.0% among countries whose previous reform occurred more than a decade earlier. This reform‐memory effect remains robust across alternative reform definitions, reform‐intensity measures and regional subsamples. By contrast, conventional determinants, including population ageing, public debt, inflation and economic growth, display weak or inconsistent explanatory power. The findings indicate that pension reforms do not occur as isolated responses to contemporary pressures. Instead, reform activity exhibits strong temporal dependence, clustering within short‐lived periods of elevated policy activity before reverting to longer periods of institutional stability. More broadly, the paper provides systematic cross‐national evidence that pension systems evolve through reform cycles rather than a sequence of independent legislative events.

title: Correction: Fearing Not Belonging: How Local Attitudes and Policies Shape Refugees’ Destination Preferences
Benjamin Franklin and Democratic Education Beyond Schooling
abstract: Political theorists have long focused their understanding of democratic education on the institution of the school, particularly the public school, to the exclusion of broader visions of education beyond schooling. But as criticisms of schooling from outside the academy mount, it becomes imperative to examine the origins of American educational thought to determine whether opposition to schooling has an older historical source. This essay locates the roots of school skepticism in an alternative American educational tradition beginning with Benjamin Franklin that drew on Locke’s pedagogical arguments to devalue institutional schooling in favor of self-education. Franklin’s educational vision harnessed the independence of the young in early America by incentivizing learning through friendship and self-interest, and resorted to schools only as a guardrail against the abuse of freedom, incorporating them but minimizing their role in education. In this, Franklin initiated the Americanization of Lockean pedagogy, or the school-skeptical tradition in American thought.

title: The efficiency paradox of majoritarian democracy
abstract: Abstract Majoritarian democracy is widely regarded as the canonical procedure for converting heterogeneous individual preferences into collective decisions, yet its welfare properties are far more fragile than legal and political theorists suggest. This paper contributes to the literature on the limits of majoritarianism by applying a spatial voting model to demonstrate that the conditions under which majoritarian democracies produce efficient outcomes are narrowly constrained by the structural features of majority rule itself. We formalize a multidimensional policy environment in which voters bargain over both the policy vector and lump‑sum transfers. We show that—even with transferable utility among members of the majority coalitions—the equilibrium chosen by the pivotal majority is generally off the Pareto frontier. Taken together, these results establish an impossibility theorem for majority rule in multidimensional policy spaces: whether coalitions are stable or cyclical, simple majority voting fails to maximize aggregate welfare. Political externalities imposed on minorities systematically exceed the surplus gains accruing to decisive majorities, and vote trading cannot redress the loss. Institutional remedies—supermajority thresholds, agenda control, or issue-bundling constraints—are therefore necessary conditions for approaching efficiency under democratic decision-making.

title: An Experimental Comparison of AI-Enabled Semi-Structured Interviews and Fixed Surveys: Respondent Satisfaction, Response Patterns, Quality, and Representation

title: When exports decelerate: The mental health consequences of China’s export slowdown
Group Identity and Belief Formation: A Microfoundation of Political Polarization
abstract: Abstract To evaluate the impact of group identity on belief formation, we conducted online experiments before and after the 2020 US presidential election. We elicit participants’ beliefs about future unemployment statistics and health system rankings and provide relevant news summaries. We find that people pay money to avoid information from political outgroups and attribute lower weight to this information when updating beliefs. An intervention which unlabels information sources decreases outgroup information avoidance by 50%, with a significant impact on only groupish participants. A debiasing intervention equalizing instrumental values of information sources reduces only universalists’ WTP for a private signal. The interventions have little effect on information processing. The evidence is consistent with a source-utility channel contributing to polarization.

title: Remote work and effort provision in teams
abstract: Abstract Remote work policies remain controversial partly because of productivity concerns, which are potentially exacerbated in team settings. Using experiments, we isolate how location-based beliefs of teammate effort affect the own-effort choices of participants assigned to work with remote and office-based teammates. Participants perform a real effort task and can contribute this effort to an individual account, paying a piece rate wage, or to a team account using a minimum-effort payment scheme. We find that remote workers do not complete fewer tasks than their office-based counterparts. Yet, teams suffer from lower effort due to workers responding to beliefs that remote teammates contribute less effort to the team. In a follow-up treatment, we demonstrate that these location-based beliefs remain salient even under a revenue-sharing team payment scheme where beliefs of free-riding may have dominated. Finally, we provide unique evidence that the COVID-19 pandemic may have shifted beliefs to be more pessimistic about the effort of remote workers but did not alter the actual effort.

title: Timetables, attendance and academic achievement in higher education
Preferential trade agreements and non-tariff measures
Entrepreneurial heterogeneity, financial development, and business cycle dynamics

When hazards don’t make law: structural resonance in global disaster-law diffusion, 1960–2025
Review of “Becoming Boundless: Indian Transnational Entrepreneurs in the Global Economy”
Modeling Culvert Failure and Community Accessibility Impacts During Hazards
abstract: Culverts (or road-stream crossings) are prone to failure during extreme events such as flooding. However, culverts are considered small-scale infrastructure and have been understudied and overlooked. The impact of culvert failure could be far-reaching and is especially damaging in rural networks where there is less redundancy in the transport system when compared to a dense urban network. Culvert failure can block road infrastructure and disconnect community members from places of interest such as hospitals. Current work on culverts has focused on improving component level condition ratings. This work allows for prioritization at the component level; however, culvert failure should be modeled as a system event where multiple culverts may fail at one time. Community characteristics are also neglected from current work focusing only on culvert condition ratings. Spatial distributions of communities and places of interest must be integrated into risk analyses to holistically understand culvert impact. This paper introduces a new methodology for simulating culvert failure during hazard events. Particular attention is given toward measuring community impact and using publicly available data to ensure transferability. Additionally, infrastructure-induced disconnection is coupled with community characteristics to identify areas of concern and propose mitigation actions. Finally, culvert importance metrics are introduced to help identify critical culverts within the system. The method is illustrated on a case study network in Western Massachusetts.

title: The governance of snarking: Anti-fandom as tiny publics
abstract: This article examines online celebrity ‘snarking’ communities, otherwise known as anti-fandom spaces or even hate forums. Specifically, we provide an analysis of the governance of these groups and how they develop a collective morality through both articulations with the celebrities’ mediation and with the logics of social justice. Using data collected from a digital ethnography of two popular celebrity snark spaces, we employ Critical Discourse Analysis to track the particular discursive repertoires and vernaculars which characterise snark across multiple platforms. We argue that despite the perceived ‘incivility’ of these online spaces, discourses of care, justice and solidarity often emerge which complicate existing narratives of these groups. Though participation in snarking collectives is often explained in pathologising or individualising narratives of anti-fandom, we demonstrate some of the reflexive work that happens in these spaces which sometimes ignites sociological discussions and frustrations at inequalities. We therefore conceptualise snark through the lens of a ‘tiny public’ that identifies and explores broader race and class injustice in contemporary society. Here, the prevailing discourses about celebrity subjects ‘failing upwards’ betrays an anger at elites who do not suffer the same material consequences at times of crisis; though many of these frustrations are misdirected back at the celebrity subject and manifest in a collective desire to see repercussions for the individual celebrity, rather than collective action aimed at the structures that make this failure possible, visible and even lucrative.

title: Assessing Civic Journalism Training: A Mixed-Method Applied Research Study
abstract: This mixed‑method applied research study examines how audiences are responding to news stories that are shaped by retraining efforts to help American journalists rebuild audiences. We wanted to know: were these trainings working? Do audiences choose stories that were influenced by these trainings over more traditional elite-focused, problem-oriented, conflict-driven stories? Working with three newsroom-training organizations, we report the results of a series of conjoint experiments that test how well stories abiding by new journalistic techniques of engagement, solutions and “good-conflict” framing play with audiences. We then use the findings from seven focus groups (n = 49) with surveys to explain why people may have responded the way they did in the tests. We found that audiences overwhelmingly selected and appreciated the re-framed content and reported that it makes them trust the news brands more. The focus group participants claimed such content would entice them to become members, subscribe, or even donate to the mainstream brand – if they came across it. However, only a few of the participants said they had heard about the news outlet. Though the principles behind these trainings may seem counterintuitive to some journalists, they offer a potential path forward in uncertain times for local news.

title: (De-)anchoring bureaucracy in liberal democracy: administrative reforms between illiberal drift and democratic renewal
abstract: Liberal democracies face mounting pressures from systemic transformations and emerging illiberal political forces, placing public administrations at a critical juncture. This introduction to the Special Issue “Mapping bureaucratic transformation in polarized polities: Comparative perspectives on democratic reform, robustness and regression” conceptualizes bureaucratic transformation along a continuum from democratic anchorage to democratic backsliding in public administration, capturing how administrative reforms can either reinforce or erode liberal-democratic governance. Drawing on normative theory and comparative empirical analysis, the contributions to the Special Issue examine how bureaucracies are reshaped by populist strategies and institutional vulnerabilities. This introductory article presents a heuristic framework that locates bureaucratic change along three relational dimensions—bureaucracy-society, bureaucracy-politics, and internal governance—and four opposing pairs of transformation, offering analytical tools to assess the democratic anchorage, resilience, and reform potential of public administration under conditions of polarization. Points for practitioners (a) Safeguard bureaucratic integrity: ensure ethical standards and professional autonomy within public administration to maintain democratic resilience, especially in polarized political contexts. (b) Balance accountability and autonomy: strive for a balance between political responsiveness and procedural integrity, fostering participatory mechanisms while protecting bureaucratic autonomy from politicization. (c) Strengthen civic embeddedness: institutionalize participatory mechanisms and sustained engagement with civil society and professional associations to sustain public trust and institutional legitimacy, particularly in polarized environments. (d) Adapt to evolving democratic needs: as representative democracies evolve, focus on reforms that strengthen connections between citizens and the executive, enhancing democratic legitimacy through inclusive governance practices.

title: Conditional Compliance: The Role of Sector and Policy Design in State Sexual Misconduct Policy
abstract: Abstract The role of principal-agent dynamics in performance and accountability reforms has been a recurring theme in public administration research. Yet, less attention has been dedicated to how the intersection of sector and policy design shapes principal-agent dynamics and subsequent policy outcomes. This study theoretically explores and empirically tests how sector and policy design shape the effects of state legislation that seeks to prevent shirking (mismanagement and underreporting) in the context of sexual misconduct outcomes in U.S. colleges and universities. We code every state policy designed to regulate higher education institutions’ management of sexual misconduct from 2007 to 2018 in the U.S. and leverage a Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood with a staggered difference-in-differences design to identify the effects. Our findings suggest that both sector and policy design matter: public institutions increase reporting in response to prevention policies that promote education and awareness, but prevention policies have no effect on private institutions. Other policies regulating enforcement and infrastructure produce null effects across both sectors. These findings have important implications for principal-agent theory and policy design research on effective methods for reducing shirking in social equity, accountability, and performance reporting.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: To Add Insult to Injury: Exploring the Impact of Policy Inequity on Administrative Burden
abstract: ABSTRACT The relationship between inequity and administrative burden constitutes a pivotal concern in the realm of public administration and policy, but how policy inequity (i.e., inequity in policy implementation) influences administrative burden has garnered scant attention. The present study employs data about public assistance programs in China spanning from 2015 to 2017 to examine the consequences of policy inequity on administrative burden. The empirical findings underscore that policy inequity augments psychological and compliance costs while concurrently diminishing citizens' participation in welfare programs, thereby indicating that policy inequity intensifies administrative burden. Notably, individual‐level social capital and contextual‐level information transparency in terms of public exposure related to welfare approval and receipt significantly moderate this relationship. Contrary to our theoretical expectations, social capital and public exposure amplify, rather than dampen, the impact of policy inequity on administrative burden. This study highlights the policy inequity lens and offers important implications for burden reduction.

title: Public sector innovation management in the shadow: why the overlooked sibling still matters
abstract: This paper examines innovation management as a deliberate organizational arrangement through which public organizations seek to remain relevant in contexts of uncertainty, technological and societal changes, and bureaucratic constraints. Drawing on a multiple-case study of five national police agencies, the study analyzes what works well and less well in systematic innovation management arrangements. While all agencies established innovation units with similar responsibilities, they differed in how innovation management systems were configured and sustained. Three configurations are identified – Strong Heavyweight, Light Heavyweight, and Lightweight – showing how enabling and constraining mechanisms help explain variation in innovation capacity across highly institutionalized public-sector contexts.
authors: Ana Paula Franco Paes Leme Barbosa

title: Debate: Is the public manager’s duty always deference?
abstract: Crisis, what crisis? To judge by the absence of consternation the arrival in power of radical-right and populist parties has not so far roused and alarmed public management professionals at large. ...

title: Systemic capacities and capabilities for mission-oriented innovation policies: the case of Brazil’s Inova programme
abstract: This paper refines, operationalizes, and empirically applies a systemic framework for analyzing the capacities and capabilities required for successful mission-oriented innovation policies. The framework identifies six critical dimensions where both structural capacities and dynamic capabilities must align: state, technical-administrative, policy, scientific-technological, industrial and demand dimensions. We illustrate the framework’s analytical purchase through a structured comparison of two contrasting subprogrammes of Brazil’s Inova programme—PAISS Industrial (bioethanol) and Inova Petro (oil and gas). PAISS Industrial combined strong capacities with effective capability mobilization across all six dimensions, whereas Inova Petro, despite substantial resources, showed misalignment between technical requirements and industry capabilities and weak market-shaping mechanisms. Read through the framework, the comparison indicates that mission-oriented success depends less on possessing individual capacities and capabilities than on aligning and mobilizing them across dimensions. Furthermore, sophisticated design and implementation capabilities are central to translating capacity into impact, particularly when building upon previous experiences. The findings have significant implications for policy design, suggesting that mission-oriented policies should consider existing capacities and capabilities, while simultaneously serving as vehicles for developing new ones through implementation.

title: Science under sanctions: The impact of the entity list on Chinese academic research
abstract: This study examines the effects of geopolitical tensions and technology-related sanctions on academic research, with a focus on the U.S. Entity List's inclusion of Chinese academic institutions. Using a comprehensive dataset of academic publications from the Open Academic Graph, we employ a stacked event study design to estimate the causal effects of the Entity List sanctions on academic research productivity. Our findings reveal that Entity List sanctions reduce the quantity but improve the quality of research output among affected Chinese researchers. Mechanism analyses, supplemented by semi-structured interviews, show that these changes are driven by research diversification and collaboration network reconfiguration. Sanctioned researchers shift toward new topics and form partnerships with non-listed Chinese institutions, which serve as intermediaries that restore access to restricted resources and expose researchers to novel knowledge. Notably, we find no significant decline in collaboration with U.S.-based researchers, suggesting that sanctions reconfigure rather than sever international networks. Theoretically, this study extends the disruption-as-catalyst logic to geopolitically imposed resource constraints, showing that sanctions can trigger productive diversification. By demonstrating that sanctions affect research quantity and quality in opposing directions through specific behavioral mechanisms, this study also reconciles inconsistent findings in prior literature and advances our understanding of how geopolitical tensions reshape the global academic research landscape.

title: Captured participatory institutions: Theory and evidence from Venezuela's Consejos Comunales
abstract: Abstract Can participatory institutions (PIs) facilitate development when captured by the government? We propose an original theoretical framework to investigate how changing incumbent priorities can shape the developmental and political effects of captured PIs. While patrons concerned with survival can force PIs to specialize in political activities, those pursuing regime consolidation may incentivize PIs to multitask, delivering developmental gains and political rewards. We deploy our framework to study Venezuela's Communal Councils. Leveraging difference‐in‐differences analyses, an original survey of Council participants, and 51 interviews with government officials and grassroots Communal Council members, we find that Councils yielded both economic and political returns during an early period marked by political stability and regime consolidation. However, as Venezuela's economic collapse pushed the government into an authoritarian survival mode, Councils became politically specialized. While showing that captured PIs can foster development under certain circumstances, our findings cast doubt on PIs’ development‐enhancing potential under autocracy.

title: Distributive consequences of plurality voting versus proportional representation
abstract: Employing a game-theoretic model of electoral competition, Myerson (1993, American Political Science Review 87 ( 4 ): 856–869) finds that both single-winner plurality voting (PV) and proportional representation (PR) lead to identical equilibrium campaigning strategies, with platform inequalities increasing as the number of political competitors rises. Using the same model, this paper derives and compares the resulting post-election income distributions and associated Gini coefficients. Key findings include: (1) The identical campaigning strategies under PV and PR lead to considerably different post-election income distributions. (2) For any given number of competing parties, PV exhibits comparatively higher inequality. (3) Inequality rises with the number of parties in both electoral systems but increases more rapidly under PV. Notably, when PV is fixed at two parties (Duverger’s law), once the simulated number of parties exceeds five, PR exhibits slightly higher inequality, challenging the belief that PR is inherently the more equal electoral system.

title: Governing Party Issue Ownership and How Citizens Assess Conditions
abstract: It is well-documented that Americans perceive conditions more favorably when their preferred party is in power. This study considers a second, more subtle, but potentially impactful partisan bias: that the governing party’s policy reputations lead voters to perceive better conditions on the issues it “owns.” In US politics, voters trust Democrats more on environmental, healthcare, education, and safety net issues while Republicans are favored on immigration, crime, defense, and keeping taxes low. In two studies, I observe whether these reputations also impact perceptions when each party is in power. First, I analyze hundreds of survey toplines from Gallup Trends, dating from 1956 to the present, about public perceptions on a variety of party-owned policy areas. Second, to leverage greater variation in control of subnational government, I analyze seven surveys that ask about state-level conditions as well. While results from the former analysis are only suggestive, both approaches point toward an association between the governing party and how citizens assess conditions on the issues it owns.

title: How Election Fundamentals and Racialized Considerations Shape Asian American Vote Choice Through the Trump Era
abstract: Racial minorities voted for Trump at higher rates in 2024 than in previous elections, prompting renewed interest in the factors driving minority vote choice. Here, we focus on Asian Americans, the fastest growing single-race group in the United States. Bridging theories of economic voting and race-centered explanations, we present a comprehensive, up-to-date account of Asian American vote choice through the Trump era. We analyze the 2024, 2020, and 2016 Collaborative Multiracial Post-Election Surveys to assess indicators of Trump support over time among Asian Americans, with comparative analysis of Black, Latino, and White voters ( N = 24,061). We find that economic considerations shaped vote choice in 2024 among Asian Americans, and all other racial groups. Linked fate remained associated with lower Trump support among Asian Americans in 2024, indicating that race continued to matter even years after the peak of anti-Asian hate. In comparison, linked fate also shaped opposition to Trump among Black voters but not Latinos in 2024. Throughout the Trump era, racial resentment among non-Black racial groups and anti-immigrant sentiment among all racial groups consistently predicted greater Trump support, including Asian Americans, despite their predominantly immigrant-origin backgrounds. This research contributes to growing scholarship that addresses conservatism among minoritized communities.

title: A rationale for political disengagement
Money talks, moderation walks: the centripetal impact of campaign contributions in the U.S. house
Partisan conflict and economic policy uncertainty: insights from a time-varying causality approach
abstract: Abstract How does partisan conflict (PC) relate to economic policy uncertainty (EPU)? When does uncertainty feed back into conflict, and how stable is that link? We examine these dynamics using a time-varying Granger causality framework applied to United States monthly data from 1985 to 2025, combining the PC Index with aggregate and disaggregated EPU subindices. PC consistently precedes spikes in fiscal, tax, spending, and health care uncertainty. In contrast, the predictive direction reverses mainly during large shocks, such as trade conflicts or financial regulation crises, and largely disappears during recessions. Generalised forecast error variance decompositions show that PC shocks account for a modest but non trivial share of forecast error variance in fiscal, tax, spending, and health care uncertainty, while policy shocks in trade and regulatory domains explain a much larger share of the variance in partisan conflict itself. These results reveal asymmetric, time-varying predictive linkages between political polarization and policy uncertainty. The findings, which are based on the decomposition of EPU into its components and time-varying Granger causality, contribute to theories of veto players, gridlock, and signaling by identifying the institutional conditions under which political conflict is associated with greater economic volatility and when policy uncertainty appears to reinforce partisan division.

title: Pension’s resource-time trade-off: the role of inequalities in the design of retirement schemes
Dual regulation and the cost of electricity rents to households: evidence from Texas
From sanctions to incentives: the impact of NextGenerationEU on the European Semester
abstract: Whereas the EU has been effective in designing ex ante conditionality for accession and Euro adoption, it has struggled to influence domestic reforms once membership is secured. Soft coordination instruments, notably the European Semester, have therefore been regarded as weak. In response to the Covid-19 crisis, NextGenerationEU (NGEU) introduced an incentive-based model of conditionality, moving beyond the Semester’s ineffective sanctions. Using binary logistic regression models, this article shows that Country-Specific Recommendations benefiting from NGEU incentives, i.e. CSRs issued in 2019–20 and included into National Recovery and Resilience Plans, display higher implementation rates than those issued before or after. Based on multi-annual evaluations, the analysis reassesses the Semester’s limited impact and examines how legal-institutional, macroeconomic, domestic-political, and sectoral factors shape reform compliance. Overall, the evidence favours incentive-based over sanction-driven conditionality, suggesting that the NGEU experiment offers credible lessons for recasting EU economic governance, with broader implications for theories of supranational compliance.

title: How to fund nonprofits?
abstract: Governments support nonprofits through direct grants and tax incentives for private donations, but the optimal mix of these tools remains unclear. I develop a model in which households donate to multiple causes and the government can use both instruments to support nonprofit funding. A key determinant of the optimal policy mix is tax discrimination, defined as the ability to vary tax incentives by cause. When tax discrimination is feasible, warm-glow giving makes private funding more efficient, reducing the need for grants. However, when tax discrimination is constrained, grants become essential to compensate for the rigidity of the tax system. In a calibrated example, the optimal government share of nonprofit funding rises from 0% to 60% as tax discrimination becomes more limited. When donations are leaky, delivering less than a dollar of value per dollar given, the importance of tax discrimination declines. In the extreme case of uniform leakage, Pareto efficiency can be achieved with grants and a linear tax credit, uniform across causes, similar to the systems currently implemented in Belgium, France, or New Zealand.

title: Safety net payment digitization and participant outcomes: Evidence from the WIC EBT transition
Turning inward and/or outward: Which socioemotional skills pay for agribusiness entrepreneurs in Nigeria?
Road to Resilience: Floods, Highways and Indian Informal Manufacturing
Not All Tides Lift the Boat: Boundary of Informativeness of Uncertainty Indices
abstract: In this article, we model the endogenous boundary of informativeness of uncertainty indices (UIs) using a panel threshold framework, employing both static LS and dynamic system-GMM specifications, and gauge the predictive power of these thresholds on economic outcomes. Specifically, we identified critical thresholds where UI shifts from background noise (uninformative) to a decisive factor (informative) in renewable energy (RE) adoption decisions. We find that the negative relationship between the UIs and energy transition is only significant and identified in the regime where uncertainty is relatively low, whereas the prediction power fails (becomes insignificant) in the high-uncertainty regimes. This suggests that the informational utility of UIs in driving (or forecasting) RE adoption operates conditionally upon moderate uncertainty levels. To explain the heterogeneous informativeness of UIs and validate the variations in our identified thresholds, we further conduct channel analyses. Relying on theoretical frameworks from risk literature, we show that risk preference, information overload, and priority concern theories can explain the level of threshold effects (informativeness) of UIs on economic outcomes. These findings provide an actionable insight for policymakers towards designing preemptive risk triggers when uncertainty crosses a critical threshold by frontloading investment activities in clean energy technologies to safeguard green energy transition pathways from headwinds of uncertainties.

title: Survival Is Triumph Enough: Rhythmic Resilience Amid Chronic Adversity and Acute Shocks
abstract: Contexts of adversity generate a wide range of challenges that expose entrepreneurs to compounding hardship yet paradoxically stimulate entrepreneurship as a means of regaining control. Existing research often portrays adversity in two distinct ways, either as a one-time disruptive event or as a persistent condition of the same underlying hardship, overlooking how adversity increasingly unfolds as chronic adversity compounded by multiple acute shocks—a setting that characterizes the lived reality of many entrepreneurs in today’s turbulent world. In such contexts, entrepreneurial resilience is not oriented toward recovery or thriving but toward enduring recurring crises, resource scarcity, and persistent uncertainty. We conducted an inductive, longitudinal study of 32 displaced entrepreneurs living in conflict-affected regions of Iraq. Our analysis reveals a process model of rhythmic resilience in a context of chronic adversity compounded by acute shocks. We show that resilience unfolds through dynamic cycles of withdrawal, reengagement, and adaptation over time that sustain survival across household, venture, and community levels. Yet these processes entail difficult trade-offs, giving rise to a resilience–survival paradox in which entrepreneurs protect survival at the expense of personal well-being, business growth, and social ties.

title: Constructing a laissez-faire narrative of industrialization: Hong Kong at the 1970 World Expo
abstract: In 1970, the Hong Kong pavilion at the World Exposition in Osaka offered a narrative of free trade and laissez-faire. It was a narrative that came to impact all subsequent interpretations of the territory’s economic development right up to the present day. This article examines the circumstances behind the pavilion and analyses the ideas and interests involved in creating the narrative. It argues that this narrative was a particular interpretation of Hong Kong’s development and contrary to existing understandings, it was not natural but rather actively constructed in response to an unstable international context that threatened economic development. Drawing on local archives, the article further argues that the narrative presented at Expo ’70 came to be appropriated by economists not only in explanation of Hong Kong, but also to support neoclassical theories of national economic development.

title: Social Work on the China-Myanmar Border: State-NGO Synchronization
abstract: This article investigates the evolving relationship between the Chinese state and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) through the case of Ruili, a county-level city on the China-Myanmar frontier. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and extensive archival records, we develop an analytical framework of synchronization for the Chinese state and NGOs to capture how the relationship between them has changed. The analysis identifies four stages: a compensatory phase, in which foreign NGOs filled governance gaps and nurtured local capacity; a parallel growth phase, in which domestic NGOs and local governments expanded activities together; an alignment phase, in which NGOs reoriented themselves to implement national strategies such as rural revitalization and public health security; and a global outreach phase, in which selected NGOs extended their services abroad within the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). We present a case in which a welfare NGO working on cross-border social problems developed its operations alongside local state agencies. This article contributes to current debates on the adaptation of Chinese NGOs to a new environment by showing how coproduction, strategic alignment, and bounded negotiation have unfolded over time in a politically sensitive frontier setting.

title: Three Configurations of In‐House Government Consulting: Public‐Value Purpose and Organizational Viability
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments have created in‐house consulting organizations to reduce dependence on external firms and retain public capability and control. Yet organizations grouped under this label pursue different forms of public value that require different designs. This article distinguishes three reasons for a dedicated unit: retaining control over consequential work, capturing returns from problems that recur across government, and mobilizing expertise dispersed across public and adjacent institutions. It develops three corresponding configurations—Strategic Transformation, Scalable Solutions, and Expertise Platform—and shows how choices about work, staffing, knowledge, authority, client relationships, financing, and evaluation must fit together. Documentary comparison of eight units in five countries grounds the analysis. The cases show that viability depends on whether work renews the conditions needed for subsequent work and that evaluation must reflect configuration and stage. Internalization is therefore organization‐building, not the reversal of a procurement decision: a unit creates public value only when work reproduces the conditions on which that value depends.

title: Managers as message makers: a conjoint experiment on information framing and citizen support for local sales tax referenda
abstract: Local option sales taxes in the United States are an interesting form of direct democracy that is influenced directly by public managers. The referenda, or ballot measures, in which people vote on sales taxes have multiple features that can be presented in a variety of ways. As such, they represent a unique opportunity to study the behavioral impact of options and information on citizen choice. With this research, we develop a novel experiment that uses the logic of a conjoint design by varying all of the key features in the referenda, but presents that information in a paragraph form that mimics the format of actual referenda. Results of this sales tax ballot conjoint experiment show that, in general, people only focus on a few key pieces of information, but specific sub-groups are interested in more and different features of the proposed sales tax. This suggests that managers may have more influence among key demographics, and knowing the attributes that matter to those demographics may help shape how sales tax ballot referenda are presented.

title: Expansive Public Service Delivery: Advancing Public Value Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT Public administration has traditionally emphasized the normative ideal that public agencies have a responsibility to improve the lives of communities through public service delivery. We turn to public libraries to explore possibilities for what we call Expansive Public Service Delivery. Expansive Public Service Delivery is defined by a mission to serve all, professional and ethical responsibilities, and proactive responsiveness through outreach and (re)assessment. Public libraries have long aimed to improve communities and advance democracy by providing open, free information access to all. Today, they also proactively seek to expand their services to underserved groups ensuring their relevance and mission achievement. This research draws from 25 in‐depth qualitative interviews to explore librarian narratives to identify four core responsibilities that constitute Expansive Public Service Delivery. We conclude with a discussion of how service for all, professionalism, ethical responsibility, and reflexive decision‐making around community needs can result in more vibrant, sustainable public organizations.

title: Democratic Backsliding and Governance Outcomes: Measuring Administrative and Political Channels of Decline
abstract: ABSTRACT Democratic backsliding has emerged as a defining political challenge of the contemporary era, yet systematic cross‐national evidence linking it to governance outcomes remains scarce. This article argues that backsliding affects governance through two analytically distinct channels: a political accountability channel, whereby weakened contestation and oversight reduce the external costs of poor performance; and an administrative channel, through which executive politicization erodes meritocratic recruitment and bureaucratic impartiality. Using a country‐year panel of 86 countries from 1996 to 2024 and generalized structural equation models, we decompose the direct, indirect, and total effects of backsliding on government effectiveness, regulatory quality, and control of corruption across stages of democratic decline. The findings show that governance deterioration is stage‐specific, channel‐specific, and outcome‐specific, following a nonlinear, U‐shaped pattern in which complete erosion—rather than autocratic reversion—produces the largest governance losses.

title: Why Comply? Explaining Sectoral Patterns in GRECO 'S Anti‐Corruption Recommendations
abstract: ABSTRACT Why do states vary in their compliance with international anti‐corruption recommendations? Research often treats the state as a unitary actor and explains variation at country‐level. This article challenges that assumption by examining variation in compliance across institutional sectors within countries. Using original data from the Council of Europe's Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), the analysis shows a clear sectoral pattern. Recommendations addressed to prosecutors are implemented most frequently, followed by those targeting judges, while recommendations directed at members of parliament show the lowest levels of compliance. The article explains this variation through the political economy of target compliance. Reform outcomes depend on the interaction between the political costs imposed by reform and the degree of control that targeted actors exercise over its implementation. We find little evidence that country‐level factors shape reform outcomes, while sector‐specific incentives provide a stronger explanation for compliance patterns. By highlighting the importance of the target population, the article contributes to research on international compliance, anti‐corruption governance, and international monitoring mechanisms.

title: Partisanship, Public Service Values, and Public Service Recognition Week Proclamations
abstract: Since 1985, Public Service Recognition Week acknowledges the role of government employees in American democracy. Building upon the study of public service values, this research investigates gubernatorial proclamations issued in 2025, treating that years as a crucial case for the study of government employee recognition. Despite instability in the U.S. federal government, state-level proclamations illustrate a consistent emphasis on common public service values, including commitment, integrity, and professionalism. The analysis of proclamation content shows some variation in the values emphasized by the two major political parties, but no statistically discernable relationship between gubernatorial party and proclamation issuance. Still, only about one third of U.S. governors issued proclamations for Public Service Recognition Week in 2025, pointing to the need for ongoing scrutiny of employee recognition practices at the state and national level. This research closes by comparing state-level action to presidential proclamations from 1987 to 2024 and discusses implications for the application of public service value theory to the study of state government employment and employee recognition.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: From Policy Design to Implementation: An Evaluation of Inclusive Employment Policies in Quebec
abstract: Abstract This article critically evaluates inclusive employment policies in the Canadian province of Quebec. Through a review of inclusive employment literature, we first find that the current Quebec policy landscape does not align with best practices. Using the policy cycle framework, we then compare the design of Quebec's employment policies to their implementation, finding that there are tensions between the two. A review of what is happening on the ground in Quebec, through an analysis of government spending documents, sheds light on the discrepancies between policy design and implementation.

title: Normalizing and abnormalizing prostitution: the productive role of policy implementation practices in shaping governmental problematizations
abstract: This paper examines how governmental understandings of prostitution are shaped and transformed through policy implementation. While prostitution policies are often based on implicit governmental problematizations, these are traditionally studied through textual and discursive analysis. Using a case study on the local governance of prostitution, this study explores how implementation practices also actively reshape these problematizations. Drawing on a typology of normalizing and abnormalizing approaches, the paper analyzes two policy programs: (1) sex worker exit programs and (2) the prohibition and policing of prostitution from homes (PFH). Although both originate from abnormalizing perspectives, the study shows how implementation practices introduce and reinforce normalizing ambitions. The findings demonstrate both the adaptability and persistence of governmental problematizations, emphasizing the productive role of implementation in policy development. Ultimately, the paper highlights the resilience of the Dutch “normalizing” approach to prostitution governance.

title: Evidence-based policy making in Japan (2016–23): institutional setting, administrative interpretation and barriers to implementation
abstract: Introduction: This article examines how evidence-based policy making (EBPM) has been institutionally situated and interpreted within Japan’s central administrative system, and what this reveals about barriers to its implementation. Methods/Data: The study uses document analysis of Policy Evaluation Expert Committee minutes from 17 central ministries and agencies from 2016 to 2023. The dataset comprises 131 meeting minutes and 374 EBPM-related statements. The study first examines the institutional setting in which EBPM has been introduced, then analyses how EBPM is interpreted, and finally identifies barriers. Findings: Japanese EBPM is operationalised through existing policy evaluation and administrative project review arrangements. It is interpreted mainly as a reform-oriented practice aimed at improving policy rationality, reviewability and internal coordination, while policy effectiveness validation remains limited. The main barriers are primarily institutional, especially conceptual ambiguity and fragmented institutional alignment. Conclusion/Implications: The study provides a systematic and empirically grounded account of how EBPM is interpreted and operationalised within Japan’s central ministries. It shows that EBPM is a context-shaped practice, whose operation is shaped by administrative systems, institutional settings and evidence demand. These findings highlight the need to analyse EBPM in relation to the institutional environment in which it is embedded.

title: Comparative study on the evolution of elderly attitudes towards government welfare responsibilities in East Asian welfare regimes
abstract: This study employs quantitative analysis of ISSP Role of Government modules to examine the elderly attitudes towards government welfare responsibilities in Japan, South Korea, and the Taiwan region of China. Findings reveal significant shifts over decades. In 2006, seniors in South Korea and the Taiwan region of China reported the highest scores, and the Taiwan region of China continued to lead in both 2006 and 2016. Across the survey waves, Japan experienced the most pronounced attitudinal fluctuations, South Korea showed moderate variability, and the Taiwan region of China demonstrated remarkable stability. Further analysis indicates that these differential patterns within the same welfare regime are shaped by temporal, national/regional, and individual-level factors. This comparative study illustrates that the East Asian welfare regime exhibits significant internal diversity alongside common traits. By documenting divergent attitudinal trajectories (e.g. Taiwan’s stability vs. Japan’s fluctuations) and linking them to distinct national institutional pathways, this research challenges the static and homogeneous conception of the ‘East Asian welfare model’. It contributes to the theorizing intra-regime variation and offers a foundation for crafting context-sensitive welfare policies.

title: How exceptionalism endures: incumbents’ ideational power and narrative strategies in the Common Agricultural Policy
abstract: Despite growing pressures for reform, the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) exhibits strong policy endurance. As core incumbents in EU agricultural policy-making, farmers’ organisations have successfully neutralised criticism and sustained dominance of exceptionalist ideas. This article analyses how farmers’ interest groups, as incumbent actors, exercise ideational power to resist challenges in CAP’s policy-making. Combining a discursive institutionalist lens with the Narrative Policy Framework, it shows how incumbents deploy power through ideas by engaging in narrative strategies aimed at preserving the CAP ideational core. Focusing on the 2017–2021 reform process and using Discourse Network Analysis, the article reveals that farmers’ organisations strategically combine exceptionalist narratives with selective co-optation of alternative ideas to legitimise the policy core while responding to criticisms. In doing so, they actively contribute to the CAP endurance by adapting the ideational core without transforming it. By demonstrating how incumbents sustain and adapt dominant ideas though narrative strategies, this article advances discursive institutionalism by offering an operationalisation of ideational power in empirical policy analysis.

title: Whose Digital Future? Civil Society and Alternative Imaginaries in Transnational Digital Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT This article investigates different visions of digital futures, examining how desired futures are discursively constructed within civil society in transnational digital governance. The analysis builds on discourse theory and a growing body of research on imaginaries in digital governance. Through a discourse‐theoretical analysis of submission papers to the United Nations' Global Digital Compact, the article examines how different collective actors within civil society construct and mobilise desired futures in the institutional context of the UN. The study finds discursive elements that articulate three distinct digital futures: technological progress, societal balance and transformative change. While their objectives, obstacles and enablers are constructed in diverse ways, in all three, digital technologies are considered necessary. By illuminating different normative values and the affective potential through which individuals and collectives are positioned in relation to desired futures, these findings show a variety of articulations within civil society and offer insights into its normative and political roles. In doing so, this study contributes to an understanding of the possibilities and limitations of alternatives in digital governance.

title: Puzzling through a pandemic: theorizing the effect of public puzzling on policy decision making and public trust
Up or Down? Experimental Evidence on Spillover Effects of Corruption on Political Trust in Hierarchical Governance
Data and methods for identifying artificial intelligence-related patents
abstract: This paper evaluates existing approaches to identifying artificial intelligence (AI)-related patents and introduces a novel, scalable framework for improving classification performance. Motivated by growing reliance on patent data in innovation research, we assess widely used methods, including patent class-based approaches and the USPTO’s Artificial Intelligence Patent Dataset (AIPD), with an independent, human-expert-annotated ground-truth dataset. We document substantial performance limitations in existing approaches, particularly in terms of precision and generalizability. To address these challenges, we develop a CPC-informed, iterative positive-unlabeled (PU) learning framework for constructing high-quality training data. Our approach integrates hierarchical patent classification with data-driven refinement procedures to reduce label noise and improve representativeness. Using this refined dataset, we train a range of machine learning, deep learning, and transformer-based models. Our results show that models trained within our framework significantly outperform existing methods, including AIPD, achieving improvements over AIPD in F1 scores of approximately 18–21% on the same benchmark dataset. These gains are primarily driven by enhanced precision without sacrificing recall, highlighting the central role of training data quality in classification performance. We further demonstrate the empirical value of improved AI patent identification through two applications, showing that the release of ChatGPT increased both the market valuation of AI patents and firms’ allocation of innovative effort toward AI technologies. To support future research, we release our training data, source code, and patent-level predictions, with ongoing updates to reflect the evolving nature of AI innovation.

title: When marriage ends: Divorce and the erosion of conservative political alignment
Defending water, defending place: Water insecurity and neighbour-based organising in Mexico City's popular neighbourhoods
Electoral incentives when the stakes are low: a case study from an economics department
abstract: Abstract Since the pioneering work of Lizzeri and Persico (2001), it has been well known that, in winner-take-all systems, office-motivated politicians may favor targeted redistribution over the provision of public goods. Motivated by the possibility that similar incentives may arise even in small organizations, we examine a policy proposal to revise a journal-ranking system in a medium-sized Economics Department. At the same time, a majority of faculty members signed a petition on an unrelated issue publicly supporting the department’s governance. Using individual publication records, we analyze whether the distributional consequences of the proposed reform were systematically related to such support. We find that faculty members who signed the petition were significantly more likely to benefit from the initial proposal, while this association became considerably weaker after an open departmental discussion and a subsequent revision of the proposal. The observed pattern is consistent with theories emphasizing distributive incentives and the disciplining role of transparency in collective decision-making though alternative readings of the revision cannot be excluded.

title: Escaping temporary traps? Evidence from age-based incentives to permanent employment
abstract: This paper studies how reducing the cost differential between permanent and temporary contracts affects firms’ use of each contract type. We analyze a 1997 Spanish reform that lowered non-wage labor costs for new open-ended (OE) contracts for workers under 30 and over 45, while leaving short-term (ST) contracts unaffected. Exploiting sectoral exposure and age-based discontinuities, we show that firms substitute strongly from ST to OE contracts for young workers but respond little for older workers. We find partial wage incidence of the subsidy on directly affected permanent jobs. The implied elasticity of substitution between ST and OE contracts is 6.5 for workers below age 30 and close to zero for workers above age 45. We also document that young workers’ wages rise in unsubsidized ST jobs consistent with the expansion of OE employment strengthening their outside options. Overall, the results reveal sharp age asymmetries in contract substitution. They suggest that monetary incentives can facilitate transitions from temporary to permanent employment for young workers, but are less effective for workers above age 45.

title: From prison peers to co-offenders
abstract: International audience

title: Race-to-the-bottom dynamics in industrial land pricing: Asymmetric effects of China’s 2009 price floor adjustment policy
Gender quotas and female entrepreneurship: evidence from Italian municipalities
The impacts of high-speed Internet access on monopsony power
The comparative statics of dominance
abstract: In finite problems comprising objects, cases, and an object- and case-contingent payoff function, we study the comparative statics of the set of undominated objects, meaning those for which there exists no mixture over objects that is superior in every case. We consider both weak and strict dominance (corresponding to different degrees of ‘strictness’ in the definition of superiority). Our main theorem characterises those payoff transformations which robustly expand the not-weakly-dominated and not-strictly-dominated sets: the necessary and sufficient condition is that payoffs be transformed separately across cases, in either a monotone–concave or a constant manner. We apply our results to Pareto frontiers and games.

title: Intergenerational Cultural Transmission with Social Interactions as An Evolutionary Game
The Dynamics of Gender Norms and Fertility Decline
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper models fertility as the outcome of gender‐biased technological progress interacting with endogenous social norms governing childcare. When rising female wages outpace norm adjustment, the inherited norm makes reallocating childcare toward fathers costly, so mothers bear a disproportionate burden and the shadow price of children rises. In cross‐country data, fertility falls faster where women's relative standing rises, especially where norms are tighter or more rigid. Calibrated to South Korea (1976–2016), the model shows that strong, slow‐adjusting norms deepen the decline. Despite smaller short‐run effects, male childcare subsidies yield larger long‐run gains than female subsidies by accelerating convergence to egalitarian norms.

title: How IoT Enables the Protective Action Decision Model (PADM) During a Wildfire Event
abstract: This article highlights the growing importance of air quality assessment, particularly given the increased frequency and severity of climate-driven wildfires. Recent research suggests that wildfire particulate matter may be more toxic than equivalent amounts of ambient PM2.5, with smoke composition and the different stages of biomass combustion having varying health impacts. This article examines how public managers and decision-makers can use Internet of Things (IoT) devices to make decisions using hyper-local, real-time data on air quality, particularly data on levels of fine particulate matter (PM2.5). We surveyed Oregon residents following the 2020 wildfires, the region's most severe fire season in modern history. We received a total of 1200 responses from June to August 2021 to help assess how individuals responded to several major wildfires that hit the state in 2020. Results indicate that residents were overwhelmed by the data and were provided with inadequate guidance on how to respond to the dangers posed by the smoke.

title: Web crawling in public administration research
abstract: Improvements in computational power and artificial intelligence technology are transforming science, including public administration research. Techniques from the computer sciences, such as web crawling, can improve data collection and analysis. However, they remain underutilized, and the literature exploring their potential in public administration research is limited. This paper aims to fill this gap by analyzing the opportunities and limitations of web crawling for data collection by answering two research questions: what opportunities and limitations does web crawling offer compared to manual web data collection, and under what conditions is web crawling an effective data collection method in public administration research? We draw on theoretical considerations from existing literature, prior empirical evidence, and insights from our own research. Based on our analysis, we highlight the benefits of the immense scalability, efficiency, and consistency that a web crawler can provide for creating large datasets, while cautioning against their use in smaller-scale research, where high setup costs, expertise requirements, and limited flexibility may outweigh potential advantages. Additionally, we provide guidelines on when and how to use web crawlers usefully in public administration research. Points for practitioners The paper evaluates the opportunities and limitations of using web crawling as a data collection technique in public administration research. The evaluation is based on existing empirical evidence, as well as experience from a research project. Web crawling can be a highly useful tool that complements traditional qualitative and quantitative methods in various contexts. When comparing web crawling to the manual collection of web data, two points stand out as particularly relevant, both within and beyond research contexts: first, web crawling generally comes with significant setup costs but is highly efficient in execution. This makes it highly scalable and particularly suitable for collecting large amounts of data. Second, proper implementation of a web crawler requires significant information technology expertise.
