Close collaboration between those who want to use the data and the information technology experts implementing the data collection is recommended to ensure that relevant, high-quality data can be obtained.

title: Face‐to‐Face With Administrative Burdens: Design Simplification, Emotional Costs, and Procedural Outcomes in Digital Welfare Applications
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent scholarship on administrative burden has increasingly focused on psychological costs, design interventions, and digital burdens. This study combines these interests and examines the psychological costs of negative emotions during administrative encounters at varying levels of digital maturity. Building on affective events theory and employing facial coding in a controlled experiment, the study demonstrates that negative emotions rise during bureaucratic encounters, with frustration resulting in more errors made by applicants. Simplifying the procedure through pre‐filled forms does not reduce negative emotional arousal; however, it enhances satisfaction with the procedure. Vulnerable citizens, as indicated by low education and foreign citizenship, benefit more from this informational integration than other groups, suggesting that procedural redesign can enhance the inclusiveness of public service delivery. Overall, the research advances both scholarly and practical understanding of the emotional dimension of administrative burdens from a process‐oriented perspective, highlighting the persistent challenge of reducing emotional costs to enhance citizen experiences.

title: Clarifying Public Policy for Stronger Public Administration in Development
abstract: ABSTRACT Public policy is ubiquitous, yet its meaning is often unclear. This ambiguity is not just conceptual. Because policy work is a large part of what public administrations do, how we define policy shapes how we structure and organize our administrative mechanisms. Varying, incomplete, or misguided views of what policy work involves can thus easily lead to fragmented or misaligned administrative systems. This is a particular challenge in developing country contexts, where views of policy work may not fit what this work requires—setting countries up for administrative confusion and functional failure. This article responds to such challenge by attempting to clarify what public policy work involves. Through a study of 150 public policy definitions, it identifies six essential elements of public policy work—or the fundamental abilities that administrative systems need to facilitate for this work: to establish policy purpose and objectives; to devise solutions and strategy; to mobilize actors and authority; to ensure effective decision‐making; to engage with context; and to accomodate appropriate process choices. These elements are presented as a set of core questions that policy work must engage, providing a practical framework for designing administrative systems that are better structured to do such work. In clarifying what public policy work involves, therefore, the article aims to help strengthen public administration in and for development.

title: Towards inclusive prosperity: comparative analysis of Indigenous procurement policies in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand
abstract: Indigenous procurement is widely promoted as an instrument of economic reconciliation, yet headline gains often mask limited transformational impact. Applying McCrudden’s social procurement framework, we conduct a systematic cross-national comparison of identity-specific procurement architectures across Canada, Australia, and Aotearoa New Zealand. We show that contract values cluster heavily within major metropolitan hubs and narrow industry sectors, leaving remote and early-stage community enterprises marginalized. Furthermore, persistent cross-national data gaps and aggregated reporting conceal these structural inequities while enabling policy distortions like fronting. We recommend structural reforms including regional benchmarks and independent auditing to align procurement with genuine Indigenous economic sovereignty.

title: Why Street-Level Bureaucrats Leave: The Effects of Organizational Transparency and Role Conflict
abstract: Street-level bureaucrats often lack workplace clarity, which contributes to higher turnover. Drawing on street-level bureaucracy theory and the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines how organizational transparency and role conflict, two dimensions of workplace clarity, shape turnover intentions among social workers in Chinese nonprofit organizations. Using multilevel data from the China Social Work Longitudinal Study, we find that organizational transparency reduces and role conflict increases turnover intentions. Value fit mediates both relationships, and job autonomy moderates them by enhancing the benefits of organizational transparency and buffering the harms of role conflict. Findings validate the extension of street-level bureaucracy theory to the nonprofit context and offer actionable insights for improving workforce stability in a complex governance environment.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Developing and implementing a large-scale summit to improve health services delivery for rural, remote and Indigenous populations
abstract: Inequities persist in health services delivery for rural, remote and Indigenous populations internationally. These populations require attention to improve health outcomes for individuals, communities, providers and the health system. Strong collaboration and trusting relationships in rural and Indigenous communities in British Columbia (BC), Canada enabled rapid health services delivery changes in rural BC in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. In June 2020, the Rural Coordination Centre of BC and First Nations Health Authority co-hosted the BC Rural and First Nations Health and Wellness Summit to collaborate with community and organizational partners to identify needs and co-create actions required to address priorities in rural health services delivery. The aim of this article is to provide information on the innovative practices of the 2020 Summit as a knowledge-to-action approach for health services delivery redesign and to share these learnings with other organizations planning large events featuring dialogue among participants distributed throughout a large area. Key learnings from the Summit include: (1) the importance of building on pre-existing and current relationships to facilitate Summit discussions in a virtual environment; (2) detailed planning and technological expertise are needed to implement large events; and (3) a carefully co-created agenda are necessary to generate buy-in and participation from partner organizations.

title: Strengthening international evidence-informed policy making: lessons from the Global South
Diagnosing Institutional Design‐Implementation Gaps: A Dual‐Layer Systems Modeling Language Protocol for Visualizing Institutional Change Mechanisms
Global market integration, national security salience, and new product development alliances in aircraft manufacturing
Constructing Responsibility in Mental Health Policy: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Educational and Vocational Support for Young Adults in Sweden's National Strategy
abstract: ABSTRACT How mental health policy is formulated shape interpretations of responsibility and actions, making language analysis crucial for understanding its impact on welfare practices. This paper explores how responsibility for educational and vocational support for young adults with mental health problems is constructed in Swedish mental health policy. Using Critical Discourse Analysis and legitimation analysis, three key national policy documents are analysed. Findings reveal that responsibility is constructed as collective yet expressed through language diffusing accountability. While moral legitimation strategies are prevalent, rationalization and neoliberal principles such as efficiency, activation and individual responsibility are prominent. Young adults are positioned as both vulnerable and responsible, expected to participate in education and employment, reflecting an activation discourse, instrumentalizing mental health as a resource for economic productivity. Neoliberal discursive patterns shift responsibility from central authorities to local actors and individuals, risking unequal support. Despite emphasis on education as a protective factor, higher education is notably absent risking to exclude support for young adults in this arena. National policy should strengthen clarity of responsibility to prevent diffusion and promote equality. Otherwise, mental health policy risks becoming an aspiration rather than a framework for justice. Social work practice should advocate structural solutions and inclusive policies that recognize mental health as a social right to prevent further marginalizing young adults with mental health problems.

title: A theory of political divergence and gradual institutional change
abstract: Abstract Why do some societies succeed in breaking away from historical traditions while others remain trapped? This paper proposes a formal theory to investigate the interaction between short‐run and long‐run political dynamics, highlighting a co‐evolution of political institutions and social structures. A society consists of various social groups, such as the rulers, the elites, and the commoners. Short‐run strategic considerations give rise to different coalitions among these groups, which determine not only political regimes but also redistribution policies. In the long run, these policies shape the accumulation of wealth and power, where small initial differences can lead to divergent paths of development. Finally, the paper examines three historical case studies on medieval Europe, imperial China, and the medieval Muslim world to illustrate potential pathways of long‐run political development.

title: Correction: Irregularities in Perez Brower (2024), “Reframing Gendered Issues: Intersectional Identity Frames and Policy Agendas”
Not‐so‐great expectations: Outgroup indifference facilitates conflict resolution in negatively interdependent contexts
abstract: Abstract We examined how responses to outgroup indifference in conflict are shaped by the perceived nature of interdependence, which changes expectations of outgroup emotions toward the ingroup. Unlike conflicts perceived as positively interdependent, we hypothesized that in conflicts perceived as negatively interdependent, outgroup indifference would constitute a positive expectancy violation, thereby inviting favorable responses. Moreover, we examined affective and inferential processes as mediators across four studies ( N = 2521). In Study 1, outgroup indifference (vs. anger and hatred but not hope) reduced negative emotions (but did not affect expected collaboration), subsequently increasing support for cooperation. Study 2 added qualitative measures and showed that outgroup indifference (vs. anger) increased support for cooperation through decreased negative emotions and increased expected collaboration. Study 3 provided correlational evidence that perceptions of interdependence predict participants' expectations of outgroup emotions. Lastly, in Study 4, outgroup indifference increased expected collaboration and emotions when interdependence was perceived as negative.

title: Does disability trump family background? Determinants of electoral participation among young individuals with intellectual disability
abstract: Abstract Systematic differences of electoral participation between various social groups indicate crucial constraints of comprehensive democratic inclusion. Yet, there is a dearth of research on electoral participation among individuals with intellectual disability (ID), whose participation rates are considerably lower than among non‐ID citizens. This study examines determinants of electoral participation among individuals with ID based on administrative records covering five cohorts of individuals from the Swedish upper‐secondary school for pupils with ID ( N = 8438), and their parents. Our main results indicate that the severity of the disability and parents who have voted are the strongest predictors of voting among individuals with ID. The latter suggests that family background is vital. However, the socioeconomic status of the families, such as parents' level of education, income, and occupation, are less pivotal factors.

title: Supporting learning in and out of school: Experimental evidence from India
abstract: Although targeted educational interventions for primary school children in low-income countries have led to substantial improvements in learning, the extent of their effectiveness varies considerably across studies, raising questions about how to adapt them to different settings. This paper examines a novel primary education program that combines a conventional in-school targeted pedagogical intervention with an out-of-school study group initiative facilitated by the community. We use a cross-cutting randomized experiment design across 200 villages in Assam, India. Our results show that standalone implementation of either component has no significant effect on learning outcomes, but when the components are combined in the full program they improve children’s test scores in mathematics and language by 0.11 and 0.09 standard deviations, respectively. The analysis highlights that the combined program increases program awareness and take-up, thereby increasing program effectiveness.

title: Is drug-related violence fueling emigration from Central America?
Sailing in calmer waters: Trade policy uncertainty and product quality
Review of “Fighting for a Foothold: How Government and Markets Undermine Black Middle-Class Suburbia”
Defended neighborhoods, vulnerable routines: routine activities, collective efficacy, and the social ecology of discrimination
Review of “Detroit Never Left: Black Space, White Borders, Latino Crossings”
When Communication Enables Catastrophe: Nuclear Risk and the Short Lifetimes of Technological Civilizations
abstract: The Fermi paradox may partly reflect technological self-destruction acting as a Great Filter during post-industrial development. Because the empirical record consists of a single civilization observed over an eighty-year nuclear age, the exercise reported here is best understood as a structured, historically anchored scenario analysis rather than a data-driven statistical estimate. We develop a time-varying hazard model to estimate civilizational survival under nuclear risk, using Earth's documented close calls as an illustrative case. A Bayesian survival-analysis framework with regime-switching hazards captures temporal non-stationarity between Cold War and post-Cold War periods and propagates parameter uncertainty. Under high-alert nuclear postures, estimated annual hazards range from roughly 0.1% to 2%, implying median survival times on the order of decades to millennia conditional on institutional configuration. These hazards plausibly exceed natural extinction risks but may decline substantially with improved governance and control systems. The results bound detectable civilizational longevity and offer conditional implications for existential-risk prioritization and SETI expectations under deep uncertainty.

title: Incident Risk Prediction for Global Maritime Networks Under a Changing Climate
abstract: Maritime risk is a fundamental component of operational cost and decision-making in global container shipping, yet quantitative, route-comparable risk estimates, especially in monetary terms and under future climate conditions, remain limited. This study develops a climate-driven Bayesian network (BN)-based Global Maritime Incident Risk Assessment and Prediction tool to quantify how projected future climate conditions may alter maritime incident risks at the grid-cell, link, and route levels. Global open waters are partitioned into 2° × 2° grid cells, and route risk is computed by aggregating cell-level risk along a path. The framework combines: (1) an estimate of incident occurrence probability derived from historical traffic and incident patterns, (2) two tree augmented BN models that predict incident type and then severity using discretized climate and bathymetry variables, and (3) monetary consequence values to express risk in real units ($ per voyage). Using monthly climate projections for 2025-2069, the approach is demonstrated on container routes in the 2M alliance network. In addition to grid cell, link and route-based incident probabilities and their projections, a key contribution is interpretable, global monetary risk values and predictions that enable direct comparison of competing routes.

title: Lisa Robinson: Benefit–Cost Analyses for Evidence‐Based Decisions
Adverse selection with sequential risks
Countering Organizational Rigidity Through Operational Resource Bundling: Integrating Resource Orchestration and Dynamic Capabilities
abstract: As organizations mature, standardized systems help meet increasing needs for efficiency. However, this often results in resources being used in rigid ways, compromising the flexibility necessary to leverage opportunities, create value, and address customers’ emerging needs. Here we address solutions to this drift to rigidity, focusing on how operational managers bundle resources to create value for the firm. Our qualitative study is based on data collected from an organization with operations across 252 locations. This data consists of 92 interviews with strategic and operational managers, ethnographic observations, and archival records. We uncovered three pathways for resource bundling that are focused on markets, customers, or organizational renewal. In each, senior-level strategic managers initially provided resources, including channels for standardization, information systems, and technical infrastructure that became rigid in their usage. When operational managers sensed this drift to rigidity, they seized flexible resources (connection, solution development, and employee development processes) to combine with the rigid resources. We refer to this as Operational Resource Bundling (ORB). Strategic managers collaborated with the operational managers to adapt how resources were used, helping to ratify, endorse, and mobilize the bundles to achieve value creation and competitive advantage. We extend earlier work by specifying how a particular type of resource orchestration—ORB—constitutes a value-generating micro-mechanism of dynamic capabilities. ORB uncovers the role of operational managers in balancing standardization versus customization through identifying and combining resources.

title: How Followers Respond to Leader Differentiation: The Importance of Considering All Leader Differentiation Properties
abstract: A central tenet of many leadership theories is that leaders treat their followers differently. Although leader differentiation is ubiquitous, its effects on leaders and followers are not well understood and theory and research have not simultaneously considered its three key properties: Leader–member exchange (LMX) differentiation, LMX quality, and LMX social comparison. We developed a theoretical model in which these three properties interact to influence followers’ supervisory interactional justice perceptions and subsequently their supervisor-directed deviance and supervisor-directed organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs). To test our model, we conducted a pre-registered experiment (Study 1), a single-level, multi-wave study (Study 2), and a multilevel, multi-wave, multisource study (Study 3). Results consistently supported our theoretical model. First, LMX differentiation indirectly influenced supervisor-directed deviance and OCBs via supervisory interactional justice. Second, the three leader differentiation properties interacted to predict supervisory interactional justice. Specifically, when LMX quality and LMX social comparison were both high, the negative impact of LMX differentiation on followers’ supervisory interactional justice perceptions was the weakest and did not reliably differ from zero. Third, when LMX quality and LMX social comparison were both high, LMX differentiation’s positive indirect effect on supervisor-directed deviance, and its negative indirect effect on supervisor-directed OCBs, via supervisory interactional justice perceptions, were the weakest and not reliably different from zero. These are among the first studies to simultaneously theorize and investigate the interactive effects of the three central properties of leader differentiation, and to demonstrate its effects for both followers and leaders.

title: Hold That Thought: Enhancing the Durability of Fact-Checking Effects Through Low-Cost Accuracy Reminders
abstract: Prior evidence suggests that fact-checking can update beliefs regarding factually incorrect information in the short term but its effects often decay rapidly. Such decay raises normative concerns about its sustainability and real-world impact. Here, we examine whether a cognitively efficient, low-cost intervention – called an “accuracy reminder” – can enhance the durability of fact-checking effects. In a large-scale pre-registered panel longitudinal experiment (N = 7,188), participants were randomly assigned to receive fact-checks and, under some conditions, follow-up prompts to reevaluate the same claim at interval-optimized time points. Across topical domains and partisan identities, reminder conditions produced durable belief correction effects lasting up to four weeks, more than doubling the persistence observed without reminders. Effects were robust across reminder frequency and timing, as well as against individual differences, suggesting implementation flexibility and theoretical generalizability. These findings identify retrieval-based reinforcement as a scalable means of sustaining factual belief correction and reinforcing shared factual baselines in spite of cognitive decay and partisan resistance.

title: Rethinking Assumptions About Moral Content Selection: Moral-Emotional Content May Be Less Appealing Than Assumed
abstract: Recent work has shown that moral-emotional content spreads rapidly on social media platforms such as X (Twitter). These patterns have led to concerns that social media facilitates the spread of moral outrage – potentially exacerbating political conflict and animosity. While most past work has focused on the supply side of this phenomenon, i.e. the transmission of morally charged political content, we consider the demand side: do people actually want to see this type of content in their information environment? In this paper, we first theoretically contextualize the motivations to engage with or avoid moral-emotional content. Then, through three pre-registered studies conducted in the U.S. in 2022 and 2023, we test whether people actively choose information that includes moral-emotional elements. Contrary to our initial expectations, we find that participants do not actively select moral-emotional content compared to neutral or emotional content. Despite previous findings on transmission, our results suggest that people may not want to see this type of content in their information environment. By focusing on selection rather than transmission, the findings presented in this paper add another nuance to an ongoing debate on the prevalence and consequences of online political outrage.

title: Tax Mobilization in Africa: Is the Secret Hidden in Women's Political Empowerment?
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the effects of women's political empowerment (WPE) on tax revenue mobilization using a panel sample of 41 African countries over the 2000–2022 period. Utilizing the system Generalized Method of Moments, the empirical results demonstrate that WPE significantly enhances tax revenue mobilization in Africa. This finding remains robust to alternative measures of both WPE and tax revenue. Furthermore, beyond a specific turning point, increased WPE tends to diminish tax revenue mobilization. Finally, the study highlights that WPE operates through several transmission channels, including corruption control, the size of the informal economy, and female labor force participation. In terms of public policy, strengthening gender quotas within the African political sphere is crucial to enhancing tax mobilization. Nonetheless, given the threshold effects identified in this relationship, policymakers must prioritize the quality of women's political representation rather than focusing solely on increasing their numerical representation within political decision‐making circles.

title: Informal Authority, Legitimacy Transition, and Institutional Change: A Theory of Advisory Capture
abstract: ABSTRACT How do informal actors achieve rapid bureaucratic dismantlement without formal authority? Analyzing the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiative, this article argues that when performance‐based legitimacy displaces procedural legitimacy as the dominant evaluative framework, informal actors can bypass established safeguards and reshape government institutions. Three concepts capture this process: advisory capture , legitimacy regime transition , and constrained coercion . The analysis reveals that dismantlement targets agencies based on political vulnerability rather than functional logic, that informal authority becomes institutionalized through formal rulemaking such as the Schedule Policy/Career rule, and that judicial review operates as ongoing contestation rather than definitive constraint. Protecting democratic governance requires defending not only formal rules but the legitimacy regimes within which those rules derive meaning.

title: Sifting Through: Federal Separations in 2025 and Their Implications for Knowledge Loss and Agency Capacity
abstract: ABSTRACT The federal service experienced unprecedented turnover in the first year of the second Trump administration. Early reports have documented the substantial losses of personnel and the politicization and antagonism underlying those changes. This research breaks down separations over the past year, with a focus on the Deferred Resignation Program (DRP), to understand where turnover occurred and how it affected organizational knowledge and capacity. The analysis examines federal workforce data from January 2015 to December 2025 and reveals that the federal service lost substantial expertise and experience through both voluntary and involuntary means of separation. These results shed light on the fallout from 2025 executive actions, clarify the implications for government capacity, and point out prospective pathways for mitigating damages to the federal service moving forward.

title: Power circuit alignment and reform trajectories: a dynamic framework for public management research

title: How we embraced methodological and ethical challenges in our community–academic partnered research about equity in organizational leadership
Tearing social safety net: platform fast-fashion and marginalization of garment workers
abstract: Existing research on platform labour has predominantly focused on service-sector gig workers under direct algorithmic control, leaving manufacturing workers who face indirect algorithmic pressure unexplored. This study investigates why informal garment workers in China’s fast-fashion industry remain excluded from social insurance system. Rather than blaming weak government enforcement, it argues that the platform-driven production regime systematically decouples the production-welfare nexus. First, highly flexible production fragments employment into daily spot-market transactions, dismantling the stable labour relations that employee-based social insurance requires. Second, algorithmic pricing squeezes profit margins, leaving workers’ wages too thin and volatile to sustain fixed social insurance contributions. Third, the industry’s ultra-fast turnover relies on urban villages, where informal spaces make the workforce administratively untraceable to the statutory social insurance system. Together, these three mechanisms accelerate garment workers’ marginalization from existing social insurance system, revealing a fundamental clash between fluid platform capitalism and rigidly status-based East Asian welfare regime.

title: Game of Mirrors for Complex Policies: The Narratives on Differentiated Autonomy in Italy
Federalism, Geography, and the Representation of Cities in the US Congress
Constitutional drafting processes and constitutional success
abstract: Abstract Several recent constitution-making processes have been celebrated for being participatory, inclusive, and representative. However, many of these processes also failed. We theorize that aspects of these kinds of constitutional drafting processes could reduce the probability of constitutional success. To show why, we construct a “Constitution Drafting game” (CD game) in which representatives from different interest groups must draft a constitution. We consider the case where the probability of constitutional success is single peaked, but the value from successful adoption is increasing in the degree of issue protection chosen. The drafting process then leads to protection choices that are above those which maximize the odds of constitutional success. Moreover, when the CD game is equivalent to a “nice aggregative game”, as in Acemoglu and Jensen (2013), the maximum and minimum equilibrium probabilities of constitutional success are decreasing in the number of representatives. Within a more specific game structure, we show that the symmetric equilibrium degree of protection chosen by each representative is decreasing in the number of interest groups represented, while the total degree of protection is increasing in it, leading to lower probabilities of constitutional success. We explain how optimism can exacerbate the degree of protection chosen by each party.

title: Electoral cycles and consumption in India
Do prosecutor and defendant race pairings matter? Evidence from random assignment
Recruiting Talent
abstract: Abstract We study a parsimonious model of a competitive labor market in which firms privately screen workers to identify talent. The equilibrium exhibits dispersion in wages and productivity; when talent is scarce, firms with superior screening skills post higher wages, attract better applicants, and recruit more talented workers. High-wage firms impose a compositional externality on low-wage firms, leading to equilibrium inefficiency: Welfare would be higher if low-skilled firms posted high wages and selected first. We also provide a micro-foundation for firms heterogeneous screening skills. When talented workers are better at screening (e.g. via superior referrals), a dynamic version of the economy converges to a unique steady state in which differences in talent, profits and screening skills persist forever.

title: Field Experiments to Reduce Inequality: Introduction to the Special Issue
Bridging Economic Efficiency and Perceived Fairness: A New Framework for Collaborative Disaster Material Reserves
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban agglomerations increasingly confront disaster risks that overwhelm individual cities’ reserve capacities. Collaborative emergency reserves offer a potential remedy but also introduce coordination burdens and distributional concerns. To address this, this study formulates a multi‐objective optimization problem that integrates economic utility with perceived fairness. The model explicitly accounts for residents’ shortage and delay experiences alongside managers’ perceptions of coordination costs, reserve burdens, and cross‐city disparities. It is solved using an enhanced multi‐objective particle swarm optimization algorithm coupled with the ε‐constraint method and driven by Monte Carlo disaster scenario generation. A numerical illustration based on 21 mainland prefecture‐level cities in Guangdong Province evaluates the framework under heterogeneous risk, budget, and coordination conditions. Sobol's global sensitivity analysis identifies regional budget, inter‐city collaboration experience, disaster intensity, and nonlinear perceived‐loss parameters as dominant drivers of collaborative advantage, whereas transportation costs and standalone city resilience exert weaker effects. The results demonstrate that collaboration generally outperforms independent reserves, especially under severe disasters and fiscal constraints. This advantage diminishes when disasters are widespread or when transaction and coordination costs are prohibitive. Distributional stress tests further reveal that resource‐abundant hub cities may perceive lower fairness when acting primarily as providers yet stand to gain substantially when severe shocks occur locally. This research provides a decision‐making framework for jointly evaluating efficiency and perceived fairness. It highlights mutual‐aid agreements, fiscal compensation, contribution‐credit mechanisms, and joint exercises as institutional complements to optimized reserve strategies.

title: Communicating Risk in the Age of Misinformation: Empirical Frameworks for Understanding Stakeholder Trust
abstract: This systematic literature review examines how stakeholder trust is conceptualized and measured in risk and science communication amid increasingly complex information environments shaped by misinformation and disinformation. Following PRISMA procedures, which provide a framework for conducting a systematic review with transparency, replicability, and completeness, we searched major databases and screened studies using explicit inclusion criteria. For instance, trust had to be operationalized and measured in risk or scientifically complex contexts; credibility studies were retained when credibility was a trust-related dimension related to stakeholder communication. Scientifically complex contexts are taken to refer to settings where information is inherently complex and nuanced, and understanding requires advanced knowledge. The final corpus (k = 69) includes quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods designs, with a post-2020 increase aligning with pandemic-era scholarship. The findings identify three roles for trust. First, stakeholder trust as an outcome is strengthened more by transparency, empathy, and perceived value similarity than by expertise claims alone. Second, trust as a broad concept often embodies more than just detailed technical understanding; rather, trust predicts acceptance of technologies and policies and lower perceived risk. Third, as a mechanism, stakeholder trust mediates links between credibility, transparency, or value similarity and downstream outcomes such as compliance and cooperation. From organizations to interpersonal interactions, stakeholder trust formation reflects the characteristics of trustors, trustees, and context. We integrate these strands into a communication approach that emphasizes clarity about uncertainty, engagement, and visible accountability as preconditions for trust. Practically, the review underscores the design of transparent messaging, alignment with public values without oversimplification, and participatory approaches that treat stakeholders as partners. Conceptually, we separate judgments about whether information seems credible from trust in the people or institutions behind it. We argue that trust helps connect what people think and feel to what they are willing to do, especially when they must make decisions under uncertainty in today's complex information environment.

title: Brand governance in the platform economy: From political to regulatory recognition
abstract: This article reconceptualises corporate advocacy as brand governance, a techno-normative promotional practice that regulates the conditions of political visibility within networked publics. Drawing on a sociosemiotic analysis of global advocacy campaigns (2017–2022), the analysis identifies three strategies, Visionary (“Feeling the Other”), Sensitive (“Feeling for Others”) and Reflexive (“Feeling with Others”), each operating through distinct affective and narrative logics. The argument advances a distinction between political and regulatory recognition. Political recognition acknowledges claims in their structural and collective dimension; regulatory recognition extends legitimacy only to claims aligned with the promotional regime’s affective and reputational logic. The evidence suggests that brand governance operates predominantly in this regulatory mode, producing a conditional visibility that privileges individualised emotional appeals over structural political demands. This study focuses on US and Western European promotional cultures; comparative research across other regions remains a necessary next step.

title: Does alternative news media inform or misinform voters during election campaigns?
abstract: A growing body of literature has studied the audiences and effects of alternative media use. We contribute by examining how such usage shapes political knowledge during election campaigns. Given their partisan orientation, lack of professional verification, and often provocative style, alternative media are found to produce and circulate misinformation, even as their users are often politically engaged, active news consumers. We ask whether alternative media inform rather than misinform citizens during election campaigns. Adopting a two-dimensional conception of political knowledge, we examine both surveillance knowledge and confidence in that knowledge – along with misinformation understood as the combination of the two. Utilizing individual-level panel data from Norway, our findings suggest that alternative news use is not associated with being better or worse informed, but with being more confident in one’s political knowledge. We discuss how these effects may differ in more polarized or lower-quality information environments.

title: Gender-Responsive Budgeting in Higher Education: An Examination of Collegiate Athletics Student Aid
abstract: Literature in public administration and public budgeting examines how budgetary processes affect the allocation of public resources across different populations. Using a gender-responsive budgeting (GRB) framework, this study examines patterns of athletic scholarship funding in the context of Title IX mandates in federally funded higher education institutions. Drawing on Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act (EADA) data from 2010 to 2022, the analysis focuses on scholarship allocations across National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I institutions. Distinct from much of the existing GRB literature, the study incorporates legal guidelines, panel data methods, and explicit distinctions by biological sex. Fixed-effects regressions indicate that total athletic student aid is positively associated with the scale of male student athletic participation, particularly in public institutions. Participation-adjusted analyses further show that both public and private institutions allocate athletic student aid to female student-athletes at levels broadly consistent with Title IX’s proportionality standards after accounting for enrollment composition. Specifically, private institutions exhibit stronger per capita adjustments favoring female student-athletes, pointing to meaningful heterogeneity in how funding allocations are implemented across institutional contexts. Overall, the findings demonstrate how a GRB-informed approach aids in interpreting aggregate funding patterns and highlight variation in institutional responses to mandates and policies pertinent to gender issues in collegiate athletics.

title: EU implementation and compliance in Justice and Home Affairs – the case of the European Arrest Warrant
abstract: Research on EU implementation has largely focused on social and environmental policies, while the area of Justice and Home Affairs (JHA) remains understudied, even though noncompliance is highest in this sector. Moreover, most studies address legal compliance but overlook practical implementation. This paper tackles both gaps by analysing the implementation of the European Arrest Warrant, a key instrument in police and judicial cooperation, that replaced diplomatic extradition with mutual judicial recognition. Drawing on data from 27 member states, we examine patterns of noncompliance and explanatory factors. Building on Börzel’s Power-Capacity-Politicisation (PCP) model, we extend it to encompass both legal and practical compliance. Our findings not only reveal a decoupling between legal and practical compliance but also show that practical compliance itself is fragmented. Moreover, we find different explanatory factors to shape different phases of implementation: legal compliance is primarily shaped by power, while practical compliance depends on capacity, particularly the availability of key institutional actors such as judges. This study advances EU implementation research by examining JHA as an underexplored policy area and by extending the PCP model to practical compliance, offering new insight into sector-specific mechanisms of (non)compliance.

title: Behavioral profiling for compliance: the role of legitimacy, norms, and prior conduct
Political trust revisited: theoretical and empirical insights into political distrust and mistrust
abstract: There remains a lack of clarity about what low political trust precisely entails. Based on long-standing discussions, recent works have sought to verify the existence of distinct political trust attitudes, namely, trust, mistrust, and distrust. While insightful, multiple criticisms have emerged on the contributions to this literature. Notably, despite growing attention, a comprehensive overview of different trust attitudes and their empirical basis has yet to be fully established. This study seeks to provide a theoretical and empirical examination as to the distinctiveness and relatedness of political trust attitudes. Drawing on novel survey data with 12,000 respondents across 8 European countries, this article shows that it is insufficient to use measures of political trust to understand political distrust. Yet, results are less supportive of mistrust as a distinct concept. Importantly, this study indicates that traditional conceptualisations and operationalisations of trust do not cover the full range of trust attitudes of citizens.

title: Crisis Learning in Local Governments: Organizational Adaptation and Policy Change During the COVID-19 Crisis
abstract: Crises can trigger multi-dimensional transformations in public administration systems. This study focuses on the integrated mechanism of learning during crisis to enhance our understanding of emergency management optimization in complex crisis environments. This study constructs an integrated analytical framework that integrates organizational adaptation and policy change to explain crisis learning in local governments and examines the sequential adaptive evolution of Xi’an City’s responses to the Delta and Omicron COVID-19 variants using network analysis and policy text analysis. The findings reveal that learning during crisis in Chinese local governments follows a practice emergence-policy institutionalization feedback loop: ad-hoc special work teams emerged to break rigid bureaucratic labor divisions, and their proven successful practices were institutionalized as permanent emergency working groups in revised emergency plans. This transition from a pure hierarchical structure to a function-led hybrid governance structure shifts local crisis governance from passive reactive response to proactive risk preparedness.

title: Does Gender Budgeting Improve Women's Well‐Being, Equality, and Empowerment?
abstract: ABSTRACT The United Nations' fifth Sustainable Development Goal calls for gender equality and empowerment. Gender budgeting (GB) has been proposed as a potential mechanism to reduce gender disparities. This is a novel approach to budgeting that considers the impact of public spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite its growing popularity, spreading to over 80 countries since its launch in the 1980s, the effectiveness of GB remains less understood. This study tests whether GB has led to tangible improvements in women's well‐being, equality, and empowerment. We use an event study research design with staggered adoption to analyze data across 47 countries from 2000 to 2023. Our analyses of average and heterogeneous treatment effects reveal short‐ and long‐term impacts; notably, we find significant reductions in maternal mortality ratios and adolescent birth rates, as well as improvements in women's political empowerment.

title: Rethinking Top Public Management Through Relational Dynamics: A Systems‐Informed Study of Senior Executives
abstract: ABSTRACT The complex nature of top public managerial work is widely acknowledged in theory but rarely examined empirically. Existing research has mostly analyzed bivariate relationships among core components of top managerial work in government, including managers' attributes, practices, outcomes, and contexts. Drawing on a systems‐based framework, we investigate how effective top managerial work unfolds as a complex relational practice. We analyze seven cases of long‐serving, distinguished Chilean senior executives through a comprehensive and process‐oriented lens, based on 27 semi‐structured interviews with the managers and members of their personal and professional networks. Our findings indicate how the relational dynamics in which senior public executives engage shape their managerial attributes and practices. Specifically, strategizing, motivation building, and technical expertise are best understood as emerging primarily through interactions within agencies and with external sociopolitical environments. These results qualify perspectives that explain senior public management effectiveness by overemphasizing executives' individual attributes and views, and underscore the need for personnel policies and governance environments that equip managers with the capacities called for by a systems approach to top public management.

title: Cultural Theory, Political Ideology, and Burden Tolerance: The Role of Core Beliefs in Shaping Support for Administrative Burdens
abstract: Administrative burdens embedded within many public policies are often politically contentious, such that core values and belief systems can drive either support or opposition. In this paper, we use survey data from US respondents to replicate and extend previous research on the public acceptance of administrative burdens in general. First, we confirm the measure's validity by examining its effects on beliefs across policies that range from highly polarized to less politically contentious. Second, we test the relationship between tolerance of administrative burden and cultural theory (CT) variables that tap into worldview orientations related to hierarchy, egalitarianism, individualism, and fatalism, which previous research has found predictive of policy preferences across a wide range of domains, even after accounting for political ideology and partisanship. We hypothesize that egalitarians and individualists will generally be less tolerant of burdens, while hierarchs will be more accepting of burdensome requirements. However, this effect varies depending on the nature of the burdens and how they relate to perceived threats for each worldview.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: The human backend of smart shipyards: data stability and precarious work in the South Korean shipbuilding industry
abstract: The digitalization of manufacturing industries has generated extensive scholarship on job displacement and the invisible labour sustaining platform economies, yet the human work required to build data infrastructures within traditional industries remains underexamined. This paper examines the backend of smart shipyard initiatives in South Korea’s shipbuilding industry. Drawing on interviews with workers, managers, engineers, and industry experts at a major shipyard, we show that data stability – the consistency and reliability of data inputs necessary for digital twin operation – is not a technical parameter but an institutional outcome shaped by the shipyard’s three-tier employment structure. The secured core, the buffered middle, and the exposed periphery respond to backend labour demands through surveillance resistance, shallow compliance, and structural detachment, producing fragmented datasets that undermine the smart shipyard’s data foundation. We conceptualize this as the paradox of automation in segmented labour markets: automation depends on the very labour it seeks to displace, and dependence falls most heavily on those with the weakest incentives and least protection. Situated within the East Asian developmental welfare state, the study reframes data stability as a problem of institutionalized datafication, extending research on digital precarity beyond platform work to the backend labour of traditional industries.

title: Triage Bureaucracy: The Organizational Challenge of Implementing Growing Policy Stocks

title: ‘Undeserving winners’ or ‘undeserved losers’? Two types of societal discontent and their relation to vote choice
abstract: Normative evaluations of shifts in social hierarchies have emerged as a central factor in understanding recent electoral transformations. In particular, far right supporters have been shown to resent challenges to the traditional social order championed by the progressive left. In this paper, we theorise and study a still more fundamental difference in the social discontent expressed by these political camps. While far right supporters tend to resent the ascent of perceived-to-be ‘undeserving winners’ of status, progressive left voters should focus relatively more on groups seen as unjustly underprivileged, i.e., ‘undeserved losers’. The former is in line with a zero-sum mindset, while the latter is consistent with endorsing a more universalist political agenda. Drawing on open-ended survey responses from an original survey conducted in Germany, we explore how individuals normatively assess changes in the social order. Through a combination of word embedding techniques and qualitative analysis, we investigate the gap between respondents' ideals and their perceptions of evolving status hierarchies. Our findings reveal that concerns about ‘undeserving winners’ are prevalent among far right voters, but less so among progressive left (Green) voters. Electoral realignment, we argue, has made this difference more central to political competition.

title: Correction: A framework for fragility: guiding measurement for policy
Rethinking policy capacity: integrating deontological and human dimensions
Effects of Perceptions of Corruption on Citizens' Trust in Religious and Customary Service Providers in Africa
The Korean national assembly elections dataset, 1948–2024: Complete candidate-level records
The Role of Religion in Civil War – Are We Really Getting It?
Affective Polarization, Media Outlets, and Opinion Dynamics
abstract: Abstract We study opinion dynamics in a social network consisting of two groups. Agents update their opinions by conforming to members of their own group while rejecting the views of the opposing group (affective polarization), and by listening to a media outlet that may provide biased information. We characterize the long-run opinions and identify when affective polarization and media bias lead to ideological polarization, persistent disagreement, or failures of learning. We also derive when information interventions or censorship improve the accuracy of average opinions} and reduce disagreement, and when they backfire: better information helps only under specific media bias configurations and when directed to the agents we identify as most effective at propagating it through the network.

title: Local Shocks and Regional Dynamics in an Aging Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how population aging shapes regional adjustment to local shocks. I develop a dynamic spatial general equilibrium model that incorporates aggregate demographic change, life‐cycle variation in migration and employment choices, and forward‐looking investment in local capital. Applying the model to Japan, I find that aging can mitigate welfare losses from a negative local shock. Although older populations are less mobile, reduced outmigration sustains local capital demand and slows capital disinvestment, limiting declines in labor productivity. An extension illustrates the model's use for post‐disaster policy evaluation, highlighting a potential tradeoff between spatial equity and aggregate welfare.

title: Does Digitalization Widen Labor Income Inequality?
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a growth model that endogenizes the occupational choice of workers with different ability levels to study how digitalization affects labor income inequality. The framework incorporates digitalization's multifaceted effects on the economy: (i) it influences economic growth through automation, and (ii) it affects labor income inequality through labor productivity (demand side) and labor time modulation (supply side). We examine how these channels influence wage inequality between skilled and unskilled workers, within each skill group, and economy‐wide. The analysis reveals that digitalization's impact on labor income inequality—whether exacerbating or mitigating disparities—depends on the inequality metric employed.

title: Paths to well-being through SDG 5 Gender equality achievements: Evidence from the EU
The Rational Design of Space Agreements: How Bilateralism Shapes Powerful States' Design Preferences
abstract: ABSTRACT The global governance of outer space relies heavily on international agreements, yet the institutional forms of these agreements remain underexplored. This article introduces a new dataset on various design features of 952 space agreements, offering the first large‐N overview of institutional design in space governance. Building on rational design theory, this article analyzes how these design features interact with one another and with negotiation structures. Our results reveal systematic trade‐offs and suggest that power asymmetry has contrasting effects depending on the context: Powerful states tend to favor greater delegation, precision, and enforcement in bilateral agreements, while often resisting them in multilateral settings. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for both power dynamics and bilateralism, two contextual factors often overlooked in rational design theory. By making the dataset publicly available, the article seeks to foster further research on the causes and consequences of institutional variation in space governance and to advance comparative institutionalist scholarship across issue‐areas of global governance.

title: Civil Servants' Compliance with Conflict‐of‐Interest Regulation: Evidence from a List Experiment
abstract: ABSTRACT While regulatory governance scholarship has paid significant attention to the normative importance of ethics reform in government, empirical evidence on compliance remains scant. Drawing on insights from the social value activation model and behavioral ethics, this study examines civil servants' compliance propensity under conflict‐of‐interest regulation. Specifically, we examine how a legitimate ethics reform is associated with the voluntary compliance of two legally treated groups: those with policy implementation duties and those with frequent stakeholder engagement. The results of our list experiment with a representative sample of South Korean civil servants ( n = 1977) show that both target groups exhibit higher estimated compliance propensity with the second provision of the Act, restricted and prohibited actions, but that only policy implementation duties are associated with higher compliance propensity with the first provision, reporting and disclosure obligations. Our findings suggest that ethics reform compliance is shaped not only by formal rules and deterrence, but also by administrative role exposure, perceived legitimacy, and the value‐based dimension of civil servants.

title: The Conditional Promise of Open Data: A Cross-Country Qualitative Comparative Analysis of Corruption Control
abstract: To explore the conditions under which open data facilitates or hinders the reduction of corruption, this article proposes a configurational framework linking transparency, publicity and accountability. A fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of 82 countries reveals that open data is neither necessary nor sufficient on its own. The article identifies three equifinal pathways to low corruption: two include open data as a peripheral element of broader configurations, while a third achieves low corruption through state–society synergy even without it. It also identifies three distinct pathways to high corruption. These findings illustrate the “conditional promise” of open data, underscoring the need to align transparency initiatives with existing publicity and accountability infrastructures.
