title: Governance on the big screen: How visual ethnography enhances governance research
abstract: Visual ethnography presents a valuable methodological approach for governance research because it offers unique contributions to the understanding of governance practices. This paper demonstrates that visual ethnography offers this by providing rich contextual data, fostering emotional openness, enhancing collaboration and adaptability, and engaging viewers in recollection, empathy, and reflection. Through an exploration of three key phases (visual fieldwork, data analysis and editing, and film screenings), this paper centers around a detailed case study on the ethnographic film Loose Ends about the COVID-19 pandemic in Dutch nursing homes. Results from this case study highlight the distinct contributions of visual ethnography in governance research. Visual ethnography not only deepens the research process but also increases the understanding of lived experiences within governance frameworks. By encouraging a more reflexive approach to decision-making, visual ethnography fosters an environment where the experiences of those affected by policies are acknowledged and valued, thereby extending the insights gained beyond the scope of traditional qualitative research methods.

title: Capturing the classroom: disinformation as discursive reconstruction of education in Orbán’s Hungary
abstract: Introduction: Debates on educational disinformation typically target false content in curricula or online. This study reconceptualizes the phenomenon as the discursive reconstruction of education’s purpose, the strategic redefinition of its values and social functions that becomes naturalized as common sense. Existing scholarship documents Hungary’s institutional capture but neglects the discursive mechanisms transforming political rhetoric into educational meaning. The study asks how Viktor Orbán’s speeches construct education’s societal role and how these representations become embedded in curricular content. Methods/Data: The primary corpus comprises Orbán’s official speeches (2022–2025) from the Hungarian government website; an education-keyword search yielded 110 speeches, from which 236 relevant segments were retained. Purposively sampled grade 5–12 textbooks (civics, history, literature) and selected 2015–2021 speeches provide illustrative, intertextual triangulation. Analytic Plan: The study applies Fairclough’s three-dimensional Critical Discourse Analysis, examining discourse as text, discursive practice and social practice. Through iterative open and focused coding of speech segments, three discursive representations were derived inductively and analysed across all three dimensions. Results: Orbán constructs education through three interlocking representations: national preservation (schools as guardians of Christian-national identity), economic engine (vocational training as sovereignty), and ideological resistance (schools as fortresses against liberal ‘contamination’). Together they achieve hegemonic closure, rendering pluralism unthinkable; textbook content materializes this rhetoric as pedagogical fact. Conclusion/Implications: Educational disinformation operates through meaning reconstruction, ‘epistemic engineering’, not only factual falsehood, making fact-checking insufficient in itself. Monitoring democratic backsliding should track discursive shifts in institutions’ self-described purposes, since classroom meanings shape future citizens’ political imaginations.

title: Cultural values, value congruence, and trust: examining the origins of trust in information regarding hydraulic fracturing among local policy elites
abstract: Trust is an important component of information-seeking, particularly as related to the policy-making process. For policy-relevant information to be utilized by decision-makers and, in turn, impact policy, the information source must be viewed as trustworthy. Thus, understanding the origins of trust in sources of information regarding a particular policy issue is necessary in understanding the policy process associated with that issue. In this paper, I examine the origins of trust in information regarding hydraulic fracturing (“fracking”). Specifically, this paper examines the role of cultural value predispositions in shaping trust in information from various sources (e.g. energy industry, environmental groups, and government) regarding fracking. Further, the moderating role of perceived value congruence is examined. This study utilizes a survey of local policy elites in Arkansas (a state with fracking operations) and Oregon (a state without fracking operations). Findings indicate that, for local policy elites (1) trust in sources of information is largely derived from culturally held values, (2) the perceived compatibility of values between local policy elites’ and those within their community impacts these relationships, and (3) the triadic relationships between cultural values, perceived value congruence, and trust in information sources are distinct between contexts.

title: From Fragile Leadership to Algorithmic Accountability: A Hybrid AI‐Human Governance Framework for Equitable Pandemic Response
Partisan bias in a sorted party system: A problem of epistemic inequality
abstract: Abstract Normative and empirical scholars typically treat partisans’ distrust of their political rivals as a product of individual cognitive biases. But even if bias is inevitable, it is parties’ coalition‐building and messaging strategies that determine who bias is directed toward. This paper argues that the social sorting of party conflict exacerbates the epistemic and democratic harm of partisan distrust by generating distinctive patterns of epistemic inequality. I show that when voters associate parties with particular social groups, members of those groups suffer greater risk of testimonial injustice and related credibility deficits owing to their perceived partisanship. These dynamics are most damaging for members of marginalized groups, as party–group overlap can reinforce the prejudices they already face. Addressing these harms, I argue, requires looking beyond individual partisans to the background features of party systems that shape how elites mobilize group identities and animus in the struggle for office.

title: The nature of party cues: A theoretical and empirical investigation
abstract: The question of why people are influenced by party cues is still heavily debated. We argue that lack of progress is partly the result of a too narrow, individual-centered, perspective on cue taking, resulting in weak links between theory and empirics. The dominant theories in the field make more nuanced predictions that are rarely considered jointly in empirical studies. We design a two-wave panel experiment, fielded during the 2022 Swedish election campaign, that allows us to test a broad set of theoretically derived hypotheses about party cues in a real-life context. The results show that cue effects vary with many different factors at the individual, issue-specific, and political environment levels, demonstrating the relevance on a dynamic perspective of cue taking. At the same time, the direct predictions of existing theories receive uneven support across individual, issue-specific, and political-environmental contexts, pointing to a clear need for theoretical development.

title: The impact of using a voting advice application on young voters’ motivation to turn out: A randomized survey experiment and observational panel study
Disentangling public opinion on European integration: On the multidimensionality of integration attitudes
abstract: This study explores citizens’ attitudes towards European integration, moving beyond a simplistic ‘yes’ or ‘no’ perspective. Focusing on the EU–Swiss relationship, it examines a variety of integration questions using 2019 Swiss Election Study data. Latent profile analysis identifies five citizen groups that share similarities in support and opposition patterns regarding the studied questions: ‘pure sovereignists’, ‘neutrals’, ‘pure integrationists’, ‘cultural sovereignists’ and ‘economic integrationists’. The latter two groups are both comparatively more favourable of economic than cultural European integration, substantiating the claim that integration attitudes are multidimensional. Investigating the predictors of adherence to these two groups, the study finds education, income and party vote intentions to have a differentiated effect. Relevant group comparisons show that education and radical right vote intentions differentiate positions along the cultural, but not the economic, European integration dimension, whereas income, radical left and liberal vote intentions differentiate positions along the economic, but not the cultural, dimension.

Law and Political Violence against Women in Central America
abstract: Cristiana Chamorro Barrios is a Nicaraguan journalist and founder of the Nicaraguan Foundation for Freedom of the Press, a nonprofit focused on promoting freedom of expression and public access to information, as well as providing training and support to local journalists. Cristiana was arrested on June 2, 2021, in Managua, Nicaragua, on accusations of tax evasion (International Society for Human Rights 2025). At the time of her arrest, Cristiana, a member of a prominent Nicaraguan family, had recently announced her intention to challenge Daniel Ortega in the November 2021 presidential election and was widely considered the favorite in the race. The charges against Cristiana 1 — including the vague claim of “abusive management and ideological falsehood” — though made with no evidence, disqualified her from running for office. She was later tried in sham proceedings and sentenced to eight years in prison. In 2023, Cristiana was one of hundreds of political prisoners forcibly expelled from the country and later stripped of their citizenship (Abi-Habib 2023; Confidencial 2021). 2

title: Contesting Norms and Challenging Order: Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 and the Geopolitics of LGBTIQ+ Human Rights
abstract: Abstract Uganda’s adoption of the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023 reveals significant contestation among domestic and external actors regarding LGBTIQ+ human rights norms. This article argues that opposition to LGBTIQ+ rights has become central to contemporary challenges to the liberal international order by contesting the authority of liberal human rights norms as universal benchmarks of state legitimacy. Drawing on critical IR theories of norm violation, it analyzes how external actors responded to the Act and how Ugandan state actors defended the legislation. The article concludes that political opposition against LGBTIQ+ human rights in Uganda, akin to anti-LGBTIQ+ politics observed elsewhere in the world, has become central to political critique of “the West” and the existing international order.

title: Law enforcement with rent dissipation
abstract: Abstract We consider a framework which brings together losses arising from rent-dissipation and the workhorse model of law enforcement. Governmental actors engage in a contest to share the proceeds from the enforcement of the law through monetary fines, which leads to rent-dissipation. This causes monetary sanctions to be costly, rendering the model used for studying nonmonetary sanctions a better fit for their analysis. The effect of rent-dissipation on optimal sanctions is directly related to the sanction elasticity of offenses measured at the classic optimum (i.e., where the expected sanction equals the direct harm from the offense). When offenses are inelastic, the optimal sanction is smaller than the classic optimum and it is decreasing in the degree of rent-dissipation; and a legislator who does not fully internalize contest costs chooses an overly punitive sanction which is smaller than the classic optimum. The opposite results are obtained when offenses are elastic. We discuss implications and extensions.

title: Logrolling affects the relative performance of majority and unanimity rule
abstract: Abstract We consider a committee facing binary decisions on a number of proposals. If members vote sincerely and payoffs are symmetrically distributed, we show analytically that simple majority rule is the best q-majority rule in an aggregate or expected payoff sense. We argue that this (well known) pattern changes systematically if the committee faces multiple decisions and members engage in logrolling deals. In a simulation exercise, we find that unanimity rule outperforms majority rule when the number of proposals considered is large enough. We complement our analysis with a laboratory experiment designed to investigate whether human subjects engage in the logrolling deals assumed in our simulations. We find that deals associated with large negative externalities are less likely to arise than others, as are “complex” deals involving many voters or proposals. These results suggest that the impact of logrolling on the relative performance of the decision rules considered may be mitigated by cognitive constraints and other-regarding preferences.

title: Gubernatorial partisanship and housing outcomes: evidence from close elections
Beyond six versus twelve: Kian v. Florida and the design of the criminal jury
Gary D. Libecap, Where’s Coase? The implications of economic property rights or rent-seeking in forming institutions
Larry M. Bartels and Katherine J. Cramer. The Politics of Social Change: From the Sixties to the Present Through the Eyes of a Generation

The economic gains from breaking boundaries: Reformulating index insurance zones to maximize lower tail dependence
abstract: Index insurance intended to help low-wealth households manage risk is hampered by downside basis risk, meaning that the insured suffers a loss, but the insurance index fails to signal a loss. Existing index insurance contracts use statistically ad hoc administrative boundaries to demarcate insurance zones. We develop an algorithm that creates zones that maximize lower tail dependence amongst individual units included in each zone. Breaking boundaries in this way minimizes basis risk. Using data from a satellite-based index insurance program in Kenya, we show that replacing administrative with optimized zones can as much as triple the value of insurance using an expected utility-based metric of insurance quality.

title: Beyond hiring: the dynamics of ethnic disparities in unemployment
When prevention cannot learn: evaluability failures in risk-control regimes
abstract: Governments and regulators often respond to corruption, accidents, administrative error, and regulatory failure by adding preventive controls. Some controls improve safety and integrity. Others remain in place even when their contribution and organizational costs are uncertain. This article develops the Evaluability Loop of Risk-Control Regimes, a process model explaining how evidence about a control becomes, or fails to become, an authorized decision about its future. A control is evaluable when a regime can explain how it should affect risk, observe how it operates, interpret the resulting signals, assess both performance and burden, and decide whether it should be retained, recalibrated, replaced, suspended, or retired. The model rejects the assumption that preventive instruments are inherently difficult to evaluate or that ex post accountability naturally produces learning. It identifies six failure modes and explains how their interaction with political and institutional asymmetries can produce a procedural ratchet. Illustrations from safety management, regulatory enforcement, and crisis accountability show that preventive controls can support learning, while observable ex post events can still produce weak evidence or blame displacement. The article’s central contribution is to specify the institutional passage from control experience to control revision.

title: Foundations of societal safety and security
Outdoor learning in a post-conflict context: transforming crisis habitus through critical pedagogy of place
abstract: While research on Outdoor Learning (OL) has largely focused on its environmental and emotional benefits in stable and safe contexts, this study examines OL in the post-conflict setting of Bosnia and Herzegovina, marked by ongoing tensions. Its main contribution is the reconceptualization of risk as a didactic and ethical category. Rather than something to be eliminated, risk is understood as a pedagogical resource that enables contested spaces to foster critical thinking and civic learning. Drawing on Critical Pedagogy of Place, the study shows how teachers can move beyond a pedagogy of neutrality and transform crisis habitus into reflective, ethically engaged practice. The article advances a framework for working with contested spaces and underscores the need for institutional support to ensure teachers’ professional and legal security. Through this lens, Outdoor Learning becomes a vehicle for critical, ethical, and civic education, rather than ecological recreation alone.

title: The intended and unintended affordances of post-separation parenting apps
abstract: Little research has examined the role of specific technologies in relationships characterised by unequal power, such as those which underpin post-separation domestic and family violence. Drawing on the mechanisms and conditions framework of affordances and the methods of feature analysis, this study analyses 32 post-separation parenting apps along with in-depth interviews with 18 Australian victim–survivors who used these platforms with a perpetrator. We identify intended outcomes embedded in app design and contrast them with unintended outcomes emerging in practice. Analysis revealed that the design and promotional materials of the apps influence their use as a reinforcer of litigious mindsets and actions. This combination appears to change user behaviours, leading to communication becoming anticipatory and strategic with mixed outcomes.

title: Audible, Spotify, YouTube & Co.: The German Digital Audiobook Market in the Context of Platformization
abstract: This article examines the contemporary digital audiobook through the lens of platformization and develops a conceptual framework for understanding platformized audiobook culture. Drawing on an integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship, supplemented by market reports, industry statistics, and audience studies, it uses the German audiobook market as an analytically illuminating example through which broader processes of platformization can be explored. The article situates audiobooks within wider transformations of everyday digital media practices, highlighting the shift from physical formats toward downloads and subscription-based streaming services. Conceptually, it distinguishes platformized audiobook culture from digital audiobook culture through two complementary analytical perspectives adapted from book studies, digital publishing, and media and communication studies: an integrative platform model and a data-environment model of streaming services. Building on this synthesis, the article proposes an ecosystem model of platformized audiobook culture to support future theoretical and empirical research.

title: The Roles of Source Citations in Identifying Misinformation and Disinformation: Moderating Effects of Digital Literacy and Information Types
abstract: This study investigates whether source citations enhance detection of false information and whether their effects depend on digital literacy and information processing style. In an experimental survey of 1,013 South Koreans, citations show no overall effect. However, they significantly improve detection of disinformation—but not misinformation—among individuals with higher digital literacy. Intuitive processing lowers detection ability, and citations do not counteract this tendency. The findings challenge assumptions that transparency universally improves evaluation, showing that citation effectiveness depends on user capabilities and the type of falsehood, and highlighting the need to strengthen digital literacy alongside transparency initiatives.

title: Forgiving the Government: The Waning Effect of Citizen Grievances in China
abstract: Public grievances do not automatically translate into collective or even individual resistance, but pent-up grievances threaten governments because they may trigger regime-challenging actions when opportunities arise. This study examines to what extent public grievances against state authorities may become pent up. Using a longitudinal survey in China, this article finds that public grievances against local state authorities reduce citizens’ trust in the political system, but citizen grievances may not become pent up. Instead, these grievances tend to be individualized in the sense that they neither last for a long time nor diffuse in society. Individualized grievances reduce political pressure because they do not constitute threats to social stability. However, whether these grievances will last if citizens re-encounter similar conflicts warrants further research.

title: Embeddedness Under Fire: How Chinese Private Firms Navigate Conflict Risks in Northern Myanmar
abstract: As one of Myanmar’s largest sources of foreign investment, China has been exposed to the civil war that intensified after the 2021 coup. Drawing on a mixed embeddedness perspective and interview-based fieldwork, this article examines how Chinese private firms operate in Myanmar’s conflict-affected regions without formal state protection or legal guarantees. It argues that their resilience rests on embedding commercial activity within fragmented governance. Institutionally, firms align with non-state armed authorities, adapt across shifting jurisdictions, and benefit from protective norms tied to Chinese identity. Socially, they mobilize ethnic and kinship ties, intermediaries, and localized information networks. These mechanisms, though costly and imperfect, convert unstable environments into workable orders. The article contributes to Global China scholarship by foregrounding private enterprises as adaptive actors in conflict settings.

title: The Virtue of Bias? China’s Stakeholder Mediation in the Iran and North Korea Nuclear Crises
abstract: Why does China mediate differently across similar security crises? Challenging mediation theory’s neutrality assumption, this article conceptualises ‘stakeholder mediation’ as engagement by third parties whose security, economic, or reputational interests are exposed to a conflict’s outcome. Such mediators hold leverage but risk entrapment and reputational costs. Using a most-similar design, process tracing, diplomat memoirs, declassified documents, and elite interviews, we examine China’s role in the North Korean and Iranian nuclear crises. Despite structural similarities, China adopted markedly different postures. Variation in stake exposure shapes risk calculations, entry timing, and leverage strategies: high immediate security stakes in Korea raised China’s intervention threshold through entrapment fears, whereas economic and reputational stakes in Iran lowered the risks of early multilateral engagement, while US–China relations operated as a scope condition.

title: Nothing Ventured, Nothing Gained: A Scoping Review and Future Research Directions for Public Sector Intrapreneurship
abstract: The acceleration of transformations in governance systems, organizational designs, and state-market relations in the 2020s has placed organizational intrapreneurship at the heart of adaptive capacities. Despite the rapid growth of research on intrapreneurship, public entrepreneurship, and organizational entrepreneurship, the literature remains fragmented across sectors, levels of analysis, and theoretical traditions. This scoping review synthesizes 61 empirical, conceptual or theoretical studies from 2020s and repositions intrapreneurship as a multilevel governance capacity embedded in evolving institutional dynamics. The synthesis articulates an integrated framework encompassing macro (institutions and governance architectures), meso (leadership and hybrid structures), and micro (professional identity and sensemaking) levels in the public sector. It also formulates a forward-looking agenda that aims to strengthen theoretical cumulativeness, methodological robustness, and the translatability of results into actionable policies and initiatives.

title: The Destruction of the Accountability of Federal Officials for Constitutional Torts
abstract: The manuscript seeks to determine whether constitutional tort lawsuits against federal executive-branch public administrators constitute an effective remedy for such administrators’ unconstitutional conduct. The article also seeks to answer whether plaintiffs alleging mistreatment of federal law enforcement officers and agents may invoke the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) to hold them accountable for unconstitutional conduct. The examination of constitutional tort jurisprudence applicable to the conduct of federal executive-branch public administrators finds that the U.S. Supreme Court has effectively barred so-called Bivens constitutional tort actions against them. The manuscript argues that the U.S. Supreme Court’s constitutional tort jurisprudence has had a direct impact on efforts by the second Trump administration to sharply increase the number of deportations of immigrants without legal authorization to reside in the United States. This has left victims of unconstitutional conduct by ICE agents without the ability to recover monetary damages for their mistreatment. Finally, the manuscript argues that academic public administration has paid insufficient attention to situations in which federal public administrators openly violate the rule of law and invoke utilitarian moral reasoning to justify their actions. Academic public administration provides explanations for such behavior by examining administrative evil and utilitarian moral reasoning. Academic public administration, however, has failed to provide a remedy for a growing number of bureaucrats who refuse to embrace higher-order moral values and turn their backs on deontological moral reasoning.

title: Redefining Performance in Hybrid Public Organisations: The Case of French Prisons
abstract: Hybrid public organisations are characterised by the coexistence of multiple institutional logics, which are sometimes contradictory. However, there has been little theoretical work on how this hybridity shapes organisational performance. Existing performance management systems tend to fragment these logics rather than articulate them, and the mechanisms by which logics translate into performance criteria in a public hybrid are not well understood. Drawing on the institutional logics perspective and the value creation framework, this article examines French prisons as a case study of segmented hybrid organisations. Using a qualitative methodology combining 47 interviews, 47 days of non-participant observation and 50 institutional documents, we address the following questions: How does institutional hybridity translate into performance criteria, and how do current performance management mechanisms affect hybridity in turn? Our findings reveal that reconciling contradictory institutional logics constitutes a performance criterion. We further observe a differentiated distribution of institutional logics across performance dimensions, with internal dimensions mobilising a broader plurality of logics than external ones.

title: Leadership Style and Organizational Performance in Nigerian Local Governments: Evidence from Ondo West
abstract: This study examines the relationship between leadership style and organizational performance in Nigerian local governments, using Ondo West Local Government, Ondo State, as a case study. While leadership and organizational performance have been widely studied in corporate and broader national contexts, limited empirical attention has been given to Nigeria’s local government institutions. This gap constrains understanding of how participative leadership shapes employee engagement and organizational performance at the subnational level. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining questionnaires and interviews with staff and management. Quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis respectively. Findings reveal a largely non-participative leadership structure, characterized by minimal employee involvement in decision-making, particularly outside top management, with adverse effects on organizational performance. Although the single-case design limits generalizability, the study provides insights into leadership dynamics in subnational governance. It recommends institutionalizing participative leadership and inclusive decision-making frameworks to enhance organizational performance.

title: Anti-corruption, market segmentation and regional innovation: evidence from China
Toward a Gender Sensitive and Locally Rooted co‐Production Approach: Insights From Implementing Child Stunting Eradication Program in Indonesia
American Society for Public Administration Code of Ethics
Fiscal Transparency for Sustainable Development: The Global Evidence
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable development (SD) has been a primary policy effort in government globally to address various key challenges in development and the environment. Transparency, as an accountability tool, is critical for stakeholders holding government administrations accountable for SD policy outcomes. Given the very limited literature on the role of administrative transparency in SD, this study creates a comprehensive global panel database covering the period from 2006 to 2022 to examine the effect of fiscal transparency on sustainability policy performance. The results indicate a significant role of developing transparency institutions in promoting SD goals, and distinctive effect of such development in countries of different development stages. The findings point to different paths for achieving accountability goals under different institutional conditions, which is significant for establishing and strengthening accountability enhancement strategies for policy outcomes.

title: Can cooperation between a city and a region lead to a robust solution during a polycrisis? – the case of Czechia
abstract: The goal of this article is to explore whether municipal and regional cooperation can provide robust governance solutions during a polycrisis. The methodology of the article is based on a single-country case study from Czechia. The case study focuses on coping with the COVID-19 pandemic and the refugee crisis resulting from the war in Ukraine. We demonstrate how cooperation between a city and a region contributed to robust solutions and improved the lives of local communities. Although municipal and regional cooperation can potentially create significant positive effects that align with the definition of robust governance, this potential is not fully realized in Czechia. The main reasons for this untapped potential are failures of the central government, a lack of leadership and strategic focus, and the absence of formalized learning.

title: Legislative Financial Asset Disclosure, Firm Motivations, and Macroeconomic Outcomes in the US States
abstract: ABSTRACT Financial asset disclosure laws are widely implemented to combat conflicts of interest among policymakers, yet their economic impact remains poorly understood. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of how these transparency measures affect macroeconomic outcomes across the 50 US states. We theorize that these disclosure and recusal laws could have divergent impacts on macroeconomic performance: they might enhance economic outcomes by curtailing the exploitation of political connections by business firms, or conversely, they could impede economic growth by altering firm behavior and deterring business leaders from seeking public office, thereby potentially reducing the pool of economically savvy policymakers. Using new data on state‐level disclosure policies, we find that asset disclosure laws are associated with a worsening macroeconomic environment in states. To uncover the mechanisms driving these counterintuitive results, we conduct two pre‐registered survey experiments with 2000 small business owners. Our experimental evidence suggests that stringent disclosure requirements deter business investment and expansion. This research has implications for legislative challenges for legislative design, transparency, and economic policy.

title: Dependent contractors in South Korea’s incomplete multi-pillar pension system
abstract: Drawing on a survey of 1,053 dependent contractors (DCs) in ten occupations, conducted by the Korea Platform and Freelancer Worker Mutual Aid(KPFWMA), this study examines how DCs are positioned within South Korea’s ‘incomplete’ multi-pillar pension system (MPPS), conceptualized along three dimensions: statutory, administrative, and functional incompleteness. The results show precarious integration: about 40% of respondents lack any pension coverage, while only one in ten attains full multi-pillar protection. Coverage is stratified primarily by age and income, occupational differences are comparatively muted, and second-pillar coverage obtained through DC work itself is nearly absent. Latent demand for a collective retirement mutual-aid scheme is nonetheless substantial within the sample, including 43.8% of KPFWMA non-members. The findings indicate that an incomplete MPPS converts labour-market precarity into old-age insecurity from the point of enrolment onward, and support mandatory contributions by business owners, contribution subsidies for low-income participants, and transitional collective arrangements.

title: When and how do governments succeed in introducing electronic voting (e-voting)? A qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 35 OECD countries
abstract: Abstract Electronic voting (e-voting) is pivotal for modern democratic institutions in the digital age. Despite nearly six decades of e-voting technology development, significant disparities exist in its global introduction. Existing studies primarily focus on country-specific experiences, leading to limited generalizable insights into what defines successful e-voting introduction and its enablers. This study bridges this gap by proposing a comprehensive definition of successful e-voting introduction. We then explore on what grounds e-voting introduction succeeds or fails by applying fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to data from 35 OECD countries. Results reveal that the broader policy environments, digital readiness and citizens’ trust and ability to use technology significantly shape e-voting policies. Government commitment and policy alignment are identified as plausible complementary explanations for both success and failure. The study underscores the interplay of institutional and societal factors, rather than isolated influences, is the key driver of e-voting success.

title: Conditional Autonomy, Discursive Gatekeeping, and Patterns of Action: How Experts Influence Policy in China's One‐Party System
R&D investment, technology adoption and productivity dynamics: An empirical study of the productivity dispersion in Canada
Burning bridges or bridging divides: Geopolitics and collaboration in research and innovation
Where Are the Most Influential Articles in Political Science Published?
abstract: ABSTRACT Where are the most influential articles in political science published? Drawing on citation data from the Web of Science, this article identifies the most-cited political science journal articles each decade from the 1940s through the 2020s. The results depict a changing discipline: the American Political Science Review still leads the field, but its once-dominant position has attenuated as a wider range of journals have become homes for highly cited work. Methodological papers now account for a substantial share of the discipline’s most influential research, reflecting the growing centrality of technical innovation.

title: Striving for Peace through Personal Narratives of Genocide and War. By Julia Chaitin & Elad Avlagon. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2025. 238p.
Legal Consciousness and the Rule of Law in Post-Conflict Societies: Emergent Hybrid Legality in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. By Holly Dunn. New York: Routledge, 2023. 172p.
Reversing Ethnic Cleansing through Minority Returns: An Intellectual History of a Novel Idea. By Rebecca A. Brubaker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. 256p.
Sovereignty in Motion: Militarization and the re-making of territory within the post-socialist Yugoslav space
Echoes of conflict: quantifying redundancy in fatality time series
abstract: Abstract Do wars follow predictable patterns, or are they chaotic and inherently unpredictable? We explore this question by quantifying temporal redundancy—how often similar patterns recur—in conflict-related fatalities. Using entropy-based analysis—a measure of randomness—and Dynamic Time Warping, we compare conflict dynamics with other complex systems such as seismology and finance. Our findings reveal that the dynamics of fatalities within conflicts exhibit high levels of entropy: they are largely unpredictable. Conflicts generally display higher entropy than climate or earthquake data, which highlights the challenges of predictive modeling. Moreover, conflict patterns are not region- or decade-specific, which suggests a degree of universality. Our framework distinguishes stable from chaotic phases in conflict dynamics and clarifies where forecasting is feasible.

title: Just to be clear? Strategic vagueness of the European Parliament in EU policy negotiations
abstract: Abstract Vague legislative language can facilitate law adoption and implementation but reduce policy effectiveness and application uniformity. So, when do legislators employ it? Building on policymaking and responsiveness theories, we argue that legislators use vague language to overcome institutional conflict and public opinion constraints but avoid it when they seek to assert their positions in legislative output and policy outcomes. Empirically, we study the conditions under which the European Parliament (EP) introduces vague amendments to European Union (EU) legislative proposals using dictionary-based content analysis of EU legislative negotiations between 2009 and 2019. The results show that EP sticks to more concrete positions when inter-institutional conflict threatens its policy goals but employs vagueness to maintain a broad appeal and avoid public backlash given public opinion divisions and contentiousness. These results add to our knowledge of legal text formulation, EU law making, and EP representation.

title: When habit prevails: a causal test of policy feedback theory using a pension reform
abstract: Abstract Elderly voters are a growing, politically powerful electoral bloc, and their pensions often constitute the largest component of welfare state. We know that cuts can provoke electoral backlash, but it is less clear whether benefit expansions mobilize retirees. Some policy feedback theories predict increased participation following material gains, but recent evidence on policy expansions is mixed. While income and political participation appear correlated among the elderly, habit formation theory implies that older voters may be a least likely case for benefit expansion leading to mobilization. Leveraging a pension reform in Illinois that increased benefits by 36% for retirees, a regression discontinuity design on administrative data covering 93,000 public employees across twelve elections shows no turnout effect, even among low-income groups.

title: Compliant Women, Constitutive Violence: Rethinking the VAWIP Counterfactual
abstract: The literature on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) has made substantial contributions to understanding how gender shapes political exclusion. Foundational work by Krook and Restrepo Sanín (2016; 2020) defined VAWIP as a form of hate crime and as systematic backlash against women’s entry into political life. This conceptual scaffolding informs Krook’s (2022) subsequent attention to semiotic and symbolic harm, extending the VAWIP framework beyond physical violence to encompass the representational strategies through which female politicians are delegitimized. Bjarnegård and Zetterberg’s (2023) edited volume extends the framework further, recognizing that gender-based political violence operates across a broader range of contexts and along a “psychological-physical continuum” (7) that is neither temporally nor institutionally confined to election cycles or legislative chambers.

title: VAWIP in a State-Monopolized Political Field: The Case of Chinese Feminist Activism
abstract: The literature on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) implicitly treats such violence as boundary enforcement: a political field already exists; the violence women encounter marks the edge they are not permitted to cross; and the state stands as the guarantor of protection and redress under the rule of law, whether or not it delivers (Krook 2020; Krook and Restrepo Sanín2016). In high-capacity authoritarian states like China (Johnston 2019), the premise of this framing does not hold. The political field itself is monopolized and policed by the state, which determines what counts as politics, who is recognized as a legitimate political subject, and what forms of political action are permitted.

title: Violence Against Feminist Advocates: Political Violence and Anti-Gender Politics
abstract: Research on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) and research on violence against women activists have made crucial contributions by conceptualizing violence as a gendered phenomenon that targets women in response to their political participation. In these approaches, violence operates as a mechanism to discipline, silence, or expel women from political and public life. Alongside these developments, a growing body of scholarship has examined anti-gender politics as a structured and transnational political project, paying particular attention to its actors, discourses, and strategies.

title: Rationing by Race
abstract: We document how deepening resource scarcity results in rationing on the basis of race in a high-stakes setting: health care. Using detailed, time stamped data on 107,000 inpatient admissions to a large health system, we find that in-hospital mortality increases for Black but not White patients as hospitals reach capacity. These findings are not explained by differential patient selection. We identify rationing by wait times as a mechanism, documenting that sicker Black patients wait longer for care than healthier White patients at almost all capacity levels. Text analysis of unstructured clinical notes reveals rationing of provider effort as another mechanism. (JEL I11, I12, I14, J15)

title: Marriage, Fertility, and Cultural Integration in Italy
Optimal Public Transportation Networks: Evidence from the World's Largest Bus Rapid Transit System in Jakarta
abstract: Designing public transport networks involves trade-offs between coverage, service frequency, and direct service. We use the expansion of the bus system in Jakarta, Indonesia, to study these trade-offs. We analyze how new direct connections, changes in bus travel time, and wait-time reductions affect bus ridership and aggregate flows and estimate a transit network demand model by matching the route launch events. Commuters in Jakarta are 2–3 times more sensitive to wait time than bus time and inattentive to long routes. We develop a flexible framework to characterize optimal networks. A less concentrated network would increase ridership and commuter welfare. (JEL L92, L98, O18, R41, R42, R48)

title: Corporate Tax Cuts, Firm Growth, and Workers' Earnings
abstract: We study the effects of the largest corporate income tax cut in U.S. history on firms and workers. To identify causal effects, we use employer-employee matched tax records and event studies comparing similarly sized firms in the same industry that faced divergent tax changes due to their pre-existing legal status. Tax cuts cause increases in firms' investment, sales, profits, employment, and payrolls, with earnings gains concentrated among highly paid workers. In the short-run, 87% of private income gains flow to the top 10% of the income distribution.

title: The Environmental Bias of Corporate Income Taxation
abstract: We study the relationship between corporate income taxation and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions in the United States. We show CO 2 -intensive firms benefit more from the tax advantage of debt and pay lower income taxes on their capital income. Building on these new facts, we provide evidence that a cut in the corporate income tax rate leads to a larger expansion of clean firms. We develop a multisector general equilibrium model that accounts for our evidence and quantify the impact of corporate tax reforms on aggregate emissions. A policy that eliminates the tax advantage of debt could reduce aggregate emissions without affecting GDP. (JEL D22, G32, H25, H32, Q52, Q54, Q58)

title: Contextually Private Mechanisms
Defying Distance? The Provision of Medical Services in the Digital Age
abstract: Digital platforms reduce geographic frictions, enabling better matching between service providers and users. I quantify reallocation gains in Swedish online health care, using nationwide time-conditional random assignment between patients and physicians. Matching high-risk patients with doctors effective at reducing Emergency Room visits lowers such visits by 4.4 percent (SE 1.3); reallocations also reduce Counter-Guideline antibiotics by 3.1 percent (1.4). I find limited trade-offs in matching; horizontal differentiation among doctors and varied patient needs allow improvement in multiple outcomes simultaneously. Efficiency-enhancing reallocations also affect equity. The findings highlight the potential for care reorganization aligning provider heterogeneity with patient needs when geographic constraints are lifted. (JEL C78, H51, I11, I13, I14, I18)

title: Manipulation-Robust Prediction
abstract: An increasing number of decisions are guided by machine learning algorithms. But when consequential decisions are encoded in algorithms, individuals may strategically alter their behavior to achieve desired outcomes. This paper develops an empirical approach that adjusts decision algorithms to anticipate manipulation. By explicitly modeling incentives to manipulate, our approach produces decision rules that are stable under manipulation, even when the rules are fully transparent. We stress-test this approach through a large field experiment in Kenya. When implemented, linear strategy-robust decision rules outperform standard linear models such as LASSO. (JEL C45, C93, D12, D91, G51, O12, O16)

title: Intergenerational Impacts of Secondary Education: Experimental Evidence from Ghana
Risk-Sharing Tests and Covariate Shocks: Drought, Floods, and Pests in Uganda
Presidential Address: Neighborhood Effects and Missing Markets for Opportunity
abstract: Experimental and quasi-experimental studies show that childhood neighborhoods have substantial causal impacts on children's adult earnings and other long-term socioeconomic outcomes. Several market failures are likely to lead to excessive residential segregation by parental income and to an undersupply of mixed-income neighborhoods. Missing markets for opportunity originate in capital market imperfections for borrowing on children's future earnings, neighbor spillovers, behavioral biases, and housing search frictions. Customized housing mobility services combined with subsidized housing vouchers can help low-income families move to higher-opportunity areas. Place-based policies that create mixed-income neighborhoods appear to increase long-term outcomes for less-advantaged children. (JEL I12, I32, I38, J13, J15, R23, R38)

title: Mortality regressivity and pension design
The effects of education on corruption: Evidence from Vietnam’s university expansion
Public Employee Pensions and Municipal Insolvency
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how municipal governments jointly manage spending, credit market borrowing, and a public employee pension system. I model governments as levered investors who must meet non-defaultable pension obligations and may value government spending more than citizens. I quantify the model using data on California cities, including a new record of fiscal emergencies, tax increases required to maintain essential city services. After the financial crisis depleted pension funds, cities engaged in excessive risk-taking: the fiscal emergency option encouraged gambling for resurrection that kept cities vulnerable to shocks well into the recovery. To correct this problem, a savings requirement works better than a restriction on risk-taking or a pension funding requirement. The policy experiments emphasize that effective policies need to target the combined pension and bond finances, as policies that only target one, such as a pension funding requirement, are undermined by endogenous changes to the other.

title: Familiar faces, honest answers? The impacts of enumerator familiarity and modality on survey responses
Comparative advantage and the quality choice of heterogeneous firms
Listening to the experts: How trust in scientists shapes environmental hazards health risk perceptions
abstract: This study explores public risk perceptions of environmental hazards with a focus on threats such as air, water and soil pollution or toxicants spillage. We analyze how trust in expert scientists shapes people’s evaluations of possible health risks from pollution-type hazards. We present a framework that emphasizes the role of trust in expert scientists to provide unbiased, informative, and useful information that can guide policy and help reduce the health threats associated with pollution-type hazards. Based on a US national survey data focusing on environmental health hazards, we find that trust in scientists is a consistent predictor and a powerful explanatory factor of individuals’ assessments of the health risks due to potential exposure to pollution-type hazards. Our findings demonstrate that public trust in expert scientists is essential and can improve people’s understanding and awareness of the possible health ramifications from a set of environmental hazards that are currently understudied, are relatively less common, and may be a result of human intervention.

title: Reconceptualising public outrage in risk communication: the relevance of moral emotions
abstract: Public ‘outrage’ has been widely referenced in risk communication practice since Peter Sandman popularised the term in the 1980s, but remains underexplored in research. This study critically reviews how ‘public outrage’ has been understood in risk communication literature. It then empirically investigates its qualities and dimensions, using a pandemic case study (Australian teachers’ responses to school closure controversies), since public outrage was considered a challenge to pandemic management. We conducted reflexive thematic analysis of a representative sample of over 8000 free-text responses from a large-scale survey of public school teachers during April 2020. We found that teachers’ outrage was structured by cognitive, affective, and moral appraisals of early-phase pandemic control policies. Teachers’ feelings of anxiety, anger and abandonment arose from perceived gaps between the goals of preventing infection and the implementation of infection control measures in schools, and were amplified by one-way communication that was untimely, confusing, and/or ineffective. Teachers’ outrage centred on experiences of disempowerment and on perceived moral violations, including the devaluation of professional identity, and the instrumentalization of teachers for social or economic ends. These insights highlight the role of moral emotions in risk responses, suggest the value of investigating the construct of ‘moral outrage’ and its effects on risk perception, and indicate the importance of addressing specific moral concerns in risk communications. We propose a research agenda for integrating moral dimensions into risk communication strategies to better anticipate and address public outrage in future health crises.

title: Enhancing risk communication through storytelling: the power of hero narratives in facilitating public disaster preparedness
abstract: We based on the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) and examined the advantages of narrative risk communication that includes hero characters in promoting public disaster preparedness behavioral intentions. We further explored whether there are differences in the impact of narrative risk communication on public disaster preparedness behavioral intentions when the government or the public is portrayed as the hero separately or jointly, and revealed the differences in the mechanisms of the three types of heroic narrative in promoting disaster preparedness. The research results indicate that compared to traditional risk communication, incorporating hero characters narrative risk communication can significantly enhance public disaster preparedness behavioral intentions. Although there is no significant difference in the overall effect of government hero, public hero, and government public co performance heroes, their internal mechanisms have their own characteristics. Government hero promotes disaster preparedness behavioral intentions by enhancing external efficacy, public hero plays their role by enhancing internal efficacy, and joint heroes can simultaneously stimulate internal and external efficacy. We incorporate an emotion-driven NPF into emergency management research on typhoon preparedness and demonstrate that, compared with traditional rational risk communication, hero character policy narratives have distinct advantages in enhancing risk communication effectiveness. Our study not only extends the NPF application scope and explanatory power in the field of risk communication, but also provides new theoretical perspectives and research avenues for improving pre-disaster communication between governments and the public.

title: “Enthusiasts, Not Professionals”: Journalists’ Experiences of Precarity in Serbia’s Hybrid Regime
abstract: Precarity has become a defining feature of the contemporary journalistic labor market worldwide. Drawing on 20 in-depth interviews with journalists in Serbia, we explore the tension between precarity and professional journalistic aspirations. Although participants understood precarious working conditions primarily in economic terms (e.g., low wages and limited job opportunities), their accounts suggest that labor (in)security is distributed according to political rather than market logic. Some respond to these pressures by adopting nondemocratic journalistic practices or by adjusting their professional values, while others embrace precarity as a mark of professional integrity and a condition for practicing journalism in a hybrid regime.

title: Subversive Amplification: Online Dissent and the Limits of Information Control in China
abstract: Abstract Intensified information control severely constrains digital contention in China, yet online mass events occasionally occur. Using a dataset of 274,721 Weibo messages, this study examines mobilization, coordination and grievance articulation during a two-day episode of online dissent in the aftermath of the 2022 Urumqi residential building fire, which preceded the White Paper protests. It argues that users were activated by public communication failures that transformed manifold grievances into outrage, and that the associated hashtags provided anchors to which criticism could be attached. In a process this study terms “subversive amplification,” concentrated engagement amplified the hashtags’ visibility, and with it the critical content attached to them. However, absent the unifying function of opinion leaders, grievance articulation remained fragmented and did not converge on unified demands. The case illustrates the inherent vulnerabilities of information control but also the conditions and limits of their exploitation.

title: External incentives, social norms, and citizens’ participation in digital co‐production: A survey experiment
abstract: Abstract With the rapid pace of digital transformation, motivating public participation has become a critical challenge for advancing both the theory and practice of digital co‐production. Drawing on incentive theory and social norm theory, this study uses a survey experiment conducted with Chinese citizens to explore their willingness to participate in digital co‐production, focusing on the effects of external incentives and social norms. The results show that material incentives are more effective than honour‐based incentives in driving participation. Additionally, positive descriptive norms have a stronger influence on participation willingness than negative norms. Notably, when positive descriptive norms are present, material incentives further amplify public engagement. This study offers insights into the motivational drivers behind citizen participation in digital co‐production and provides practical recommendations for governments on how to strategically leverage incentives and social norms to boost public involvement. Points for practitioners Material incentives appear to be more effective than honour‐based incentives in strengthening citizens’ willingness to participate in digital co‐production. Positive descriptive social norms demonstrate stronger effects than negative norms in promoting citizens’ willingness to engage in digital co‐production. The combination of material incentives and positive descriptive social norms may generate synergistic effects in enhancing citizens’ willingness to participate in digital co‐production.

title: Coordination Costs and Homelessness Housing Form Choice
Disclosing Power Dynamics in Metropolitan Governance: An Analysis of Network Micro‐Mechanisms of Change in an Evolving Inter‐Municipal Network
Political Business Cycle and Electoral Forecast: Does Local Financial Condition Worsen When Electoral Victory Seems (Un)Likely?
Political Determinants of Tax Policy: How Central and Local Governments Respond to Political Incentives
Congressional Oversight Reports as Legislative Branch Work Product and Research Resource
Coincidental Representation: How Congruence and Influence shape Public Satisfaction with Government
abstract: A much-cited finding in recent political science is that average citizens in established democracies appear to have little influence on public policy, while the affluent have strong influence. Yet, as critics have pointed out, average and affluent often want the same from government, meaning that even without influence, average citizens often get the policies they want ‘by coincidence’. This raises an important question: Do citizens care about ‘who governs’ if government regularly adopts their preferred policies anyway? Using a preregistered survey experiment, I show that political inequality causes just as much popular dissatisfaction with government when policy outcomes are highly consistent with a respondent’s policy preferences, as it does when policy outcomes are inconsistent with those preferences. While opinion-policy congruence remains an important predictor of satisfaction, citizens also appear to value political equality independently of policy outcomes. These findings suggest that coincidental representation may not fully compensate for perceived inequalities in political influence.

title: Cool Citizens? How Affectively Unpolarized Citizens View and Participate in Democracy
abstract: Abstract Does affective polarization change how citizens view and participate in democracy? We posit that the answer to this crucial question depends on how affectively un polarized citizens view and participate in democracy. Yet, the most common operationalization of affective polarization––measuring sympathy ratings for one party relative to another––does not differentiate between people’s absolute sympathy ratings for the parties, which may mask essential heterogeneity among unpolarized citizens. This paper theorizes the methodological origin of this heterogeneity, describes it, and highlights its implications. Cluster analyses and regressions from three nationally representative surveys in the US provide three conclusions. First, substantial shares of the US population are affectively un polarized. Second, unpolarized citizens cluster into two groups: one feeling lukewarm and one feeling cold toward both parties. Third, these unpolarized groups report diverging democratic attitudes and participation patterns. We discuss the methodological implications and the need for future research on affectively unpolarized citizens.

title: Payroll taxes, firm dynamism, and aggregate productivity
Gone with the wind: Productive response to agricultural shock
Connectivity and Selective Rural Migration
abstract: ABSTRACT How does infrastructure shape rural development? Using household panel data from a nationally representative sample of Chinese villages, matched to high‐resolution highway maps, we find that road expansion between 2000 and 2015 operates mainly through reallocation, with less productive farmers scaling down or exiting and more productive farmers remaining and expanding. We quantify the aggregate and distributional consequences in a dynamic spatial equilibrium model with heterogeneous households and endogenous migration. Improved connectivity not only accelerates urbanization but also increases aggregate rural output by 2.2%–5.3% in the long run, even as the rural workforce declines.

title: Minimizing Risk of Load Redistribution Attacks on Electric Grids in the Presence of Insider Threats
abstract: Malicious and negligent insiders pose significant security risks to mission-critical systems like electric power grids due to their high privileges in increasingly digitized infrastructures. This paper investigates the vulnerability of smart power grids to load redistribution (LR) attacks in the presence of insider threats. We introduce a stochastic optimization model to minimize the expected risk of high operation costs due to LR attacks by protecting critical grid components and deploying detection technologies, such as honeypots, to detect insider threats and prevent information leakage. Our model accounts for uncertainties in insider presence, honeypot effectiveness, and attack targets, and uses the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) measure, which can be adjusted based on the decision-maker's conservatism. In addition, it accounts for real-time power demand variations and dynamic false-data injection by attackers. To enhance tractability, we transform our model, originally formulated as a trilevel mixed-integer nonlinear programming (Tri-MINLP) problem, into an approximate single-level mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. We apply our proposed model to the IEEE 14-bus test system, and our results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in lowering the risk of high operation costs due to LR attacks. In addition, we present several insights by assessing the impact of key factors on the expected financial risk of attacks, including the protection budget, insider-threat likelihood, honeypot-detection effectiveness, and the defender's decision-making conservatism.

title: A Bayesian Model for Estimation of Virus Reduction in Potable Reuse Treatment Trains and Quantitative Microbial Risk Assessment of Waterborne Viral Pathogens
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding virus occurrence and reduction at advanced treatment facilities for potable water reuse constitutes a high‐priority research need to protect human health and to enhance available water supply alternatives. The objectives were to (1) determine log reduction values (LRVs) of 15 viruses by advanced wastewater treatment; (2) evaluate suitability of the final wastewater effluent for potable reuse; (3) evaluate viruses or groups of viruses as indicators of wastewater treatment efficiency. Reduction data of seven human enteric and eight surrogate viruses were obtained from three potable reuse facilities. LRVs were estimated using a Bayesian model that can handle nondetects and identifies groups of viruses with similar LRVs. Quantitative microbial risk assessments were conducted for adenoviruses, enteroviruses, and noroviruses GI and GII. Mean total LRVs ranged from 5.4 to 11 log 10. Required mean total LRVs for the four pathogenic viruses ranged from 11.3 to 13.4 log 10 . Both male‐specific and somatic coliphages, detected by classical enumeration of infectious virions, are recommended as indicator viruses. Of the pathogenic viruses, adenovirus was found to be the most effective indicator for virus reduction. At all facilities, infection risks were higher than 10 −4 per person per year, implying that the finished water may not comply with existing safety standards. Infection risks may have been overestimated by 2–4 log 10 because only a fraction of the detected virus was infectious. Nevertheless, achieved LRVs were still too low and given the uncertainty on infectious virus fraction, one may accept overestimation of risks to stay on the safe side.

title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
abstract: This paper explores the perception of social currency as a distinct value within local news consumption among audiences. Social currency refers to the value individuals derive from engaging with and sharing news content within their social networks, allowing them to connect, express identity and signal awareness. Drawing on a large-scale mixed-methods study of local news audiences in Australia (survey: n = 7919; interviews and focus groups: n = 84), this study operationalised key dimensions of social currency using factor analysis. The findings confirm that social currency is a separate and measurable construct, distinct from traditional news motivations. It is significantly higher among younger people, men, urban residents and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, reflecting how news consumption intersects with social interaction, identity expression and symbolic practices of everyday life.

title: Ambivalent algorithms, fragile connectedness: How algorithm awareness facets shape responsiveness and insensitivity on TikTok
abstract: This study examines how distinct facets of algorithm awareness are associated with perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR), perceived algorithm insensitivity (PAI), and social connectedness on TikTok. I draw on the algorithm responsiveness process and also treat algorithm awareness as four distinct dimensions (content filtering, automated decision‑making, human–algorithm interplay (HAI), ethical concerns) to examine how each dimension is differentially associated with PAR and PAI and, in turn, with feelings of inclusion and belonging. Using survey data from 305 TikTok users and structural equation modeling, I show that user‑agency‑oriented dimensions, particularly filtering and HAI, are indirectly associated with connectedness via higher responsiveness and lower insensitivity. By contrast, automation operates as an ambivalent structure: it boosts responsiveness yet is negatively associated with connectedness, marking a boundary condition for personalization. Platforms should pair automation disclosures with clearer user recourse, traceable feedback, and human review in high-stakes contexts.

title: The year is a dropdown menu: Platformed provenance and the viral afterlives of AI-generated retro music
abstract: This article examines how generative AI media becomes believable and shareable when it is packaged as a rediscovered archive and distributed through commercial platforms. Drawing on multi-sited digital ethnography, targeted platform walkthroughs, and cross-platform trace analysis of a viral “lost song” circulating in Italy in 2025, I show how listeners in this case mobilized sonic cues and platform metadata, including release dates and credits, as practical evidence. I use metadata realism to describe everyday reliance on database fields as documentary testimony, and provenance play for situated practices of verification and narration through which people negotiate synthetic pasts. After public debunking, circulation continued through humorous and artistic reframings, while verification itself became part of the artifact’s social life. The analysis foregrounds platformed provenance and considers what the case implies for synthetic media governance and content credentials.

title: Analyzing Regional Cooperation in Southwest Saskatchewan through Partnerships among Eastend, White Valley, and Arlington Municipalities
abstract: Abstract This case study examines regional cooperation between the Town of Eastend and the Rural Municipalities of White Valley and Arlington in southwest Saskatchewan. It explores how these municipalities overcome institutional inertia to deliver essential services and sustain community viability. Drawing on five interviews with local elected officials and administrators, alongside a targeted literature review, the study analyzes collaborative initiatives including shared fire protection, recreation funding, water infrastructure upgrades, and the development of a regional ambulance service. Using a framework grounded in historical institutionalism, status quo bias, and veto player theory, the study finds that cooperation emerges incrementally through project‐specific agreements rather than full municipal mergers. These arrangements rely on trust, fiscal practicality, and strategies that preserve local identity while reducing risk aversion. The findings highlight best practices for coalition‐based governance and offer recommendations to support service sharing while maintaining municipal autonomy and long‐term rural sustainability.

title: The Relational Character of Canadian Nation‐Building Infrastructure in the 21 st Century
abstract: Abstract Infrastructure development is central to Canada's nation‐building process. This article argues that the federal government has recalibrated its nation‐building mandate from unilateral state command to relational orchestration. Through thematic analysis of thirty‐eight policy documents related to three federal infrastructure plans (2007–2016), we show that “nation‐building infrastructure” has evolved from large‐scale projects to an umbrella term encompassing community‐focused initiatives and both hard and soft infrastructure. The federal government now channels investment through partnerships with provinces, municipalities, territories, private capital, and Indigenous rights holders. This shift represents not federal withdrawal but a strategic repositioning of federal power through coordinated, multi‐actor arrangements.

title: Canada's Ethics Commissioner and the Watchdog Model of Ethics Enforcement
abstract: Abstract Despite notable progress, the OECD recently noted that conflict of interest regulation still suffers from poor implementation and how to ensure effective enforcement of ethics rules remains an important challenge. One popular but under‐examined approach is to rely on an ethics watchdog: an independent agency with few powers that can nevertheless investigate and publicly blame violators as a form of sanction and deterrence. To better ascertain the effectiveness of this model of ethics enforcement, we examine how Canada's Ethics Commissioner used investigations to enforce ethics rules over a fifteen‐year period, the media coverage that they have received, and the career consequences that adverse findings have had for the officials blamed by the Commissioner. We find that, while used to scrutinize even the most powerful officials, ethics investigations had little impact, casting doubt on the potential effectiveness of relying on publicity, shaming and reputational costs as tools of ethics enforcement.

title: Imagining infrastructure, Encountering friction: Green hydrogen development in Morocco and Namibia
Bordering standards: The politics of verifying the Korean military demarcation line
abstract: The Military Demarcation Line (MDL) on the Korean Peninsula is often treated as the archetype of a clear, militarized border. Yet it is increasingly described as ‘unclear,’ a puzzling claim for a boundary long regarded as rigid and well enforced. This article argues that such ‘unclearness’ does not reflect the absence of a border, but rather uncertainty in its operational reference: which baseline is actionable, which representations and markers can be relied upon, and which institution can authoritatively verify and reconcile discrepancies. Bringing border studies into dialogue with science and technology studies, the article reframes border clarity as an ongoing infrastructural achievement sustained through the alignment of maps, markers, records, and verification procedures. Drawing on armistice texts and annex maps, Military Armistice Commission records, operational regulations, and subsequent geospatial updating efforts, it shows why the MDL is a critical case: militarization sustains strong behavioral prohibitions while simultaneously constraining inspection, maintenance, and supervised access—the practical work that keeps representational layers mutually useable. When these conditions deteriorate, the line does not disappear; it persists through partial, contested, and sometimes incompatible operational versions. The article develops the concept of versioned demarcation to capture how demarcation is repeatedly reassembled across changing technical systems and institutional routines. It demonstrates that disputes that appear to concern ‘where the line is’ are often conflicts over verification, access, and custodianship, and offers a framework for analyzing ‘unclear borders’ beyond the Korean case.

title: Populism and academic freedom
abstract: Abstract Academic freedom empowers scholars to influence public discourse and debate, cultivate critical reasoning, discuss ideas that challenge traditional values, and impose a soft check and balance on governments. For those reasons, governments have specific preferences regarding the extent of academic freedom, especially when led by populists, whose ideology, values, and strategic features are frequently at odds with the implications of this freedom. Using a quasi-experimental design, we confirm that academic freedom declines significantly under populist governments, a pattern largely independent of their host ideology. Those negative consequences increase after multiple populist terms, and extend more broadly to the substance of speech and the flow of information. Altogether, these results highlight the incompatibility of populism with democratic guarantees.

title: Election results and democratic discontent: Expectations, extremism, and democratic values in post-election Brazil
How evolving institutions shaped China’s economic geography
How did empirical economic research improve over the last decades: Recent trends and prospects
Captured Gatekeepers: Structural Conflicts of Interest in U.S. Higher Education Accreditation
Non-verbal uncertainty cues impact assessments of verbal probability information
abstract: In spoken communication, verbal probability phrases (e.g. likely, almost never, certain) play a central role in conveying uncertainty. While prior research has largely focused on how such expressions are interpreted in written form, growing attention is being paid to the role of non-verbal cues in shaping uncertainty interpretation in multimodal communication. This pre-registered 2×2 within-subjects experiment (N = 100) contributes to this emerging field by investigating how auditory (rising intonation) and visual (marked facial expressions) uncertainty cues influence assessments of verbal probability information, by focusing on recipients’ perception of speaker certainty and the numerical interpretation of probability phrases. Both rising intonation and marked facial expressions independently reduced perceived speaker certainty and, in most cases, increased recipients’ variability in numerical interpretations. Notably, the combination of both cues produced the lowest perceived speaker certainty, though no additive effect on interpretive variability was observed. These findings highlight the importance of integrating non-verbal signals into theoretical models of risk and uncertainty communication and invite future research to investigate how multimodal uncertainty cues work in real-world, high-stakes contexts such as medical consultations or public risk communication.

title: O*NET Plus: A Review and Organizing Framework Extending O*NET’s Content Model in Management Research
abstract: The Occupational Information Network (O*NET) is a database of occupational descriptors sponsored by the U.S. Department of Labor. Since its release around the turn of the century, O*NET has taken on a broad and important role in management and organizational research as a key data source for occupational characteristics. It is common practice for researchers to combine or adapt descriptors from O*NET’s content model to measure constructs that O*NET does not capture directly (e.g., job complexity, emotional labor demands). This practice has enabled a great deal of research and poses potential extensions to O*NET’s content model, but has also come with challenges, including the proliferation of redundant measures with varying levels of validation. The purpose of this review is to synthesize the studies using O*NET-based measures and curate a database of measures with considerable evidence supporting their validity. In doing so, we contribute to the literature in three ways: (1) we introduce an extended content model that we call “O*NET Plus” and offer it as an expanded organizing framework for occupational description; (2) we review evidence for the psychometric soundness of O*NET Plus measures, highlight those with considerable evidence, and amass these measures in a central location to offer a “one-stop-shop” for researchers looking to leverage O*NET Plus; and (3) we offer guidance and implications for further expansions to O*NET Plus.

title: Understanding youth participation in public policy: Insights from applying the CLEAR framework
abstract: Background Currently, insight into factors that encourage or hinder youth participation in public policy is limited. This study explores whether the dimensions of an influential theoretical framework (CLEAR) are applicable to youth participation. It also examines how these dimensions are currently addressed to organize youth participation (12–30 years) in public policy.Methods The study is based on qualitative data, conducted in the Netherlands. Thematic coding was used to analyze interviews with thirty-five representatives of organizations involved in youth participation (n=16) and public officials at the municipality of Rotterdam (n=19).Results Respondents’ experiences with youth participation in public policy relate to the five dimensions of the CLEAR framework: “Can do”, “Like to”, “Enabled to”, “Asked to”, and “Responded to”.
